0.title: Holy Exiles: Living the Gospel Under Pressure
0.overview:
First Peter is the New Testament's sustained theology of exile. Peter writes to Christians scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor — Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia — identifying them with three words that frame everything: elect, resident aliens, of the Dispersion. They are chosen by God and displaced in the world. These two facts stand in permanent tension throughout the letter: you are precious beyond calculation to the God who elected you; you are strangers and foreigners in the world you inhabit. Both are true at the same time, and both must shape how you live.

The recipients were primarily Gentiles — 2:10 quotes Hosea's 'not a people' passage, and 4:3 describes their former lives as pagan. Yet Peter addresses them with the vocabulary of Israel: elect exiles of the Dispersion, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. The church has stepped into the covenant identity of Israel and now carries it into a hostile empire. The suffering they face — social ostracism, slander, economic disadvantage, possibly intermittent persecution — is the normal cost of that identity. The letter does not explain why suffering comes; it explains how to endure it and what it means.

The letter's Christological center is 2:21–25 and 3:18–22: Christ's own suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension are the template for Christian existence. He suffered unjustly; he did not retaliate; he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly; he was vindicated. The pattern is not merely an example to follow but a participation to enter: believers share Christ's sufferings (4:13) so that they will share his glory. The theology of suffering in 1 Peter is not stoic endurance but eschatological confidence — the same confidence that carried Jesus through the cross to resurrection is available to every believer in every form of suffering.

Did Peter really write this letter, given its polished Greek? Many scholars think a later follower wrote it, pointing to the style, unlikely from a Galilean fisherman, and to a setting of persecution they date later. But the letter claims Peter as author (1:1; 5:1), the early church received it without doubt, and Peter says he wrote By Silvanus (5:12), most likely Silas, Paul’s companion, who helped with the writing. The persecution described fits the 60s under Nero, and a fisherman from bilingual Galilee who had preached for thirty years could well write good Greek with help. The more likely conclusion is that Peter wrote it from Rome, the Babylon of 5:13, before his death around AD 64–67.

The letter was written from 'Babylon' (5:13) — the Jewish-Christian code word for Rome, used also in 4 Ezra and Revelation. Silvanus (Silas) may have served as secretary (5:12), which would explain the polished Greek that would be surprising from a Galilean fisherman. The likely date is 62–64 AD, during or shortly before the Neronian persecution that would claim both Peter and Paul.

1.title: Living Hope: Election, Holiness, and the Imperishable Word
1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundations of the letter. The greeting packs election, the work of the Trinity and covenant identity into two verses. The thanksgiving (vv. 3–12) shows why Christians have hope: God has given new birth to a living hope through Christ’s resurrection, and an inheritance kept in heaven, while he guards his people until it is revealed. Suffering on the way does not contradict that hope; it tests and proves it.

Then comes the call to holiness (vv. 13–25). Because of who you now are, live accordingly: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” The standard is God himself, and the motive is the price of our ransom, the precious blood of Christ. The chapter ends with the word of God, which gave us new birth and remains when everything else withers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to “elect exiles” scattered across five Roman provinces. They are chosen by God the Father, set apart by the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with his blood. Chosen and strangers, both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elect Exiles

Chosen by God and strangers in the world — both at once, and the second is no evidence against the first. Father, Spirit and Son are all at work in their salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scattered believers across five provinces were being slandered and excluded.

Now: Being out of place in the world is no sign that God has forgotten you.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 1 tells suffering exiles who they are, what they have and how to live. They are chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit, for obedience to Christ and cleansing by his blood (vv. 1–2). God has given them new birth into a living hope through Christ’s resurrection and an inheritance kept in heaven, while they are kept by his power (vv. 3–5). So they rejoice in trials that prove their faith like gold, loving a Christ they have not seen (vv. 6–9), the Christ whose sufferings and glories the prophets foretold (vv. 10–12). Therefore: hope fully in the coming grace and be holy (vv. 13–16); live in reverent fear, ransomed by the precious blood of the spotless Lamb (vv. 17–21); and love one another, born again through the abiding word of God (vv. 22–25).

The setting. Peter wrote from “Babylon” (5:13), almost certainly a code name for Rome, probably in the early 60s AD, shortly before Nero’s persecution of 64, with Silvanus (the Silas of Acts) as secretary or courier (5:12). Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia were Roman provinces covering most of modern Turkey, perhaps listed in the order of a courier’s loop from the Black Sea coast. The readers were mostly Gentile converts (1:14, 18; 2:10; 4:3), facing not yet the arena but slander, suspicion, and exclusion from guilds and family feasts (4:3–4). Tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome within a few years, as the Lord had foretold (John 21:18–19).

Who is writing. Remember who this man is. He is the one who said he would die with Christ and then, before the night was out, swore three times that he had never met him. The Lord had warned him and prayed for him: I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). This letter is that sentence being kept. A man who knows from the inside how faith can buckle under social pressure, and how Christ holds on to it anyway, writes to people under social pressure, to strengthen them. He sums up his purpose at the end: this is the true grace of God; stand firm in it (5:12).

Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ. Simon was his name; Jesus gave him another, Petros, rock (in Aramaic, Cephas) (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). It is worth noticing what he does not say. He does not call himself the chief apostle, or the rock on which the church is built, or the first bishop of Rome. He gives his name and his commission and nothing more, and later he will call himself simply a fellow elder (5:1). He is the leader of the twelve and the first preacher of Pentecost (Acts 2), and he writes with the authority of a man sent by Christ, but the authority is not his own. An apostle is one sent, and everything depends on the sender.

To those who are elect exiles. Two words held together that do not normally belong together, and the whole letter lives in the tension between them. Elect, eklektois: chosen, God’s own, the language of Israel. Exiles, parepidēmois: resident foreigners, people living somewhere that is not home and who have no standing there, the word Hebrews uses of the patriarchs who confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth (Hebrews 11:13). Peter puts the highest possible status beside the lowest and says: both, at once. You are chosen, and you are strangers, and the second is not evidence against the first. That is the pastoral problem the letter exists to answer. These people were being treated as outsiders, and the natural inference was that God had forgotten them. Peter refuses the inference in his first sentence. Their outsiderness is not a sign that they are unloved. It is the shape their belovedness takes in a world that is not yet their home, for our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

Of the Dispersion. The word is diaspora, scattering, as in James 1:1. For centuries it meant one thing: the Jews scattered among the nations after the exile, living in Babylon and Alexandria and Ephesus, turning towards Jerusalem when they prayed. Peter takes the word and lays it over a church made mostly of Gentiles. That is an astonishing move. People who had never been to Jerusalem, whose grandparents had worshipped Zeus and the emperor, are told that they now belong to the scattered people of God, living away from their true homeland and waiting to be gathered. Their homeland is not a strip of land on the eastern Mediterranean; it is the inheritance kept in heaven (v. 4). The whole story of Israel has become their story.

According to the foreknowledge of God the Father. Verse 2 is one of the most compressed Trinitarian statements in the New Testament. According to the foreknowledge of God the Father: the origin. In the sanctification of the Spirit: the means. For obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood: the end. Three persons, three prepositions, one salvation. And foreknowledge, prognōsis, is not God peering forward to see who would choose him. In biblical usage to know someone is to set your regard on them. Amos says of Israel: you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2), and God was not admitting that he had no information about Egypt. It is love fixed beforehand, not information gathered in advance (Romans 8:29; 11:2). Peter uses the same word of Christ himself in 1:20: he was foreknown before the foundation of the world, which can only mean chosen and appointed, not merely foreseen. And Peter had used the word before, at Pentecost, of the cross: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

Where Christians differ: is election based on foreseen faith? Arminians read according to the foreknowledge of God as meaning that God chose those he foresaw would believe. Verdict: In Scripture, God’s foreknowledge is his personal, loving choice beforehand, not mere awareness of future facts. Christ was foreknown (1:20) in the sense of chosen and appointed; so believers are elect according to God’s fore-love. The whole Trinity is at work: the Father chooses, the Spirit sanctifies, the Son’s blood cleanses. Faith is the result of election, not its cause: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48).

In the sanctification of the Spirit. Sanctification, hagiasmos, is being set apart. The Father’s choice in eternity does not remain in eternity. The Spirit comes into a particular life, in a particular town, on a particular day, and takes hold of that person for God, bringing him to faith (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Here the word describes the start of the Christian life, not its slow growth: the moment a pagan in Cappadocia was separated from the world and claimed as God’s own. He may have thought he was simply listening to a travelling preacher. The Spirit was drawing a line round him.

For obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood. This reaches back to Sinai. In Exodus 24 Moses read the book of the covenant, the people answered that they would do all the LORD had spoken and be obedient, and Moses took the blood and threw it over them: behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Exodus 24:3–8; Hebrews 9:19–20). Obedience and blood, in that order. That was the moment Israel became God’s nation. Peter tells scattered foreigners in Asia Minor that the same thing has happened to them, under a better covenant with better blood. He had heard that covenant made. In the upper room, the night before the cross, Jesus took the cup and said: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28). Moses had thrown the blood of bulls; the Son of God shed his own. The blood that made Peter’s readers God’s people was not splashed on them from an altar. It ran from the veins of the Lord who loved them. Election was never meant to end in a privilege to admire. It ends in a people who obey Christ and are cleansed by him, and keep being cleansed, because the sprinkling is not only the first washing but the ongoing provision for people who still fail (1 John 1:7).

May grace and peace be multiplied to you. Not merely given, plēthyntheiē, multiplied: grace and peace in ever-increasing measure. Peter is writing to people whose troubles were multiplying. He prays that grace would multiply faster. And it is worth noticing that grace comes before peace, always, in every apostolic greeting. Peace with God, and the peace of God in the heart, are what grace produces; they cannot be had first.

What it does not mean. Exiles does not mean Christians should be indifferent to the place where they live. They are to do good there, honour its authorities and win its respect (2:12–17), as the exiles in Babylon were told to seek the welfare of the city (Jeremiah 29:7). But their deepest home is elsewhere, and they hold everything here with an open hand.

Does election mean God does not want everyone to be saved? It means salvation begins with God and not with us, which is why anyone is saved at all. The gospel is still to be preached to everyone, and everyone who comes to Christ is welcomed (John 6:37). No one will ever be turned away who wanted Christ and was refused because he was not chosen; the doctrine works the other way. It tells the believer that his coming was God’s doing, and that the God who began it will finish it. Election is written for the comfort of believers, not as a riddle for outsiders. Its first effect in this letter is to steady people who felt rejected by everyone.

How can I know I am one of the elect? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, but by looking at what election produces in time. Peter names it in this very verse: the Spirit setting you apart, obedience to Jesus Christ, and the sprinkling of his blood. Are you trusting Christ’s blood, and nothing else, for your cleansing? Do you want to obey him, and grieve when you do not? Then you are looking at the fingerprints of the Father’s choice. Peter later tells his readers to make their calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:10), not by speculation but by a growing life of faith and love.

In a sentence. From Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to God’s chosen people, living as foreigners scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, who have been chosen according to the loving foreknowledge of God the Father, set apart by the Spirit to obey Jesus Christ and to be cleansed by his blood: may grace and peace be yours in abundance.

On a Tuesday. The next time you feel out of place, at work, in your family, in a conversation where everyone laughs at what you cannot laugh at, name it for what it is: the feeling of an exile, not the feeling of a reject. Then say the other word over yourself: chosen. Both are true at once. And ask the practical question Peter will spend five chapters answering: how does a chosen stranger behave here, today, among these people, so that they see something of the place he comes from?

For worship. Before there was a Pontus or a Bithynia, before Rome had an emperor or the world had a sun, the Father had set his love on a handful of people who would one day meet in a back room in Asia Minor and be laughed at by their neighbours. The Spirit went and found them, one by one. The Son poured out the blood that would make them his. Three persons, one love, one purpose, and not a single exile overlooked. The God who chose them is the God who scattered them, and the God who scattered them will gather them, every one, into a home that cannot be taken away.
verseByVerse.note: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia were Roman provinces covering much of modern Turkey. Peter probably wrote from Rome in the early 60s AD, shortly before Nero’s persecution. The readers were mostly Gentile believers, now “exiles” in their own society.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–12 — Born Again to a Living Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter bursts into praise. God has given his people new birth to a living hope through Christ’s resurrection, an inheritance that cannot perish, kept in heaven, while they are guarded by his power. So they rejoice, even in grief, because trials test their faith as fire tests gold. They love Christ though they have not seen him. And the prophets who foretold this grace searched to understand it, learning that they served a later generation, in things angels long to look into.
verseByVerse.theology:
Kept, and Keeping

Born again to a living hope, believers have an inheritance kept in heaven and are themselves guarded by God's power until it is revealed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prophets searched their own words about Christ’s sufferings and the glories to follow.

Now: Trials test faith as fire tests gold, and faith is worth far more.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God’s power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! Peter opens with praise rather than instruction, and the exclamation is in the Greek. Blessed, eulogētos: worthy of praise, to be spoken well of. It is the same opening as Ephesians 1:3 and 2 Corinthians 1:3, and it is a Jewish form, the shape of the blessings a Jew said many times a day: blessed are you, O Lord our God. But Peter fills it with new content. God is now named as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Whatever these people were suffering, his first instinct is worship, and that is itself a lesson. He does not begin with their problems. He begins with God, because the problems will look different once God has been seen.

According to his great mercy. Not according to their goodness, their potential, or their need, but according to his mercy, and great mercy, to poly autou eleos, abundant mercy. Mercy is kindness to those who deserve the opposite. Peter knew exactly how much mercy it had taken to make a Christian of him. The source of new birth is in God and not in us, and it is as large as God is.

He has caused us to be born again. The verb is anagennaō, to beget again, and Peter is the only New Testament writer who uses it (here and in v. 23). The idea goes back to Jesus’ words to Nicodemus, that a man must be born again (John 3:3–8), and James says the same: of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth (James 1:18). And note the grammar, because it is the point. He caused us. Nobody arranges his own birth, contributes to it, or consents to it in advance. It is the one experience every human being has been entirely passive in, and Peter chose the image deliberately. We did not cause our first birth, nor our second. A Christian is not a person who decided to turn over a new leaf. He is a person to whom God gave a new life.

To a living hope. Not a lively feeling but a hope that is alive, zōsan, because the one it rests on is. Most of what the world calls hope is a wish with its fingers crossed: I hope it does not rain, I hope the test comes back clear. Christian hope is a certainty not yet seen. It is alive, active, growing; and it is alive because it rests on a living Saviour.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Peter grounds the hope immediately, and he grounds it in an event. A dead man’s promises expire with him. These do not. And no one knew this better than Peter. On the Saturday after the crucifixion his hope was as dead as the body in the tomb. He had followed a man he believed was the Messiah, and the man had been executed, and he himself had denied him. Then on Sunday morning he ran to the tomb and found it empty, and later that day the Lord appeared to him, alone (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5). When Peter writes that God caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection, he is describing his own Easter. His hope was dead and was raised with Christ.

To an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading. Then the inheritance, klēronomia, described with three Greek words that all begin with the same negative letter, a deliberate triplet. Imperishable, aphtharton: it cannot decay or be destroyed. Undefiled, amianton: it cannot be polluted by sin. Unfading, amaranton: it cannot wither like a flower (the amaranth was named for this, the flower that does not fade). Every one of those is a denial of something that happens to earthly inheritances. Israel’s inheritance was the land of Canaan, and it could be invaded, defiled and lost, and had been. Death, sin and time take everything we own. This inheritance is beyond the reach of all three. And Peter was writing to people whose property in many cases had been taken, or who had been cut out of the family will for becoming Christians. He tells them what they have not lost.

What is the inheritance? Not a mansion with a number on the door, but God himself and everything he gives with himself: the new heavens and new earth, a resurrection body, the sight of Christ, sinless fellowship with all his people, and the end of every tear (Romans 8:17; Revelation 21:3–4). Peter calls it the salvation ready to be revealed. It is not something we earn as wages but something we receive as children, because inheritance is what comes to you by birth. That is why Peter puts the new birth and the inheritance in the same sentence.

Kept in heaven for you. The tense is perfect, tetērēmenēn: reserved and still reserved, guarded and remaining guarded. It is in the safest possible custody, with your name on it. No thief, no inflation, no confiscating magistrate in Bithynia can touch it.

Who by God’s power are being guarded through faith. And then the answering promise. Guarded, phrouroumenous, is a garrison term: soldiers posted around a city, keeping the enemy out and the inhabitants safe. The tense is present: continually guarded. So the inheritance is kept for you, and you are kept for it. Both ends of the journey are under guard, and the middle is where the reader currently is. By God’s power: the guarding is God’s work, not ours. Through faith: the means God uses. He keeps us by keeping us believing.

Does through faith mean that our security depends on our holding on? Faith is the means by which God guards us, not a condition that hands our safety back to us. The faith itself is his gift and is kept by his power. Those who are guarded by God’s power will reach the salvation ready to be revealed. Think of a father holding a small child’s hand on a busy road. The child holds on too, but the child is not safe because of the strength of his grip. He is safe because his father’s hand is round his.

For a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. Ready, hetoimēn: prepared, waiting, finished. Revealed, apokalyphthēnai: unveiled. Salvation is not something still being assembled in heaven. It is complete, and it is waiting to be uncovered at Christ’s return. We are saved now (v. 9), and we will be saved then, and what is hidden now will be shown.

Where Christians differ: can a believer lose this inheritance? Some traditions teach that a true believer can fall away finally and be lost. Verdict: Peter teaches a double security: the inheritance is kept in heaven for us, and we are guarded by God’s power through faith for it. Neither can fail. This is the perseverance of the saints: those whom God has begotten again he will keep to the end, not apart from their faith but through it, which he himself sustains (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; Jude 24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers can be careless. God guards us through faith, and we are called to keep believing. But God himself guarantees that we will.

What about people who seemed to believe and then walked away? Scripture is honest that some do (1 John 2:19; Matthew 13:20–21), and it explains them: they went out from us because they were not of us. Not everyone who joins a church has been born again, and seed on rocky ground can spring up quickly and then wither. That is a sobering truth, but it is not a threat to the believer who is anxious about it. The person who fears falling away and runs to Christ is showing the very faith by which God is guarding him. If someone you love has drifted, do not conclude too quickly either way. Pray, keep the door open, and remember that some who wander are sheep who will be brought back.

In a sentence. Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! In his great mercy he has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. This inheritance is kept in heaven for you, who through faith are protected by God’s power until the coming of the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of what you are afraid of losing: health, a job, a reputation, someone you love, your own mind in old age. Beside it, write the three words Peter uses: imperishable, undefiled, unfading. Not to make the first list unimportant, but to put it in its place. Then, when the fear comes, pray it to God in Peter’s order: first blessing, then the request. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is very hard to panic and bless at the same time.

For worship. Blessed be the God who did not wait for us to deserve a second birth, but gave it according to his great mercy. Blessed be the Father who raised his Son from the dead, so that our hope could never die again. He has written our names on an inheritance that rust cannot touch, sin cannot stain and time cannot fade, and he has posted himself as the garrison round our weak and wavering faith. The treasure is kept for us, and we are kept for the treasure, and the hands that keep both are the hands that hold the stars.

verseByVerse.quote: In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

In this you rejoice. In what has just been described, not in what is about to be. The joy has an object outside the circumstances, which is the only way it survives the rest of the sentence. Rejoice, agalliasthe, is a strong word: exult, leap for joy, the word Mary used when her spirit rejoiced in God her Saviour (Luke 1:47). And the tense is present. Peter does not say you will rejoice when this is over. You are rejoicing now.

Though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials. Three qualifiers in half a verse, and each is a mercy. Now: present, and therefore temporary. For a little while, oligon: measured against the imperishable inheritance, and Peter has just set the scale (5:10; 2 Corinthians 4:17). And if necessary, ei deon, which is the tender one: the trials are not random and not routine. They come when there is a reason for them, and somebody is deciding. Not one ounce of suffering lands on a believer that God has not weighed and judged needed. Various trials, poikilois peirasmois, is the same phrase as James 1:2: many-coloured trials, every shade and variety. Peter will later use the same word for God’s varied grace (4:10). The trials come in many colours, and so does the grace.

You have been grieved. Note that Peter says it plainly. Grieved, lypēthentes: distressed, sorrowful, the word used of Jesus in Gethsemane. He does not pretend the joy cancels the pain or that a Christian should feel less. Both are true at once, and the letter never asks them to choose. Paul says the same: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). A Christian at a graveside is allowed to weep. What he is given is not the absence of grief but a joy underneath it that the grief cannot reach.

So that the tested genuineness of your faith. Then the purpose, and the image is a workshop. The word dokimion is the assayer’s: what is left when the fire has taken everything else, the proven, genuine part. A metalworker put the ore in a crucible over a hot fire; the dross rose to the top and was skimmed off; and he kept going until he could see his own face in the molten metal. Then it was pure. The purpose of trials is not to destroy faith but to prove it and purify it, and the refiner is never careless with the heat (Malachi 3:3).

More precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire. The comparison is exact rather than decorative. Gold is refined by fire and is still perishable; faith is refined the same way and is not. So the process is identical and the product is worth more, which is Peter’s answer to a suffering congregation asking what any of this is for. If men will put gold, which will one day melt in the final fire, through the furnace to make it pure, will God not do as much for faith, which lasts for ever? Job had found it out in the dark: when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold (Job 23:10; Zechariah 13:9).

May be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ. And see where the praise lands: at the revelation, apokalypsis, the unveiling of Jesus Christ at his return. Not now. The vindication is on a date, and the letter keeps pointing to it, which is what makes for a little while bearable rather than glib. Whose praise? Christ’s praise of the believer: well done, good and faithful servant (Matthew 25:21). And the believer’s honour, all redounding to God’s glory. The Lord who was ashamed of no one will stand before the universe and acknowledge the faith of a slave girl in Pontus who would not deny him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should seek out suffering or that God enjoys our pain. It means that when suffering comes, it is never wasted.

Is God the one sending my suffering? Scripture holds two things together. God is sovereign over every trial; nothing reaches his child by accident, which is what if necessary means. And God is never the author of evil; much suffering comes through the sin of others, the brokenness of a fallen world, or the attacks of the devil (5:8). Joseph’s brothers meant evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), and both were true of the same event. You do not need to decide whether a trial came from God’s hand or from someone else’s malice. You need to know that it cannot leave God’s hand, and that he intends it for your good.

How do I know if my faith is genuine? The fire shows it. Not by whether you feel strong, but by whether, under pressure, you still turn towards Christ rather than away from him. Genuine faith may be shaken, frightened and weak, as Peter’s was, but it keeps coming back to the same place: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life (John 6:68). Fake faith, which was always really faith in comfort, leaves when the comfort goes. If your trial has driven you to pray more and lean harder on Christ, the assay is already coming back positive.

In a sentence. In all this you greatly rejoice, though for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in all kinds of trials. These have come so that the proven genuineness of your faith, of greater worth than gold, which perishes even though it is refined by fire, may result in praise, glory and honour when Jesus Christ is revealed.

On a Tuesday. Name the trial you are in. Then say three things to God about it, using Peter’s words. It is for a little while. It is not random; you judged it necessary. And it is producing something more precious than gold. Then ask him for one specific impurity he might be burning away: impatience, self-reliance, love of comfort, the need to be thought well of. Ask him to finish the work, and to keep his hand on the fire.

For worship. The Refiner sits by the furnace and does not leave. He knows the exact heat, the exact length of time, and the exact moment to lift the crucible out. He went into the fire himself first, on a hill outside Jerusalem, where the heat was not measured and did not stop until it was finished, so that the fire his people pass through would only ever refine them and never consume them. And at the end of it all, he will hold up the faith of his weakest saint before the angels and call it gold.

verseByVerse.quote: Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory, obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory, obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

Though you have not seen him, you love him. Stop on that, and remember who is writing it. Peter had seen him. He had pulled nets with him, walked on water towards him, watched him transfigured, and denied him in a courtyard while the man looked at him: the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61). Of all the people who could have written this sentence, he is the one for whom it is not true. And there is no hint of superiority in it. He does not say you have not seen him as I did. He states their position and honours it, and the Lord had already said where the greater blessing lay: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29).

You love him. Peter puts love before faith in this verse, and perhaps he could not help it. Beside a charcoal fire on a beach the risen Lord had asked him three times, do you love me? and Peter had answered, grieved: Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you (John 21:15–17). Now, thirty years on, he tells Gentiles who were never on that beach that they love him too. The question Jesus put to Peter is the question that marks every Christian. Not merely: do you agree with him? But: do you love him?

How can I love someone I have never seen? In the same way you can love a person through letters before you meet them, only more so, because Christ is not absent. He speaks in his word, he is present by his Spirit, and he has shown you who he is in the Gospels. Love for Christ is not mainly a warm feeling you work up. It grows as you look at what he is and what he has done for you, and it shows itself in wanting to please him, trusting him, missing him and longing to see him (John 14:21). If you are drawn to him, grieved when you dishonour him, and glad when he is honoured, you love him, even if the feeling is quiet.

Though you do not now see him, you believe in him. Now, arti: at present. The not-seeing has a time limit. We shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2), and faith will give way to sight. Until then, faith is the eye that sees what the eye cannot.

And rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory. Two adjectives, and both are reaching past the end of language. Inexpressible, aneklalētos, means it cannot be spoken out: Peter, describing their joy, admits he has no words for it. And filled with glory, dedoxasmenē, glorified, most likely means the glory of the age to come has already leaked into it. This is not cheerfulness. It is a foretaste, arriving in people whose lives were hard. It does not depend on circumstances, because it does not come from them.

Obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls. Obtaining, komizomenoi, is a word for receiving what is due, carrying off a prize. Outcome is telos, the end, what a thing arrives at. And the present tense matters: not you will obtain but you are obtaining, now, in the middle of the trials. The salvation is being received while the grief of verse 6 is still going on. Souls, psychōn, means the whole person, not a ghostly part of us that floats free of the body; the salvation Peter has in view includes the resurrection. It is both a present experience and a future completion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians never feel sad. Peter has just said they are grieved (v. 6). Joy and sorrow coexist (2 Corinthians 6:10).

What if I do not feel this joy at all? Then you are in the company of many saints, and of the psalmists, who wrote whole songs from the dark (Psalm 88). Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, not a test you pass or fail each morning. It can be buried under depression, grief, exhaustion or illness, and none of those is a sign that Christ has left you. Keep looking at him, keep using the means of grace, and tell God honestly that you want to rejoice in him and cannot. The joy Peter describes rests on facts, not feelings: you are loved, kept and being saved. The feeling will come back; the facts never left.

In a sentence. Though you have not seen him, you love him; and even though you do not see him now, you believe in him and are filled with a joy too deep for words and full of glory, for you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

On a Tuesday. Speak to Christ today as to someone you love, not only as someone you need. Tell him one thing you admire in him, from the Gospels: the way he touched the leper, the way he looked at Peter, the way he prayed for his murderers. Love grows by attention. And if the day is heavy, notice that Peter places this joy in the same people who are grieved by various trials. You do not have to wait for the grief to finish to begin.

For worship. He is the one whom angels see face to face, and he has chosen to be loved, for now, by people who have never seen him. He hides himself in a word and a Spirit, and somehow, from a back street in Cappadocia to a hospital bed tonight, he wins hearts that have never looked into his eyes. He is worth loving unseen. And the day is coming when the unseen will be seen, the faith will become sight, and the joy that has no words will at last find its voice in a song that does not end.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look.

Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours. Peter now does something remarkable: he tells a small, harassed congregation of foreigners that they are the point of the entire Old Testament. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and the rest were speaking of the grace that was to be yours, the grace that would come in the Messiah’s age. People who had grown up on Homer, and had perhaps never heard of Moses until a year or two ago, are told that the prophets were writing to them.

Searched and inquired carefully. Two verbs, both intensive. Searched, exezētēsan, and inquired carefully, exēraunēsan: investigated diligently, like miners tunnelling for ore. The men who wrote Scripture studied their own words, trying to work out what they meant, which is an extraordinary thing to be told about inspiration. They were not passive dictation machines. They were readers of what they had written, and puzzled by it. Daniel read Jeremiah and tried to understand the seventy years, and asked about his own visions and was told the words were shut up until the time of the end (Daniel 9:2; 12:8–9).

Inquiring what person or time. Literally, what or what sort of time: when would it happen, and what would the circumstances be? Some translate it who or when, the person and the time. Either way the prophets knew the main lines of what they foretold and lacked the details, and they were hungry for them.

The Spirit of Christ in them was indicating. Note the phrase: the Spirit of Christ in them. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), and Peter says the prophets were carrying the Spirit of a Christ not yet born. Christ was already at work in the Old Testament prophets, centuries before the incarnation, which can only mean that he existed before Bethlehem. Prophecy was not the prophets’ own invention: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21).

When he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. Predicted, promartyromenon, testified beforehand. And what the prophets could not resolve is named exactly. Both were there in the text, and the order made no sense: a suffering figure (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22) and a glorified one (Psalm 110; Daniel 7). Two Messiahs, or one in sequence? Nobody could tell until the sequence happened. Then on the road to Emmaus the risen Christ asked: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:25–27, 44–46). Peter was in the upper room that evening when the Lord opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. Here he passes the lesson on. And note glories, plural: the resurrection, the ascension, the reign, and the return. The pattern is the one Peter’s readers must follow too: suffering first, then glory (4:13; 5:10).

It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you. They were told, in effect, that the answer was not for their generation. And they went on writing. Isaiah wrote of the Servant who would be pierced for our transgressions and died seven centuries before anyone saw it happen. Anyone labouring at something whose usefulness he will not live to see is in very good company. The Sunday school teacher who never learns what became of the children, the missionary translating a Bible he will not see printed, the mother praying for grandchildren not yet born: the prophets served people they would never meet, and Peter tells his readers that they were those people.

In the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. The same Spirit who spoke through the prophets spoke through the apostles and evangelists who brought the gospel to Asia Minor. The Spirit sent from heaven is Pentecost (Acts 2), and Peter had stood in the middle of it. So the Old Testament and the New Testament are one revelation by one Spirit about one Christ. The unnamed preacher who came to Pontus was finishing a sentence Isaiah had begun.

Things into which angels long to look. Then the last clause, and it is one of the most arresting in the New Testament. Long, epithymousin: desire, eagerly want. Look, parakypsai: to stoop down and peer in. It is the word used of the disciples bending to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5, 11), and of the man who looks intently into the perfect law (James 1:25). Peter himself had stooped and looked into that tomb (Luke 24:12). He pictures the angels leaning over the edge of heaven, trying to see. They have never needed redeeming and cannot experience it, and it fascinates them. Through the church the manifold wisdom of God is being made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10), and there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10). What angels long to see, believers possess.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the prophets understood nothing of what they wrote. They knew the main lines; they lacked the details of time and circumstance. Nor does it mean the Old Testament is only about the future; it spoke to its own time too. But its deepest meaning is Christ.

So should I read the Old Testament looking for Christ in every verse? Read it looking for Christ in its whole story, not hunting for him under every stone. The Old Testament is God’s account of creation, fall and promise, and every part of it is heading somewhere: the sacrifices show what sin costs, the kings show what a true king must be, the prophets show both judgment and a coming rescue, the psalms give the very words Christ would pray. Ask of each passage: what does this show me about God, about sin, about the need for a Saviour, and how does Christ fulfil it? He himself said the Scriptures bear witness about me (John 5:39).

Why do angels not experience salvation? Because no Saviour came for fallen angels. Christ took on human nature, not angelic nature (Hebrews 2:16), and died for human sinners. The angels who stayed loyal never needed saving, and those who rebelled have not been offered it. So the angels watch, with wonder, something done for a race lower than themselves, and see in it depths of God’s love and wisdom they would not otherwise know. It is a humbling thought: the gospel you heard as an ordinary Sunday sermon is a thing the highest creatures in the universe study.

In a sentence. The prophets who spoke of the grace that was to come to you searched intently and with great care concerning this salvation, trying to find out the time and circumstances to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when he testified in advance to the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, when they spoke of the things that have now been told you by those who have preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Even angels long to look into these things.

On a Tuesday. If the gospel has become familiar to you, ordinary, the thing you already know, read Isaiah 53 slowly today, and remember that the man who wrote it did not know the name of the one he was describing, and longed to. Then think of an angel bending down to look. Ask God to give you back some of the wonder. And if you are doing work for God whose fruit you may never see, take heart from the prophets: they were serving people they would never meet.

For worship. For a thousand years the Spirit of Christ spoke of him through men who could not see his face. Moses saw his day in a lamb, David in a forsaken sufferer, Isaiah in a Servant crushed for others, Daniel in a Son of Man coming on the clouds. All the lines of all the prophets ran towards one hill and one empty tomb, and now we stand at the place where they meet, and what prophets searched for and angels stoop to see is ours. The whole of history has been leaning towards Christ, and the whole of heaven is still leaning in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — Be Holy, for I Am Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the basis of the salvation he has just described, Peter calls his readers to get their minds ready for action, stay clear-headed, and set their hope completely on the grace they will receive when Christ appears. As obedient children they must no longer be shaped by the desires that ruled them in ignorance, but be holy in all their conduct, because God, who called them, is holy, as the law says. Since they call on a Father who judges everyone impartially by what they do, they should live reverently during their time as exiles, knowing they were bought free from an empty inherited way of life not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless lamb, chosen before creation and revealed now for their sake. Through him they trust God, who raised him and glorified him, so their faith and hope rest in God. Having been purified by obeying the truth, they must love one another earnestly from the heart, for they have been born again from imperishable seed, the living and lasting word of God. Human life fades like grass and flowers, but the Lord’s word stands for ever, and that word is the gospel preached to them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of a Child

Be holy, because the one who called you is holy. Call on him as Father who judges impartially, and remember the price of your ransom: the precious blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had been ransomed from empty ways handed down from their ancestors.

Now: All flesh withers, but the word of the Lord remains, and that word is the gospel preached to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

Therefore, preparing your minds for action. Therefore: and everything from here rests on the twelve verses behind it. Peter never gives a command until he has given a reason. Because of this great salvation, chosen, born again, guarded, foretold by prophets and gazed at by angels, now the commands begin. Preparing your minds for action translates a vivid Greek idiom, anazōsamenoi tas osphyas tēs dianoias: girding up the loins of your mind. A man in that world wore a long robe, and before he could run, fight or work he pulled it up and tucked it into his belt. Otherwise he would trip.

Girding up the mind. Applied to the mind, it means gathering up whatever is loose and trailing. Peter is not asking for more feeling; he is asking for mental discipline, the deliberate collecting of a mind that would otherwise flap about. There is a memory in it of the first Passover, eaten with loins girded, sandals on, staff in hand, ready to leave Egypt at short notice (Exodus 12:11), and of the Lord’s words: stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning (Luke 12:35). A Christian’s mind is to be packed for a journey. Clear away whatever hinders your thinking: the clutter of distraction, the drift of daydreams, the half-truths you have stopped examining.

And being sober-minded. The word, nēphontes, is literally the opposite of drunk, and it means clear-headed, unintoxicated, seeing things as they are. Peter uses it three times in this short letter (4:7; 5:8). Suffering distorts judgement, and so does fear, and so does the surrounding culture’s version of reality. A person can be drunk on the world’s pleasures, or on its panic, or on its endless supply of news, and the effect is the same: he cannot see straight. Peter wants Christians who are awake.

Set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. Then the command itself, and both halves matter. Fully, teleiōs: completely, without reserve, with nothing held back for a second option. Hope is being treated here as something you place, deliberately, in one location. And the location is not what God will do for them next year but what will be brought when Christ appears. The grace that will be brought, pheromenēn, is being carried towards you: the full grace of final salvation, coming to meet us at Christ’s return, like a ship already on the horizon. Which is a demanding instruction for people who would have preferred relief now. Peter does not promise the trials will stop. He tells them where to put their hope so that it is not destroyed if they do not.

Hope is the engine. Notice that this is the first command in the letter, and it is a command to hope. Not first to be holy, or to love, or to endure. Those all follow, and they all grow out of this. Christian living is driven by hope: a person who knows where he is going, and what is waiting for him, can bear a great deal on the road. A person who has put his hope anywhere else will be crushed when that thing is taken.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring present responsibilities while waiting. Hope in the future shapes how we live now.

How do I actually set my hope on something? By deliberately thinking about it, again and again, until it shapes your expectations. Hope is not only an emotion that comes and goes; it is a direction you give your mind. Read what Scripture says about Christ’s return and the new creation (Revelation 21–22; 1 Corinthians 15). When you notice yourself hoping in something else for your security, a promotion, a relationship, a medical result, name it and turn your mind back: that would be good, but it is not my hope. Sing about heaven. Talk about it with other Christians. Hope that is never fed shrinks; hope that is fed carries you.

In a sentence. So prepare your minds for action, keep a clear head, and set your hope completely on the grace that will be given you when Jesus Christ is revealed.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you reach for when you feel low: the phone, the fridge, the news, the daydream. None of them is wicked, but most of them are the mental equivalent of trailing robes. Today, at that moment, tuck the robe in. Put the phone down for a minute and say one sentence to yourself about what is coming at the revelation of Jesus Christ. Then ask: if I really believed that grace is on its way to me, what would I do differently this afternoon?

For worship. The grace is already on its way. It set out from heaven when the Son left the Father’s side, it was paid for at the cross, it was guaranteed at the empty tomb, and it is being carried towards his people now, every day nearer, with nothing in the universe able to stop it arriving. He who promised is faithful. When he appears, he will not come empty-handed; he will bring with him everything he has kept for us, and himself above all.

verseByVerse.quote: As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, “You shall be holy, for I am holy.”

As obedient children. Literally children of obedience, hōs tekna hypakoēs, a Hebrew way of saying that obedience characterises them. It is what they are made of, not merely what they do. And the word children matters: they have been born again into God’s family (v. 3). Children resemble their father. The command to obey is not the rule of a sergeant over recruits but the family likeness a father expects to see growing in his children.

Do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance. The verb, syschēmatizomenoi, means to be shaped from outside, pressed into a mould, the same word Paul uses in Romans 12:2. The pressure is constant and it is not usually noticed, which is why it has to be resisted deliberately. A jelly does not decide to take the shape of the mould. It simply sits there long enough. Passions, epithymiai, are desires, cravings, the appetites that ran the old life.

Your former ignorance. That tells us these readers were largely Gentiles: Jews could not have been described as ignorant of God. And it is a merciful description of a pagan past: not only wickedness but not-knowing. They behaved that way because they did not know any better, and now they do. Peter does not excuse the old life, but he refuses to define them by it. That is who you were. It is not who you are. And the knowledge they now have leaves them no excuse to go back.

But as he who called you is holy. He who called you is God, whose effectual call brought them to faith (2:9, 21; 5:10). Then the standard, and it is startling. The measure is not an improvement on the surrounding culture, nor the best available human example, nor the average Christian in your church. It is God himself. Holy, hagios, means set apart, other, belonging to a different order: utterly pure and morally perfect. The seraphim cry it three times in Isaiah’s vision, holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts (Isaiah 6:3), and cover their faces.

You also be holy in all your conduct. Be, genēthēte: become, show yourselves to be. Holiness applied to conduct means a life that is visibly not from around here. Which is exactly the letter’s theme: exiles behave like citizens of the place they are from. In all your conduct, en pasē anastrophē, closes the loophole everyone reaches for. Not only in religious matters, not only in public, not only in the parts of life that show. Work, home, speech, money, relationships, the browser history, the tax return, the thoughts nobody else hears. All of it.

Since it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy. The quotation comes from Leviticus 11:44–45, and it recurs there (19:2; 20:7, 26). Peter is doing something bold with it. That command was given to Israel at Sinai, and he applies it without adjustment to Gentile converts in Bithynia. What was said to the covenant nation is now said to them, because they are the covenant people, which is the argument he will make explicitly in chapter 2. And the reason is not a rule but a person: for I am holy. Holiness is not an optional extra for keen Christians. It reflects the character of the God who has called us, and without it no one will see the Lord (Hebrews 12:14).

The Holy One in a fishing boat. Peter knew what holiness looked like, because he had met it at close range. After the great catch of fish he fell at Jesus’ knees and said, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8): Isaiah’s cry, woe is me, in a fishing boat. Later he confessed, you are the Holy One of God (John 6:69). John tells us that the glory Isaiah saw when the seraphim cried holy was the glory of Christ (John 12:41). So the holiness of Leviticus is not an abstract standard. It walked the shore of Galilee, touched lepers without being defiled, and committed no sin (2:22). And the Holy One did not depart from the sinful man. He called him, and he calls us, to be made like himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we become holy in order to be accepted. We are called and accepted by grace; holiness is the response. Nor does holiness mean withdrawing from the world; it means being different within it.

Is it possible to be holy as God is holy? In one sense believers already are: they are set apart as God’s own people (2:9). In another sense it is a lifelong work, real growth in holiness by the Spirit’s power, never complete in this life (1 John 1:8). The command is real, and God supplies what he commands; the standard is himself, and the goal is likeness to Christ at his appearing.

Does holiness mean being serious and joyless? No. The holiest man who ever lived was accused of being a glutton and a drunkard because he went to so many feasts (Matthew 11:19). Holiness is not grimness; it is wholeness, a life with nothing rotten in it. It removes the things that spoil joy: the guilt, the secrecy, the slavery to appetites. Holy people laugh freely because they have nothing to hide. What holiness does exclude is the cheap laughter that depends on cruelty or filth (Ephesians 5:4), and the joy that needs sin to be fun.

Where do I start? Start where the pressure to conform is strongest for you. For one person it is the tongue at work; for another, entertainment; for another, money, or anger at home. Ask: in this one area, what would I do if I were really from somewhere else? Then do it, relying on the Spirit and not on willpower alone, and confess quickly when you fail. Holiness grows like a garden, not like a light switched on, and it grows best in people who are not afraid to tell God the truth.

In a sentence. As obedient children, do not let yourselves be shaped by the evil desires you had when you lived in ignorance. But just as he who called you is holy, so be holy in everything you do, for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”

On a Tuesday. Pick one area of your life this week, work, money, speech or entertainment, and ask: what would holiness look like here? Then ask where the mould is pressing on you without your noticing. What do you now find normal that would have shocked you when you were first converted? That is often the place where the shaping has been happening.

For worship. He is holy, holy, holy: light with no darkness at all, goodness with no shadow of turning, purity so bright that seraphs hide their faces. And this God, who might have been content to be holy alone, has called to himself people from the brothels and temples of Asia Minor and from the half-hidden sins of our own hearts, and said: be like me. He does not lower the standard to meet us. He lifts us to it, by his Son’s blood and his Spirit’s power, until on the last day we stand before him without spot, holy as he is holy.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one's deeds, conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one’s deeds, conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile,

And if you call on him as Father. And the if is not a doubt but a given: since you do. Call on, epikaleisthe, means invoke in prayer, perhaps an echo of the prayer Jesus taught, Our Father in heaven (Matthew 6:9). Peter grants them the most intimate name available. People who had prayed to statues of Artemis now pray to the living God and call him Father.

Who judges impartially according to each one’s deeds. And then, in the same breath, the Judge. The two halves sit oddly together for modern readers, who tend to hold Father and Judge apart. Peter does not. Impartially is aprosōpolēmptōs, literally without receiving the face, the opposite of the partiality condemned in James 2:1. God does not defer to appearance, position or connection, and Peter is telling that to people at the bottom of every social ladder in Asia Minor. Impartiality is terrifying to those with advantages and profoundly good news to those with none. Having him as Father does not exempt us from his evaluation of our deeds (Romans 2:6, 11; 2 Corinthians 5:10); it means the one evaluating them loves us.

The Judge we have met. Peter learned this word in a Roman officer’s house. Standing before Cornelius, he said, truly I understand that God shows no partiality, and in the same sermon he announced that Jesus is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:34, 42). The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). So the impartial Judge whose eyes no face can buy has a face of his own, and it is the face of the one who was judged in our place, before a partial high priest and a cowardly governor. We may call God Father only because the Son taught us to and died to make it true.

Conduct yourselves with fear. This needs care, because perfect love casts out fear is also in the New Testament (1 John 4:18), and Peter is not contradicting it. The fear here, phobos, is not terror of condemnation; he has just called God Father. It is the reverence of someone who knows exactly who he is dealing with. The respect of a child who loves and honours his father and does not want to displease him. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10).

Two kinds of fear. A useful test of the difference: fear that drives you away from God is the wrong kind, and fear that keeps you careful in his presence is the right one. A child who is not frightened of his father may still not be casual with him. The wrong fear hides in the garden like Adam. The right fear comes near, takes its shoes off like Moses, and listens.

If God judges according to deeds, does that contradict justification by faith alone? No. Believers are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies shows itself in deeds, and at the judgment those deeds are the evidence of it (Romans 2:6–7; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Our standing rests on Christ; our deeds show that we belong to him, and are rewarded by grace.

Throughout the time of your exile. Exile, paroikia, is sojourning, residence as a foreigner: the exile word again from verse 1, and now with a duration attached. It has a beginning and an end, and they are living inside it (2:11). Peter’s counsel for the whole stretch is one word: reverence, because a man who genuinely fears God has very little capacity left for fearing anybody else, which is the practical liberation this letter keeps offering. The neighbours could slander them; the magistrate could fine them. But the one whose opinion finally mattered was their Father.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be judged to determine whether they are saved. Their salvation rests on Christ. But their works will be evaluated, and God takes their conduct seriously (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

How does fearing God free me from fearing people? Because fear always looks to whoever holds the final verdict. If my colleagues, my family or social media hold it, I will bend to them. If God holds it, their verdicts are reduced to their real size: real, sometimes painful, but not final. Jesus said, do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28). In practice, before a hard conversation or a moment of pressure, ask: what will my Father think of this, and does anything else ultimately matter? That question has made timid people brave for two thousand years.

In a sentence. Since you call on a Father who judges each person’s work impartially, live out your time as foreigners here in reverent fear.

On a Tuesday. Notice whose opinion you are most afraid of this week: a boss, a parent, a spouse, an online crowd. Then bring that person, in prayer, before your Father who judges impartially, and leave him there. And when you pray Our Father, pause for a second on both words: Father, so you can come close; in heaven, so you come carefully.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth has let us call him Father. He sees every deed with perfect clarity and no favouritism, and he has never yet been fooled by a face. And this same Judge has adopted the guilty, at the cost of his Son, so that the courtroom where every work will be weighed is presided over by the one who loves us most. We fear him because he is holy. We come to him because he is ours. And there is no safer place in the universe than the presence of the God we fear.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.

Knowing that you were ransomed. And the participle explains the fear of verse 17. Reverence rests on knowledge of what was paid. Ransomed, elytrōthēte, is the slave-market and prisoner-exchange word: a price handed over to secure a release. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45; Titus 2:14). And it carries the exodus behind it, where God redeemed Israel out of Egypt with an outstretched arm and the blood of the Passover lamb, the event this whole passage keeps gesturing at.

From the futile ways inherited from your forefathers. That is a striking thing to say to Gentile readers, and it names what most of them would have called their heritage. Futile, mataias, means empty, achieving nothing: the standard biblical verdict on idols. And inherited, patroparadotou, handed down by your fathers, is the sharp word. These ways came down to them; they did not choose them. Peter is describing something almost nobody escapes by deciding to: the whole handed-down apparatus of how your family has always done things, which is precisely why a ransom was needed rather than advice. Christ’s blood frees us from empty family traditions and cultural patterns, as well as from guilt.

The modern inheritance. We have our own. Not the household gods of Bithynia, but the patterns of anger, drinking, coldness, money-worship, or quiet despair that run down through three generations of a family, and the cultural assumptions we absorbed before we could read: that you are what you earn, that happiness is the point, that death is the end. Peter says these can be broken, not by the effort of a single generation, but by a ransom. Many a Christian has been the first in a long family line to be bought out of the old ways, and the last to be held by them.

Not with perishable things such as silver or gold. Peter names the two most durable currencies in the ancient world and calls them perishable, phthartois. He has already used gold as the standard of value in verse 7 and found it wanting there too. Slaves were freed with money, and a ransom price was literally counted out. But no amount of money could free a single human being from sin. All the gold in Rome would not have covered one lie.

But with the precious blood of Christ. Precious, timios: costly, of great value, honoured. Christ’s blood is of infinite worth, because he is the infinite Son of God; Paul calls it the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). The price of our redemption was his life. And the price is set by what was spent, not by what the readers thought they were worth. That is the pastoral force of it for people being treated as worthless. You may work out what something is valued at by looking at what was paid for it. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

Like that of a lamb without blemish or spot. Without blemish, amōmos, no physical defect; without spot, aspilos, no stain. The Passover lamb had to be inspected and found flawless before it could be used (Exodus 12:5), as did all sacrificial animals (Leviticus 22:19–25). Peter, whose brother Andrew heard John the Baptist say, behold, the Lamb of God (John 1:29, 36–40), applies the inspection language to Christ. He was examined by Pilate, by Herod, by the high priest, and by the devil in the wilderness, and none of them found fault in him. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter and opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). His blood is effective because he was sinless: only a spotless life could be offered in place of stained ones (Revelation 5:6–12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the ransom was paid to Satan, as some early theologians speculated. It was paid to satisfy God’s justice, as the sacrificial imagery shows: the penalty of sin was borne by Christ (Romans 3:25–26).

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to Satan, who has no rightful claim over us. The price was paid to satisfy God’s justice (Romans 3:24–26), and what we are ransomed from is the futile ways inherited from your forefathers (v. 18), slavery to sin and its penalty.

Why did it have to be blood? Because sin deserves death, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins (Hebrews 9:22). Blood in Scripture stands for a life given up in death. God could not simply overlook sin and remain just; the penalty had to be paid. In love, he paid it himself, in his Son, who bore our sins in his body on the tree (2:24). This is penal substitution: Christ took the punishment we deserved, so that we could go free. The blood is not a magical substance; it is the sign of a death, and that death was ours.

In a sentence. For you know that it was not with things that perish, like silver or gold, that you were set free from the empty way of life handed down to you by your ancestors, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or defect.

On a Tuesday. Think of one empty way you inherited: a habit of mind, a family reaction, a cultural assumption. Name it to God, and then say: I was ransomed out of this, with blood. That changes the fight. You are not trying to become free; you are learning to live as someone who has been bought free. And the next time you feel worthless, do the arithmetic Peter suggests: look at what was paid.

For worship. No one has ever paid such a price for anything. Not silver, which tarnishes, not gold, which melts, but the life-blood of the eternal Son, the spotless Lamb, poured out on a Roman cross for slaves who did not know they were slaves. He walked into the market where we were being sold and paid for us with himself. And now we belong to him, and he does not undervalue what he bought. The futile ways of our fathers end at his cross, and a new family history begins there.

verseByVerse.quote: He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.

He was foreknown before the foundation of the world. The word, proegnōsmenou, is the same one used of the readers in verse 2. Christ and his people are both foreknown, and the parallel is not accidental. Not merely foreseen, but chosen and appointed in advance. Before the foundation of the world means before there was a world to fall. The cross was not God’s response to an emergency, improvised after things went wrong, a plan B. The Lamb was in view before Genesis 1 (Ephesians 1:4). Peter had preached it at Pentecost: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

But was made manifest in the last times. Made manifest, phanerōthentos: revealed, made visible. This is the incarnation, the hidden purpose stepping into history at a date. And the last times is the New Testament’s standard description of the period the readers are in (Hebrews 1:2). The final era of history began at Bethlehem, and everything since is its outworking. We are not waiting for the last days to begin; we are living in them.

For the sake of you. Peter puts it as bluntly as it can be put, di’ hymas. The eternal purpose, hidden before the world was made, was manifested for the sake of a scattered group of foreigners in Pontus and Bithynia who were being slandered by their neighbours. The whole eternal plan of God, centred on Christ, had them in view. And it had you in view. Not as a statistic, not as one of the masses, but as one for whom the Son came.

Who through him are believers in God. Even their faith arrives by way of Christ. He is not merely the object of it but the route to it (John 14:6). Gentiles who had worshipped idols now believe in the true God because of Christ. No one comes to know God as he is except through the Son who has made him known.

Who raised him from the dead and gave him glory. The Father raised and glorified the Son (Acts 2:32–36; Philippians 2:9): the world said no to Jesus, and God said yes. Then the logic of the last clause, so that your faith and hope are in God. The resurrection is offered here not primarily as proof of an event but as the ground of a disposition: God did that, therefore your faith and hope can rest on him. It is the same argument as verse 3, and Peter has now made it twice in one chapter. A God who raises the dead can be trusted with an inheritance.

What it does not mean. Foreknown does not mean God merely knew in advance that people would crucify Jesus and decided to make the best of it. God planned it, while those who carried it out were fully responsible (Acts 4:27–28).

If God planned the cross, were the people who crucified Jesus guilty? Yes. Scripture holds both together without embarrassment. Peter told the crowd at Pentecost that Jesus was delivered up according to God’s definite plan, and in the same sentence, you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordained the event for our salvation; Judas, Caiaphas and Pilate did it for wicked reasons and were answerable for it. God’s sovereignty never makes human choices unreal. It means that even the worst thing men ever did was taken up into the best thing God ever did.

In a sentence. He was chosen before the creation of the world, but was revealed in these last times for your sake. Through him you believe in God, who raised him from the dead and glorified him, and so your faith and hope are in God.

On a Tuesday. When things feel out of control, remember that the darkest day in history, the day the Son of God was murdered, was not out of control. It was planned before the foundation of the world for the sake of people like you. If God could take that day and make it the salvation of the world, he can be trusted with yours. Put your faith and hope in God, not in how today goes.

For worship. Before the first star was lit, the Father looked on his Son and saw the Lamb. Before Adam fell, the cross was planned; before we were born, our names were on his heart. He came at the appointed time, he was rejected, he died, and the Father raised him and crowned him with glory. And the whole of it, from eternity to Easter, was done for the sake of us. Our faith does not rest on our grip, or our goodness, or our feelings. It rests on the God who raised Jesus from the dead.
