verseByVerse.quote: Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth for a sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth for a sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart,

Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth. The purification is stated as accomplished: purified, hēgnikotes, is perfect tense, having purified and remaining pure. It has happened. And the means is obedience to the truth, which for Peter means the gospel believed and acted on, repentance and faith, rather than a code kept (Acts 15:9). At conversion, their souls were cleansed.

For a sincere brotherly love. And note what the purifying produced. It had an aim, and the aim was other people. Brotherly love, philadelphia, is family affection, the warmth of brothers and sisters. Sincere is anypokritos: un-play-acted, without the mask, the word for an actor in a Greek theatre turned negative. Peter allows that love can be performed, and rules it out.

Love one another earnestly from a pure heart. Then the command, and after that description it might have seemed unnecessary. That is the pattern the New Testament always follows. You have been purified for love; therefore love. The indicative first, then the imperative, and the imperative is needed precisely because what is true of us is not yet automatic in us. Love, agapēsate, is self-giving love, the love that does good to the other whatever it costs. From a pure heart means with undivided motives, not loving in order to be thought loving. (Some manuscripts read simply from the heart; the meaning is hardly different.)

Earnestly. This is the interesting word. Ektenōs means stretched out, strained, at full extent: used of a muscle under tension and of an athlete’s effort. And Peter had reason to know it. When Herod put him in prison and meant to kill him, the church was praying earnestly for him (Acts 12:5), the same word, and in the night an angel came and led him out. He knew what stretched-out love could do. Peter is not asking for warm feeling but for love that costs something to sustain.

A realistic command. These were scattered congregations of people thrown together by nothing except Christ: different races, classes and households, with slaves and masters in the same room, former temple prostitutes beside former Pharisees. Loving that group was not going to happen by temperament. It was going to take the sort of effort the word describes.

Love one another, as I have loved you. Peter is passing on a command he first heard with wet feet. On the night before the cross Jesus knelt with a towel and a basin, washed the feet of all twelve, Peter protesting, Judas included, and then said: a new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another (John 13:34). The measure of the love is Christ’s own love, and its proof is the cross that came a few hours later. That is why brotherly love in the church is not a social nicety. It is the family likeness of people washed by the same Lord, and by this all people will know that you are my disciples (John 13:35).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we purify ourselves by our own efforts. God purifies us through the gospel, which we obeyed by faith. But we are now called to live out that purity in love.

What if there is someone in my church I find very hard to love? Then you are exactly the person this verse was written for. Peter is not asking you to like everyone or to feel the same warmth for all. He is asking you to do them good, earnestly, from the heart. Begin by praying for them by name; it is very hard to keep resenting someone you are regularly bringing to God for blessing. Then do one concrete kind thing. Speak well of them when they are absent. If there is a real wrong between you, go and seek to put it right (Matthew 18:15). Feelings often follow actions, but the command does not wait for them.

Does loving earnestly mean I must tolerate sin? No. Love rejoices with the truth (1 Corinthians 13:6) and sometimes requires loving correction, church discipline, or protecting the vulnerable. Earnest love is not soft; it wants what is best for the other person, and sometimes that means saying hard things, or refusing to enable harm. What it rules out is coldness, gossip, cliques, and the polite distance that keeps fellow believers at arm’s length while appearing friendly.

In a sentence. Now that you have purified yourselves by obeying the truth so that you have genuine love for each other, love one another deeply, from the heart.

On a Tuesday. Choose one fellow believer to love strenuously this week: in time, in effort, in sacrifice. Choose the one it will cost you something to love, not the one you naturally like. Send the message, make the visit, carry the meal, give the hour. Love that stretches is love that has been stretched.

For worship. He loved us earnestly first. In Gethsemane he prayed more earnestly, his sweat like great drops of blood, and then he stretched out his arms on a cross for people who had betrayed, denied and deserted him. That is the love that purified us, and it is the love he now pours into his church, so that slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, the respectable and the ruined, sit down at one table as brothers and sisters. Every act of genuine love in the church is a small reflection of the love that bled for her.

verseByVerse.quote: since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God;

Since you have been born again. Peter now gives the reason underneath the command, and it takes him back to verse 3. Born again, anagegennēmenoi, is perfect passive: having been begotten again, and remaining so. The logic is family. Love one another, because you have the same birth. They are brothers by regeneration, not by preference, and that is why the love is commanded rather than left to affinity. You do not choose your siblings.

Not of perishable seed but of imperishable. Seed, spora, is sowing, origin. There is that word again, the third time in the chapter. The inheritance is imperishable (v. 4), the ransom was not paid in perishable silver (v. 18), and now the seed itself is imperishable. Peter is building a single case for readers whose visible world was all too perishable. Natural birth uses seed that dies; everyone in that congregation had buried somebody. This birth does not, which means the family it creates cannot be dissolved by the thing that dissolves every other family. Death will part husbands and wives, parents and children. It cannot part brothers and sisters in Christ, because the life they share cannot die: it is the life of the risen Christ, through whose resurrection they were born again (v. 3), and Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again (Romans 6:9).

Through the living and abiding word of God. The seed is the word, and the parable of the sower is not far away (Luke 8:11); Peter had heard it explained by the Sower himself. Both adjectives are doing work. Living, zōntos: it is not inert information but something with life in it, which is why it can generate life (Hebrews 4:12). Abiding, menontos: it remains, which is the point the quotation in the next verse will drive home. The word that gave them birth is the one thing in their situation that will still be there when everything visible has gone.

Is new birth, then, by the word? God himself gives new birth (v. 3; John 3:8), and he does it through the gospel preached: of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth (James 1:18). The Spirit uses the word as his instrument. That is why the church preaches, and why the word is the seed that never perishes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the word works apart from the Spirit. The Spirit uses the word to give new birth (John 3:5–8). Word and Spirit work together.

Does this mean baptism is what gives new birth? No. Peter names the seed of the new birth, and it is the word of God, the gospel preached, not the water of baptism. Baptism is the sign and confession of a new birth that has already taken place through the word and Spirit, which is why it belongs to those who believe. When Peter does speak of baptism (3:21), he insists it is not the washing of the body that saves, but the appeal of a good conscience to God through the resurrection. Christians who baptise infants also deny that the water itself regenerates; we differ with them on who should receive the sign, not on how new birth comes.

Why does it matter that the word is living? Because it means that when you read or hear Scripture you are not handling a museum piece. The same word that gave you life goes on feeding it (2:2). It can convict you, comfort you, correct you and change you, today, because God is speaking in it. That is why a Christian who neglects the word grows weak, and why a sermon is never only information. Come to the word expecting God to do something.

In a sentence. For you have been born again, not from perishable seed but from imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.

On a Tuesday. Look around your church next Sunday and remind yourself: these are not people I chose; they are people God fathered, by the same word that fathered me, and they will be my family for ever. Then pick one of them you hardly know and find out one thing about them. And give the word a place in your day where it can do its living work, even if it is only a single passage, read slowly, with a prayer.

For worship. He did not make us his children with seed that dies, or with a promise that could be broken. He spoke, and by his living word, carried by his Spirit, dead hearts in Galatia and Cappadocia, and in our own street, woke up and called him Father. The word that said let there be light in the beginning said let there be life in us. It has never stopped speaking, it will never pass away, and the family it has created will stand round his throne when every other family on earth has gone to dust.

verseByVerse.quote: for "All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever." And this word is the good news that was preached to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for “All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever.” And this word is the good news that was preached to you.

For All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. Peter closes the chapter with Isaiah 40:6–8, and the choice of passage is deliberate. Isaiah 40 was written to exiles: people far from home, wondering whether God had finished with them. It opens: comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isaiah 40:1). All flesh means all human beings, in their mortality and weakness. And note that it is not only the grass but all its glory: the flower, the impressive part. Human achievements, beauty, power, wealth, fame.

The grass withers, and the flower falls. The picture is the one James used (James 1:10–11): the hills of Israel green after the winter rains, carpeted with wildflowers, and then the hot desert wind blowing in from the east and browning the whole landscape within a day. Peter is writing to people being outclassed and outranked by neighbours with standing, and Isaiah’s word is that the standing is the most temporary thing about them. Not merely human life but human splendour is what withers. The magistrates who fined them, the families who disowned them, the city of Rome itself with all its marble, are wildflowers on a hillside, and the wind is coming.

But the word of the Lord remains forever. The single contrast, and everything in the chapter has been arranged to arrive here. Remains, menei, abides, endures, the same root as abiding in verse 23. In contrast with everything human, God’s word lasts for ever: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matthew 24:35). In Isaiah this comforted exiles in Babylon: empires rise and fall, but God’s promise stands. Babylon fell; Persia fell; Greece fell; and the word of the Lord did not. The same comfort for Peter’s exiles, writing from another Babylon. Set the imperishable seed beside the withering flower and you have Peter’s whole estimate of the situation.

And this word is the good news that was preached to you. Then the last line, and it is the one that lands. Preached as good news is euangelisthen. Isaiah’s eternal word is not a distant abstraction. It is the specific message somebody brought to Pontus and Cappadocia and said out loud in a room: the thing these readers heard, perhaps from a travelling trader, and believed. That is a remarkable dignity to confer on ordinary preaching. The word that outlasts all flesh and every human glory is the same word an unnamed evangelist spoke to a handful of foreigners, and it is the seed that gave them a birth that cannot perish.

The chapter that opens the Gospels. Peter’s quotation comes from the chapter all four Gospels use to introduce John the Baptist, the voice crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord (Isaiah 40:3; Mark 1:3; John 1:23). And Isaiah 40 says what the good news is. The herald is told to lift up his voice and cry to the cities of Judah, behold your God (40:9), the God who comes with might and yet will tend his flock like a shepherd and gather the lambs in his arms (40:10–11). That God came. The word that outlasts all flesh is the news that the Lord himself arrived in Jesus, took the frail flesh that Isaiah calls grass, died in it, and rose in it never to wither again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean human life has no value because it is short. It means human life finds lasting value only when connected to God’s eternal word.

If everything withers, why should I work hard at anything? Because what is done in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Your job, your family, your service are not worthless because they are temporary; they become lasting when they are done for Christ and joined to his eternal purposes. What withers is the glory, the vanity of building a name for yourself. What lasts is the person you are becoming, the people you have loved into the kingdom, and the word you have passed on. Work hard, but do not build your identity on what the wind will take.

How is the gospel the word of the Lord when it was spoken by ordinary people? Because God speaks through his messengers when they speak his message. When the gospel is faithfully preached, it is not merely a human opinion about God; it is the word of God at work in those who believe (1 Thessalonians 2:13). The preacher may be unimpressive and the room small, but the word is the same eternal word Isaiah heard. That is why Christians should listen to faithful preaching with expectation, and why every believer who shares the gospel with a friend is handing on something that will outlast the stars.

In a sentence. For, “All people are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord endures for ever.” And this is the word that was preached to you.

On a Tuesday. Walk past something impressive today: a tall office building, a famous name, an expensive car, a celebrity in the news. Say quietly: flower of grass. Not with contempt, but with perspective. Then think of the gospel you heard, perhaps from someone very ordinary, and thank God for the person who said it to you. And ask who in your life has not yet heard it from you.

For worship. Every empire has withered, and his word has not. Every philosopher has been answered, and his word still speaks. Every glory of man has fallen like a flower in the hot wind, and the word of the Lord stands, exactly where it stood when Isaiah heard it, and the angels proclaimed it, and Peter preached it, and someone said it to you. He spoke the world into being, and he will speak it into newness, and in between he spoke to us. All flesh is grass. But our God remains, and his word remains, and those born of it will remain with him for ever.

2.title: Living Stones and Holy Exiles: Identity, Witness, and the Suffering Christ
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from who Christians are (vv. 1–10) to how they live in a hostile world (vv. 11–25). You are living stones in God’s house, a chosen race, a royal priesthood; therefore live so well among unbelievers that those who slander you will glorify God. Identity produces conduct, and conduct commends the identity.

The chapter ends with Christ’s unjust suffering (vv. 18–25). Peter frames submission not as mere social conformity but as following the suffering Servant, who entrusted himself to God, and then did what no one else could: bore our sins in his body on the tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Put off the sins that destroy love, and crave the pure milk of God’s word. Come to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but precious to God, and be built with other believers into one spiritual house and holy priesthood. Christ is the cornerstone to those who believe and a stumbling stone to those who disobey. And believers are now given Israel’s titles: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people, called to declare his excellencies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priesthood of All Believers

Coming to Christ, the living stone, believers are built into one spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel’s titles were given to Gentile converts with no status at all.

Now: Once not a people, now God’s people; once without mercy, now shown mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 2 tells God’s new people who they are and how to live in a hostile world. Born again by the word, they strip off malice and crave the pure milk of the word (vv. 1–3). Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by men but chosen by God, they are built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood (vv. 4–8). They are now what Israel was called to be: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people (vv. 9–10). So, as exiles, they live such good lives that slanderers will glorify God (vv. 11–12), submitting to authorities for the Lord’s sake (vv. 13–17), slaves even to harsh masters (vv. 18–20). For Christ suffered for us, leaving an example, and bore our sins in his body on the tree; by his wounds we are healed, and strays have returned to the Shepherd of their souls (vv. 21–25).

So put away all malice. So, oun, therefore: because you have been born again and are called to love (1:22–23). Put away, apothemenoi, is the verb for stripping off clothing, as in James 1:21. These are the garments of the old family, and they no longer fit. A newborn is washed before it is fed. Malice, kakia, is ill will, the settled wishing of harm, the inner wickedness from which the rest grows.

And all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Look at the five items, because they have one thing in common: malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander. Every one is a sin against other people, and four of the five are done with words or with a face. Peter has just commanded earnest love from a pure heart (1:22); this is the list of what makes that impossible. Deceit, dolos, is guile, trickery, the bait on a hook that hides the barb. Hypocrisy, hypokrisis, is the actor’s mask, set deliberately beside the sincere, un-masked love of 1:22, which is the same word negated. Envy, phthonos, is the resentment of another’s good. And slander, katalalia, evil speaking, backbiting (James 4:11), was exactly what these readers were suffering from outside (2:12). Peter will not let a congregation being slandered do to each other what is being done to them. And note the word all, three times: all malice, all deceit, all slander. Strip off every trace. A church cannot have a little backbiting.

Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk. The image follows the birth: newly born people should have an appetite. Newborn infants, artigennēta brephē, are babies just born, and long for, epipothēsate, is a strong verb: crave, yearn for intensely. It is the noise a hungry baby makes, which is not a polite request. A newborn does not want milk among other things; it wants milk with its whole body, and it will not be distracted by a rattle. Spiritual, logikon, is related to logos, word: the milk is the word that gave them birth (1:23–25). And pure, adolon, is a play on the deceit, dolon, of verse 1: guileless, unadulterated, nothing mixed in. Put off the deceit; drink the milk with no deceit in it.

That by it you may grow up into salvation. Grow up, auxēthēte, be increased, mature. Into salvation: towards its final completion (1:5, 9). Peter’s use of milk is worth noting because it differs from Paul’s. In 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12–13 milk is the beginner’s diet, contrasted with solid food. Here it is not a stage to be outgrown but the food that produces growth. The goal is maturity, and the diet does not change. The oldest saint in the church is as dependent on the word as the newest convert, and should be as hungry.

If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good. This quotes Psalm 34:8: oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! It is a psalm Peter draws on repeatedly in this letter (3:10–12). Tasted, egeusasthe, means experienced. And the Lord in Psalm 34 is the LORD, Yahweh; here Peter applies it to Christ, the living stone of the next verse. He does it without comment, as though it were obvious that the LORD of David’s psalm is Jesus. And good, chrēstos, kind, gracious, sounds almost exactly like Christos in Greek. Peter may well intend the echo: you have tasted that the Lord is kind; you have tasted Christ. The argument is from experience: an appetite follows a taste. People who have genuinely tasted something good do not need to be persuaded to want more of it.

What it does not mean. Milk here does not mean elementary teaching, as in Hebrews 5:12–13 and 1 Corinthians 3:2. Here it refers to the whole word of God, which all believers, mature or young, must crave as eagerly as a baby craves milk.

What if I have no appetite for the Bible? Then do what a doctor would tell you to do with a child who has stopped eating: look for what is spoiling the appetite, and keep offering the food. Peter puts the two together: put away malice, deceit, envy and slander, and crave the milk. Unconfessed sin, a grudge, or a diet of constant distraction will kill spiritual hunger. Confess them. Then read a little, regularly, and ask God before you open it to show you Christ there. Read the Gospels if the rest is hard. Appetite often returns by eating; and the God who caused you to be born again is the one who gives his children hunger.

How do I actually put off slander and envy? By naming them honestly, and by replacing them. Notice when you start the sentence that begins, have you heard about…, and stop it. When someone in your church is praised and something in you shrinks, recognise it as envy and thank God aloud for the person instead. Ask whether what you are about to say would be said if the person were in the room. If there is a real grievance, take it to the person, not to others (Matthew 18:15). And remember that you are stripping off old clothes because you have new ones: Christ’s love for you leaves no need to diminish anyone else.

In a sentence. Therefore, get rid of all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander of every kind. Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.

On a Tuesday. Do you crave God’s word like a hungry baby craves milk? If not, ask God to increase your appetite, and feed on it daily this week. And watch your mouth in the same week: before each conversation about someone absent, ask whether it is malice, envy or slander dressed up as concern. The two go together. The tongue that stops feeding on others begins to taste the Lord.

For worship. He is good, and kind, and we have tasted it. We tasted it the day we first understood that the blood of Christ was for us; we taste it every time his word lands on a weary heart like milk on a hungry child. He does not ration his kindness. He feeds his newborn ones with the purest food in the universe, his own word, and he grows them, slowly and surely, until they are ready for the salvation he has prepared. And the LORD whom David tasted as a fugitive from Saul, feigning madness among the Philistines, has a name now: Jesus, whose kindness we have tasted at his table and will taste at his feast for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

As you come to him. The metaphor changes from infancy to masonry, and Peter builds a whole doctrine of the church out of one word. Come, proserchomenoi, means approach, draw near, and it is the word used for coming to God in worship (Hebrews 4:16; 10:22). The tense is present: keep coming. The Christian life is not a single visit to Christ at conversion, but a continual coming, morning by morning, prayer by prayer, Sunday by Sunday.

A living stone rejected by men. The phrase is a deliberate paradox. Stone is the deadest material there is, and Peter attaches the word he has been using of hope (1:3) and of the word of God (1:23). A stone that is alive, because it has been raised from the dead. Rejected, apodedokimasmenon, is a technical word: tested and rejected, declared unfit after examination. It comes from Psalm 118:22. Builders inspected stones before using them, and set aside the ones that would not do. The religious leaders examined Jesus, cross-questioned him, put him on trial, and threw him out (Mark 8:31; 12:10).

But in the sight of God chosen and precious. Chosen, eklekton, and precious, entimon, honoured, valuable, come from Isaiah 28:16. There is the letter’s whole theme in one line, and it is applied first to Christ. Two verdicts on the same person, running in opposite directions. Men rejected him; God chose and honoured him. And the readers, rejected in Pontus and Bithynia, are being told which verdict counts. Their Lord was rejected first, and the rejection did not have the last word.

You yourselves like living stones. Believers share Christ’s life; they too are living stones. And notice who is writing. Peter’s name means rock, and the Lord had said, on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18). If anyone could have claimed to be the foundation stone, it was him. He does not. Christ is the living stone, and Peter is one stone among many, built on him. Every believer, the slave and the apostle alike, is the same kind of stone.

Are being built up as a spiritual house. The passive matters: they are being built, oikodomeisthe, and the present tense says God is still at work on it. Not building themselves, and not assembling by choice. Someone is doing it. And the singular is the point. Not houses but a house, one structure. A spiritual house, oikos pneumatikos, is a temple made of people and indwelt by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Corinthians 3:16). The temple in Jerusalem was made of dead stones and would soon be thrown down. God’s new temple is made of living people, and it will never fall. A stone on its own is rubble; it becomes masonry only by being set against other stones. Peter is writing to scattered, isolated believers and telling them they are load-bearing parts of one building.

The quarry and the chisel. Think of how a stone gets into a wall. It is cut out of the rock where it lay, often with violence. It is shaped, the rough edges chipped off, until it fits. And then it is set in place, next to stones it did not choose, bearing weight it cannot see. Every Christian knows something of all three. Being dug out of the old life, being shaped by trials and by other people’s rough edges, and being set alongside believers who are not one’s natural friends: this is the Builder at work. He is not making a pile of separate statues. He is making a house for himself to live in.

To be a holy priesthood. Priesthood, hierateuma, is a body of priests. Not some believers, but all. This is the root of what the Reformers called the priesthood of all believers, and note how thoroughly it dismantles the old arrangement. In the temple there was a building, a priesthood and sacrifices, and ordinary people had access to none of them. They stood in the outer courts while the priests went in. Peter says the congregation is the building, is the priesthood, and offers the sacrifices (Revelation 1:6; 5:10). Every believer is a priest with direct access to God.

To offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Not animals, but praise and thanksgiving, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name (Hebrews 13:15); doing good and sharing what we have (Hebrews 13:16); our bodies given to God as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1); gifts for the gospel (Philippians 4:18); prayer (Revelation 8:3–4); and declaring his excellencies (v. 9). Acceptable, euprosdektous, means well-pleasing. And the last three words keep it from being self-important: acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Even the offerings of a priesthood need a mediator. Our praise is stained and our good works are mixed, and God receives them gladly because they come to him through the hands of his Son, our one great High Priest.

Where Christians differ: is there a special priesthood in the church? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches maintain an ordained priesthood that offers sacrifice on behalf of the people. Verdict: The New Testament teaches the priesthood of all believers. Every Christian is a priest, offering spiritual sacrifices directly to God through Christ, the one great High Priest. The church has elders and deacons, who lead and serve, but no priestly caste that mediates between God and the people (1 Timothy 2:5). Peter himself, the first leader of the apostles, describes himself as a fellow elder (5:1), and Christ, not Peter, as the stone on which the church is built.

What it does not mean. The priesthood of all believers does not mean there is no church leadership or no ordered ministry. God gives elders to teach and shepherd (5:1–4; Ephesians 4:11). It means no believer needs another human being to approach God for them.

If every believer is a priest, is there any place for ordained ministers? Every believer has direct access to God through Christ and offers spiritual sacrifices; there is no need for a priestly class to offer sacrifices for others, as in the Roman Mass. But the New Testament still gives elders to teach and shepherd the church (5:1–4). They are not priests between God and his people, but servants of the word among a priestly people.

Can I be a Christian without a church? Peter’s picture says no, not in any healthy sense. A living stone is not meant to lie in a field. Christ saves individuals, but he saves them into a house, and the New Testament knows nothing of believers who refuse to belong to a local congregation. If you have been hurt by a church, that is real and grievous, and you may need time and care. But the answer is a better church, not no church. Find a congregation that preaches Christ faithfully, commit to it, and let yourself be set in the wall, rough edges and all.

In a sentence. As you come to him, the living Stone, rejected by people but chosen by God and precious to him, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. You are a priest today, wherever you are. The sink, the desk, the hospital ward and the steering wheel are altars. Offer your praise aloud in the car. Offer your work as done for him. Offer a gift to someone in need. And on Sunday, look at the people around you and remember: this is the house God is building, and I am one stone in it, set beside these stones on purpose.

For worship. The stone the world threw away is the one God chose, and he is alive. He did not only die for us; he gathers us to himself, and fits us together, and makes us a dwelling for God by the Spirit. Where once only one man could enter the holy place once a year, now a whole people, slaves and fishermen and housewives, come boldly to the throne of grace every day. And every stammering prayer and every cup of water given in his name rises to the Father acceptable, because it passes through the hands of the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," and "A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it stands in Scripture: “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” and “A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.” They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.

For it stands in Scripture. Peter now stacks three stone texts from the Old Testament, two from Isaiah and one from the Psalms, and the effect is cumulative: this was always how it was going to go. The rejection of Jesus was not a surprise that the apostles had to explain away. It was written.

Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious. The first is Isaiah 28:16. The cornerstone, akrogōniaios, was the chief stone at the corner of the foundation that set the lines of the whole building: every wall was measured from it, every angle took its direction from it. If it was true, the house was true. And God himself laid it. In Isaiah’s day the rulers of Jerusalem were trusting in alliances with Egypt; God says, I am laying a stone of my own, and only those who build on it will stand.

And whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. Notice that Isaiah’s stone is a person: believes in him. Put to shame, kataischynthē, means disappointed, humiliated, let down. Those who trust Christ will never be let down, now or at the judgement (Romans 9:33; 10:11). And that is exactly the promise a slandered congregation needed. Their neighbours were shaming them. God promised that the shame would not stick.

So the honor is for you who believe. Honour, timē, is preciousness, value, related to the precious, entimon, of verse 6. The preciousness of Christ belongs to believers; they share his honour. Two readings are possible and both are true: to you who believe, he is precious; and the honour that is his is given to you. The people the world dishonours are those God honours, because they are joined to the stone he honours.

But for those who do not believe, The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The second text is Psalm 118:22. The Lord had quoted it of himself (Matthew 21:42), and Peter had quoted it before the Sanhedrin to the very builders who had done the rejecting: this Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone (Acts 4:11). He has been preaching this text for thirty years. The builders, the religious leaders, rejected him, but God made him the chief stone. Unbelief cannot overturn God’s choice. They can throw the stone out of the building site; God puts it back at the corner.

And A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense. The third text is Isaiah 8:14, and here the images collide deliberately. Stumbling, proskomma, and offence, skandalon, a trap, a snare, a cause of falling. The same stone is a foundation to some and an obstacle to others. Nothing about the stone changes; what differs is whether a man builds on it or trips over it. For unbelievers Christ is not a foundation but an obstacle, and they fall over him to their ruin (1 Corinthians 1:23). And no one can simply walk past this stone. It is set in the middle of the road of every human life. You will either build on Christ or fall over him.

They stumble because they disobey the word. Then the hard sentence. Disobey, apeithountes, means refuse to believe, refuse to be persuaded. Unbelief is disobedience to the gospel, because the gospel is a command to repent and believe. Read the order carefully, because it is often reversed. Peter gives the reason for the stumbling first, and it is disobedience: a real refusal, genuinely theirs.

As they were destined to do. Destined, etethēsan, means appointed, placed, set. God appointed that those who disobey the word would stumble. Their stumbling is both their own guilty choice and within God’s sovereign purpose. And it will not do to soften either half. Peter has already said these readers were chosen according to foreknowledge (1:2); he is not going to pretend the other side of that is nothing. What he does not do is make God the author of the disobedience.

Where Christians differ: does God destine people to unbelief? Some read this as teaching only that God appointed the consequence (stumbling) for those who freely choose to disobey. Verdict: The verse teaches that those who disobey stumble according to God’s appointment. God is sovereign over all things, including the rejection of Christ by unbelievers (Romans 9:18–22; Acts 4:27–28). Yet the stumbling is caused by their own disobedience, for which they are wholly responsible. God passes over some, leaving them in their sin, and justly appoints them to its consequences; he does not create unbelief in an innocent heart. The doctrine is to be handled with humility and reverence, not speculation, and it is set against the glory of the chosen in the next verse.

Does as they were destined to do mean that God destined some to disobey? Within the Reformed tradition some read it to mean that God appointed the stumbling as the consequence of disobedience: those who reject Christ are destined to stumble over him. Others read it more strongly: their disobedience itself fell within God’s purpose, as the verdict above holds. Either way, their stumbling is their own act, because they disobey the word, and God’s purpose stands behind it. No one in hell will be able to say that he wanted Christ and was refused.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone is prevented from believing who wants to believe. Whoever believes will not be put to shame. Unbelief is always a guilty refusal.

Should this make me worry that I or someone I love is destined to stumble? No. This verse is not given to make anyone examine God’s secret decree; it is given to explain why so many reject Christ, and to steady believers who are puzzled by it. If you are worried about whether you will stumble over Christ, the answer is simple: come to him now. Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. And for those you love who are stumbling, keep praying and keep speaking. You do not know who is chosen. Saul of Tarsus stumbled over this stone for years, and then was knocked down by it on the Damascus road and rose up a believer.

In a sentence. For Scripture says: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame.” Now to you who believe, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” and, “A stone that causes people to stumble and a rock that makes them fall.” They stumble because they disobey the message, which is also what they were destined for.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly where Christ still offends you: a command you would rather not obey, a doctrine you would rather not believe, a claim of his that embarrasses you in front of your friends. That is the place you are tempted to stumble rather than build. Bring it to him and build on it instead. And when you meet someone who mocks Christ, do not be shaken; it was written. Pray for them, and remember how many of the mockers of the first century became the church of the second.

For worship. He is the stone God laid in Zion, chosen and precious, and everything true in the universe takes its line from him. The builders of this world have inspected him and thrown him out a thousand times, and every time God has set him back at the head of the corner. Empires have stumbled over him and lie in pieces; philosophies have broken on him; and still he stands. And we, who would have tripped over him too, have been given eyes to see his worth, and built on him, and we shall never be put to shame. To us who believe, he is precious, more precious than all the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

But you are a chosen race. But you: and the contrast with the stumblers is total. Four titles follow, and every one is lifted straight out of what God said to Israel, most of it at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Isaiah 43:20–21). A chosen race, genos eklekton, is from Isaiah 43:20: a new people, not by physical descent but by God’s choice. Consider what it would have meant to hear that read aloud. These were people with no race worth naming, no priesthood, no nation, and no possessions worth the word. Peter tells them they are all four. And every title belonged first to Christ. He is the chosen one, the stone God chose (v. 4); he is the King who is also Priest; he is the Holy One of God; he is the beloved Son in whom the Father delights. These people are chosen because they are in the Chosen One, and everything God says of them he first said of him.

A royal priesthood. From Exodus 19:6: you shall be to me a kingdom of priests. Royal priesthood, basileion hierateuma: priests who belong to the King, and who share his reign (Revelation 1:6; 5:10). In Israel kings and priests were kept strictly apart; when King Uzziah tried to burn incense in the temple, he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Only one figure in the Old Testament was both, the mysterious Melchizedek, and the Messiah was promised to be a priest for ever after his order (Psalm 110:4). Christ is that King-Priest, and in him his people are both too.

A holy nation. Nation, ethnos: set apart for God, drawn from every nation. It is a nation without borders, without an army, without a capital on earth, and it is the only nation that will last for ever.

A people for his own possession. Laos eis peripoiēsin: a people acquired, treasured, as in Titus 2:14, and Exodus 19:5: you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples. The Hebrew word behind it, segullah, was used of a king’s private treasure, the jewels he kept for himself (1 Chronicles 29:3). God’s special treasure. People whom Rome counted as nobody are the crown jewels of the King of heaven.

That you may proclaim the excellencies of him. And the purpose is stated. Proclaim, exangeilēte, means announce, publish, tell out loud. Excellencies, aretas, are virtues, praises, mighty deeds (Isaiah 43:21). A priesthood exists to represent God to people and people to God, and Peter gives the whole congregation the job. The purpose of God’s people is to make known his greatness to the world. Not chiefly to have an identity, but to point at someone else’s.

Who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Called, kalesantos: God’s effectual call. Darkness: ignorance, sin, the realm of Satan (Acts 26:18; Colossians 1:13). Marvellous light, thaumaston phōs: wonderful light, the light of God’s truth and presence. A conversion described as a relocation, a total transfer, and it echoes the exodus again: out of Egypt, through the darkness of the plague, and into the land. And the light is marvellous, which means it never stops being surprising. Christians who have walked in it for fifty years are still astonished.

Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people. Then verse 10, which is Hosea, and it is the tenderest thing in the chapter. Hosea was commanded to name his children Not My People and No Mercy, as living signs of God’s verdict on Israel, and then promised that the names would be reversed: I will have mercy on No Mercy, and I will say to Not My People, you are my people (Hosea 1:6–10; 2:23). Paul applies the same passage to Gentiles (Romans 9:25–26), and so does Peter. He applies the reversal to Gentiles who never had the names in the first place, and the sentence structure carries it: once, now, twice over.

Once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy. Hosea’s daughter was named No Mercy (Hosea 1:6). Now mercy has come. Whatever these readers are being called in Pontus, their name has already been changed once. And the God who changed it does not change it back.

Where Christians differ: is the church a replacement for Israel, or are they two separate peoples? Dispensationalists keep Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with distinct promises; some speak of replacement theology, in which the church replaces Israel entirely. Verdict: Peter applies Israel’s titles directly to the mostly Gentile church. The church is not a separate people from Israel but the fulfilment of God’s purpose for Israel: one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, the true seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22; Romans 11:17–24). This is fulfilment, not mere replacement: believing Jews were the core of the church, and God continues to graft Jews back in through faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26).

Has the church replaced Israel? Peter applies Israel’s titles to the church, Jew and Gentile together, because the church shares Israel’s calling as the one people of God in Christ (Exodus 19:5–6; Ephesians 2:11–22). That does not mean that the Jewish people have no place in God’s purposes; Paul still expects many to be grafted back in (Romans 11:23–26), and Christians differ on how and when that will happen. It means that there is one people of God, and its centre is Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not make the church an ethnic or national people. It is a spiritual people from every nation. Nor does it mean believers may be proud; they were chosen by mercy alone.

I struggle with low self-worth. How does this help? It gives you a name that does not depend on how you feel, what others say, or how well you have done this week. God calls you chosen, royal, holy, treasured, and he says it to people who were once nobody. Your worth is not something you have to build; it is something he has declared and paid for. That does not make you better than anyone else, because all of it is mercy. But it does mean that the voices calling you worthless are lying. When they speak, answer with God’s words: once I was not a people, now I am God’s people; once I had not received mercy, now I have.

How do I proclaim his excellencies if I am not a preacher? By speaking of what God has done for you, naturally and honestly, in the ordinary conversations of life. Tell a friend what you are thankful for and why. Explain, when someone asks why you are different, what Christ means to you. Sing in church as if you meant it. Pray aloud with a struggling neighbour. Live in such a way that people ask (3:15). The excellencies of God are not a script for professionals; they are the testimony of everyone who has been brought out of darkness and can still remember what it was like.

In a sentence. But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, so that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

On a Tuesday. Read verse 9 aloud this morning as a description of yourself, slowly, title by title. Then go into the day as what you are. When you are treated as nobody, remember whose treasure you are. And find one moment this week to tell someone, in your own words, one excellency of the God who called you out of darkness: something he is, or something he has done.

For worship. He looked on people who were not a people, and made them his people. He looked on those who had no mercy, and gave them mercy. He reached into the darkness of Pontus and Bithynia, and into ours, and called us by name into a light so marvellous that we have never got used to it. Chosen, royal, holy, treasured: every title is a gift, every gift is mercy, and every mercy was bought with blood. The King has made beggars his priests, and the Light of the world has made his home in people who once sat in darkness, and no one in all the universe is so worthy to be praised.
verseByVerse.note: Titles once given to Israel at Sinai are now given to the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — Submission, and the Steps of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As foreigners and exiles, fight the desires that war against your soul, and live so well among unbelievers that their slander is silenced and they glorify God. Submit for the Lord’s sake to every human authority, even the emperor. Live as free people, as God’s servants. Slaves, submit even to unjust masters, because Christ suffered unjustly, leaving an example to trace. He did not retaliate, but entrusted himself to God. And he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
Entrusting Rather Than Suppressing

Christ did not revile in return; he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly. Then he did what no follower can copy: he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter spoke directly to slaves, and told believers to honour an emperor who would soon persecute them.

Now: Follow in his steps: do good, bear injustice without retaliation, and hand the case to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.

Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles. Beloved, agapētoi: Peter does not lecture strangers; he appeals to people he loves. Urge, parakalō, appeal, exhort, plead. And the two words from 1:1 and 1:17 return together. Sojourners, paroikous, resident aliens, and exiles, parepidēmous, temporary residents. Peter uses them as the ground of the ethics that follow. Your identity shapes your conduct: you do not belong here, so do not live like those who do. Behave like what you are.

To abstain from the passions of the flesh. Abstain, apechesthai: keep away from, hold yourself back. Passions of the flesh, sarkikōn epithymiōn, are the desires of sinful human nature: sexual sin, greed, gluttony, anger, pride (Galatians 5:19–21). Flesh in this sense does not mean the body, which God made and will raise, but the whole of fallen human nature turned in on itself.

Which wage war against your soul. Wage war, strateuontai, is to campaign, to fight as soldiers, as in James 4:1. The military image is deliberate in a letter about outside hostility. Peter has spent two chapters on what the neighbours are doing; here he names a nearer enemy, and it is inside the walls. That is a genuinely important pastoral point. A community under external pressure naturally locates all its danger outside, and Peter will not let them. Sinful desires are not harmless pleasures but enemy soldiers attacking your soul, conducting a campaign against the very soul whose salvation he has just described (1:9). Lust always presents itself as a friend. Peter tears the uniform off.

Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable. Then the outward face of the same holiness. Gentiles, ethnesin, here means unbelievers, the surrounding pagan society. And that is striking, since most of these readers were Gentiles; Peter has so thoroughly reclassified them as Israel that their old category is now the outsiders’ name. Honourable, kalēn, means good, beautiful, attractive. Not merely correct but winsome. Peter does not only want Christians to be blameless; he wants their lives to be lovely to look at.

So that when they speak against you as evildoers. Not if. The slander is assumed. Speak against, katalalousin, is the slander word from verse 1. Early Christians were accused of atheism, because they rejected the gods and had no images; of cannibalism, because rumours of eating someone’s body and drinking his blood leaked out from the Lord’s Supper; of incest, because they called each other brother and sister and greeted with a kiss; and of disloyalty to Rome, because they would not worship the emperor. They were bad for business too. Fifty years after this letter, Pliny, governor of these very provinces of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan that the temples had been almost deserted and the trade in sacrificial animals had collapsed because of the spread of the Christians. He tortured two slave women, whom the Christians called deaconesses, and found nothing but what he called a perverse and excessive superstition. He also reported that the Christians bound themselves by oath not to steal, commit adultery or break their word. Peter’s strategy had worked: even the persecutor had to admit that the slander was false. And the slander had been aimed at their Lord first. The charge his accusers brought to Pilate was that he was doing evil (John 18:30); he was condemned as an evildoer, and hung between two of them, and his life was the evidence that answered the charge.

They may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation. See, epopteuontes, means observe closely, watch over time: the slow watching of neighbours who are trying to find something wrong. Good deeds, kalōn ergōn, are again the beautiful works. The strategy is not argument but visibility, and Peter expects the slander to be defeated by the evidence of ordinary life. It is his Lord’s own instruction: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16). And the man writing had heard it on the hillside.

What is the day of visitation? A day when God comes, hēmera episkopēs, whether to save (Luke 19:44) or to judge (Isaiah 10:3). Some read it as the day of judgement, when even unbelievers will be forced to acknowledge that God’s people were right; the more likely reading is that pagans who have watched Christians’ good deeds will themselves be converted and glorify God when he visits them in mercy. So good lives can win slanderers to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good conduct will always prevent persecution. Jesus lived perfectly and was crucified. But good conduct removes legitimate grounds for accusation and can lead others to faith.

How do I fight a desire that feels overwhelming? Treat it as Peter does: as an enemy, not a part of you to be negotiated with. Abstain means keep away, so do not stand near the fire: remove the apps, change the route, avoid being alone with the bottle or the person. Tell a trusted Christian friend, because sin grows in the dark and shrinks in the light. When the desire comes, turn your mind to Christ and to what is promised (1:13); a greater love expels a lesser one. And when you fall, do not give up the war; confess, receive forgiveness, and get back up. The soldier who falls is not the one who loses. The one who changes sides is.

What if people speak badly of me even though I am doing good? Then you are in good company, and Peter has written this letter for you. Keep doing good, without bitterness. Do not spend your energy defending your reputation; let your life do the talking over time. If a specific accusation is false, you may correct it calmly. But leave the verdict to God, who sees, and to the slow work of evidence. Many people who slandered Christians in one decade were Christians in the next. Your patience may be the thing God uses to bring them to himself.

In a sentence. Dear friends, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to keep away from the sinful desires that wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among the unbelievers around you that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us.

On a Tuesday. Is there a neighbour or colleague who thinks badly of Christians? Let your good deeds this week give them reason to think again: be the most reliable person in the office, the kindest on the street, the one who does not join the mockery. And look honestly at the war inside. Which desire is camped closest to your soul at the moment? Name it, and take one concrete step today to cut its supply lines.

For worship. The Lord whose disciples were called atheists and cannibals is the one who went about doing good, and was called a glutton, a blasphemer and a friend of sinners, and was crucified between two thieves. He did not argue his way out of the slander; he loved his way through it, and on the third day God vindicated him. Now he lives in his people, and his beauty shines through the ordinary goodness of slaves and shopkeepers until even their persecutors bow and give glory to God. Every honourable life among unbelievers is a lamp lit from his.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.

Be subject for the Lord’s sake. Be subject, hypotagēte: submit, place yourselves under. It is a key word in this section (2:13, 18; 3:1, 5), and it describes taking one’s place willingly in an order God has made. And the first words carry the whole weight: for the Lord’s sake. Not because the state deserves it, not because it is competent, not even mainly from fear of punishment, but because he requires it. The motive is loyalty to Christ, who wants his people to honour God-given authority (Romans 13:1–7). The Lord himself submitted to a corrupt high priest’s court and to Pilate’s, for his Father’s sake.

To every human institution. Human institution, anthrōpinē ktisis: human creation, a human authority structure. Government is a human arrangement in its forms, monarchy or republic, council or parliament. But it is ordained by God in its existence: there is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1).

Whether it be to the emperor as supreme. Emperor, basileus, king. Supreme, hyperechonti, highest authority. Remember who the emperor was. This letter was most likely written in the early 60s, which means the man as supreme was Nero, who within a few years would be using Christians as living torches in his gardens, as the Roman historian Tacitus records, and under whom Peter himself would almost certainly die. That fact should govern how the verse is read. Peter is not describing an ideal government or making submission conditional on good behaviour. He is telling a persecuted minority to be model subjects of a ruler who will kill them. And the governors sent by him were men like Pilate, Felix and Festus, and later Pliny in Bithynia. Peter knew such men: a governor had sent his Lord to the cross.

To punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. The stated function is justice, restraining evil and rewarding good (Romans 13:3–4). And Peter, who had been flogged by the council in Jerusalem (Acts 5:40) and would be executed by Rome, states it anyway. He is describing the office rather than flattering the officeholders. Even imperfect government serves this purpose to a degree: a world with corrupt police is still safer than a world with none.

For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people. Put to silence, phimoun, means muzzle, gag, as one muzzles an ox. Ignorance, agnōsia, is lack of knowledge, and foolish, aphronōn, means senseless. The best answer to slander is a life that makes it obviously untrue, and Peter’s strategy is not to win the argument but to remove its material. Good citizenship silences slanderous accusations that Christians are subversive.

Where Christians differ: when may Christians disobey the government? Verdict: Christians must submit to governing authorities as a general rule, paying taxes, obeying laws and honouring officials (Romans 13:1–7). But when the government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, believers must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19–20; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Even then, they should accept the consequences peacefully, without violent rebellion, as Peter and the apostles did. Christians may also work through lawful means to change unjust laws.

The apostle who disobeyed. The limits are not spelled out here, but they exist and Peter knew them. It was he who told the Sanhedrin, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Submission is the settled posture; it is not unconditional, and where the state commands what God forbids the same apostle disobeyed and took the beating, rejoicing that he was counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). The pattern is the three young men before Nebuchadnezzar’s statue and Daniel at his open window: respectful, unbending, and willing to pay.

What it does not mean. It does not mean governments are always right, or that Christians must approve of everything rulers do. It means our basic posture is respect and submission, for the Lord’s sake.

What about a government I believe is wicked? Peter’s readers had one, and his instruction did not change. You may disagree with your rulers, vote against them, protest lawfully and speak the truth about them. You must still pray for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), pay your taxes, obey just laws and refuse to speak of them with contempt. The limit is not whether you like them, but whether they command you to sin. Where they do, you obey God, openly and peaceably, and accept the cost. A Christian’s politics should be marked by more respect, more prayer and less rage than his neighbour’s, because he knows who is really on the throne.

In a sentence. For the Lord’s sake, submit to every human authority: whether to the emperor, as the supreme authority, or to governors, who are sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to commend those who do right. For it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorant talk of foolish people.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your government leaders by name this week, including the ones you did not vote for, and obey the laws faithfully as service to Christ: the speed limit, the tax return, the planning rules. And notice how you speak about rulers, online and at the table. Would a pagan neighbour hear contempt or respect? Peter asks for respect towards Nero.

For worship. The kings of the earth rise and fall at his word. Nero had his day, and his gardens are dust, and the Lord he persecuted reigns at the right hand of God, King of kings and Lord of lords. We can submit to earthly rulers without fear because they are not the last authority; and we can defy them without hatred when we must, because their power was given from above. Every throne on earth is a footstool of his, and he has never yet lost control of a single one.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor at the time was probably Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.

Live as people who are free. Free, eleutheroi. It is an extraordinary thing to say to a group he has just told to submit to Nero, and to slaves, two verses later. Peter’s category of freedom is evidently not political. Christians are truly free: free from sin’s slavery, from the law’s condemnation, from the fear of man and of death (John 8:36; Galatians 5:1). Submission to authorities is not slavery but the free choice of those who serve God.

Not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil. Cover-up, epikalymma, means a veil, pretext or cloak, something thrown over what is underneath. The abuse is perennial: liberty in Christ invoked as permission, and Peter names it before anyone can try it (Galatians 5:13; Jude 4). Some might use Christian freedom as an excuse to disobey authorities or to indulge sin. A freedom that is used to do evil has already become a new slavery.

But living as servants of God. Servants, douloi, slaves. Free, and slaves, and the paradox is the resolution rather than the problem. True freedom is slavery to God (Romans 6:22). We are free from everything else in order to serve him. A man wholly owned by God is beyond the reach of anyone else’s ownership, which is precisely why a Christian slave in verse 18 can be told he is free. A fish is free in water, not out of it; a man is free in the service of the God who made him, and nowhere else.

The sons are free. Peter had learned this freedom beside the lake at Capernaum. Matthew tells how the collectors of the temple tax asked him whether his teacher paid it. Jesus asked him: from whom do kings take tax, from their sons or from others? From others, said Peter. Then the sons are free, Jesus answered; however, not to give offence, go to the sea, cast a hook, and in the first fish’s mouth you will find a coin; give it for me and for yourself (Matthew 17:24–27). There is verse 16 in a story: the Son of the King, owing nothing, paying anyway so as not to be a stumbling block, and including Peter in his freedom. Christians submit as free sons, and the Son pays their way.

Honor everyone. Then four short commands, and the arrangement repays attention. Honour, timēsate, means value, respect, treat as worth something. Universal, and it comes first. Every human being, made in God’s image, deserves respect, including slaves, pagans, enemies, and the neighbours who were slandering them. In a rigidly stratified society that was close to revolutionary.

Love the brotherhood. A narrower circle and a warmer word. Brotherhood, adelphotēs, is the family of believers. The family gets love, not merely honour. Respect for all; love for the family. Then fear God, phobeisthe: reverence, and it belongs to one being only (Proverbs 1:7). And the tense of the first command is different from the others in Greek, as though Peter were giving a headline (honour all) and then three ways of carrying it out in a continuing life.

Honor the emperor. And now look at what Peter has done. The emperor gets the same verb as everyone, honour, the identical word as the first command, and he does not get the verb reserved for God. In a world where emperors were being called divine and incense was burned to them, that is a carefully calibrated sentence. Christians would not offer incense to the emperor as a god, but they would respect him as a ruler. Caesar is worth exactly as much honour as the man who cleans his stables, and not one degree of the fear that belongs to God. My son, fear the LORD and the king (Proverbs 24:21); render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Matthew 22:21). This is the balance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must agree with or admire every leader. It means they show proper respect for the office and the person, while giving ultimate allegiance to God alone.

How can I honour someone I find contemptible? By remembering that honour is given because of what a person is before God, not because of how he behaves. Every human being bears God’s image, however defaced, and every ruler holds an office God has made. You can disagree firmly, oppose a policy, even refuse an unjust order, and still refuse to mock, sneer or dehumanise. Honour looks like courtesy in speech, fairness in description, prayer for the person, and a refusal to rejoice in his downfall. If Peter could honour Nero, we can honour our opponents.

In a sentence. Live as free people, but do not use your freedom as a cover for evil; live as God’s slaves. Show proper respect to everyone, love the family of believers, fear God, honour the emperor.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have failed to honour, a leader, a colleague, a stranger, the cleaner, the person in the news you love to despise? Show them respect this week, as one made in God’s image. And ask the opposite question too: is there anyone you fear more than God? That fear is the one that makes you less free.

For worship. He has set us free with the only freedom that lasts: free from guilt, free from the fear of death, free from the tyranny of other people’s opinions, free to serve him. And his service is perfect freedom. He alone is to be feared, because he alone is God, and the one who fears him need fear nothing else. Caesar is honoured as a man; Christ is worshipped as Lord. And one day every knee will bow, emperors first, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.

Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect. The word is oiketai, household slaves, domestic servants, and it should be said plainly that these were slaves, not employees, and that a large part of the population of those cities was enslaved. Many early believers were slaves. On slavery and Scripture, see also 1 Timothy 6:1–2. Respect, phobos, is literally fear: reverence, and very probably reverence towards God shown in how they serve.

Peter speaks to slaves. Note first who is being addressed. Peter speaks to slaves directly, as moral agents with choices to make. No Greek or Roman moralist did that; slaves were tools, and you addressed their owners. Aristotle called a slave a living tool. The mere fact of the sentence assumes a dignity the culture denied. And note what is not here. Peter gives no corresponding instruction to masters, as Paul does (Ephesians 6:9), most likely because these congregations had few or none. He is writing to the bottom of the ladder, and he gives the bottom of the ladder the longest passage in the chapter and the fullest picture of Christ.

Not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. Good, agathois, and gentle, epieikesin, reasonable, kind. Unjust, skoliois, means crooked, bent, harsh, perverse; our word scoliosis, a twisted spine, comes from it. There is the hard part, and Peter does not pretend otherwise. Unreasonable people, and the household slave had no appeal against one. Submission is not conditional on the master being kind.

For this is a gracious thing. Then the principle, stated twice. Gracious thing, charis, is literally grace: this is grace, the same word as God’s favour. Something commendable, something God approves, and more than that: something of God’s own grace is present in that endurance.

When, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. And the qualifier is essential. Mindful of God, dia syneidēsin theou, means because of conscience towards God, being conscious of God. What makes it grace is not the suffering, which by itself is merely misfortune, but that the sufferer is thinking about God while it happens. Endures, hypopherei, means bears up under. Sorrows, lypas, are pains and griefs, and unjustly, adikōs, is undeservedly. Peter is not commending endurance as a virtue in the abstract; he is describing a person who takes the injustice and holds God in view through it.

For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? Credit, kleos, is glory, fame, praise. Beaten, kolaphizomenoi, means struck with the fist, buffeted, the word used of the soldiers beating Jesus (Matthew 26:67). The distinction is drawn sharply, and it protects the teaching from being sentimental. Deserved trouble borne quietly is not a spiritual achievement. Enduring deserved punishment earns no praise. The grace is in the undeserved kind.

But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God. Suffering for doing right, without retaliation, pleases God. It reflects Christ. In the sight of God: the master may never notice, the household may never know, but the slave’s patience is seen in heaven.

What it does not mean. It does not endorse slavery, abuse or injustice. Nor does it forbid escaping abuse when possible (1 Corinthians 7:21), or seeking legal protection (Acts 16:37; 22:25). It addresses how believers should respond when they cannot escape unjust suffering: with patient endurance, trusting God, not with revenge. Victims of domestic abuse are not commanded to remain in danger.

Does this mean the Bible approves of slavery? Peter addresses believers as they actually were, without endorsing the system. Scripture lays the seeds of its overthrow: a slave is a beloved brother (Philemon 16), Paul urges slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Every human being is made in God’s image, and slave and master stand equal before Christ (Galatians 3:28). It was Christians, reading their Bibles, who led the campaigns that ended the slave trade.

And must a Christian employee today simply endure abuse? A modern employee is not a slave; he can leave, seek protection under the law and report wrongdoing. Peter’s principle still applies: do your work well and honour those over you, even when they are unfair, and do not repay evil with evil. But nothing here requires anyone to stay in an abusive situation or to cover up a crime.

What if I am being harmed at home? Then hear this clearly: this passage is not a command to stay in danger. Peter is addressing slaves who had no legal way out; you are not in that position, and the apostles themselves used the protection of the law (Acts 16:37). Abuse is a sin that God hates, and the church must never tolerate it or counsel anyone to endure it silently. Tell someone you trust, contact your church leaders and, if you are at risk, the police or an abuse support service. Seeking safety is not a failure of faith. What Peter forbids is revenge, not protection.

In a sentence. Slaves, in reverent fear of God submit yourselves to your masters, not only to those who are good and considerate, but also to those who are harsh. For it is commendable if someone bears up under the pain of unjust suffering because they are conscious of God. But how is it to your credit if you receive a beating for doing wrong and endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.

On a Tuesday. If you face unfair treatment at work this week, a credit stolen, a blame misplaced, a manager who is simply unreasonable, respond with patience and integrity, trusting God who sees. Before you react, ask: am I mindful of God right now? And be honest about the other half of Peter’s distinction. If the trouble I am in is my own fault, I am not a martyr; I need to repent, not to feel noble.

For worship. No one in the Roman world spoke to slaves as Peter speaks to them here, but the God of Peter had already done more. He sent his Son in the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7), to be struck with fists, mocked, and crucified by the death reserved for slaves. The Lord of glory took the lowest place, and so the lowest place is now holy ground. Every unseen act of patience in a harsh household is seen by him, and called grace, and will be rewarded on the day when the last are first.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
