For to this you have been called. Stop there, because it is one of the most difficult sentences in the New Testament. Called, eklēthēte: God’s effectual call (1:15; 2:9). To this: to patient endurance of unjust suffering. Peter does not say suffering is inevitable, or that God will bring good out of it, though both are true elsewhere. He says it is what they were called to, using the same word he has used of their calling out of darkness into marvellous light (2:9). One calling, two faces. Suffering is part of the Christian calling: it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake (Philippians 1:29; 2 Timothy 3:12).

Because Christ also suffered for you. And there is the reason. Suffered, epathen. For you, hyper hymōn, on your behalf: Christ’s suffering was substitutionary, for us, in our place, before it was anything else. The pattern is not arbitrary; it is his. A servant who suffers unjustly is not outside the will of God but walking where his Lord walked.

Leaving you an example. The word for example is hypogrammos, and it is beautifully concrete. It is the schoolmaster’s copybook line: the letters written at the top of the page for a child to trace underneath. A teacher would write the letters perfectly; the student, tongue between his teeth, traced them below, line after line, wobbling, until his hand learned the shape. Peter’s picture of discipleship is a child’s hand moving over the master’s letters. Christ wrote the pattern; we trace it.

So that you might follow in his steps. Follow, epakolouthēsēte, means follow closely, and steps, ichnesin, are footprints, tracks. It keeps the same idea: footprints to be trodden in, one at a time. Walk exactly where he walked, placing your feet in his footprints, the way a child walks behind his father in deep snow. And Peter, of all people, chose that image. He is the man who said he would follow to prison and to death, and did not, and whose restoration on the beach ended with two words: follow me (John 21:19). He knows exactly how hard tracing those letters is, and he is writing to slaves rather than to apostles.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is only an example. His death was first a substitution (v. 24), which no one can imitate. But having been saved by his substitution, we follow his example.

Why would God call anyone to suffer? Because he is making us like his Son, and his Son’s way to glory went through the cross (1:11; Hebrews 12:2). Suffering for doing good shows the world what Christ is like, refines faith (1:7), loosens our grip on this world, and prepares a weight of glory beyond comparison (2 Corinthians 4:17). God does not call us to suffer because he is careless of our pain, but because he has a purpose in it that is bigger than our comfort. And he does not call us to anything he has not done first. The footprints in front of you were made by bleeding feet.

In a sentence. This is what you were called to, because Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example to trace, so that you would follow in his footsteps.

On a Tuesday. Think of the hardest person or situation you will meet today. Before you go in, picture the copybook: Christ’s letters at the top of the page, your hand underneath. Ask, what would his hand do here? Then trace one letter: a gentle answer, a silence instead of a retort, a prayer for the person. You will wobble. Children always do. Trace it again tomorrow.

For worship. He did not send us down a road he had not walked. He went ahead, through Gethsemane, through the judgement hall, up the hill outside the city, leaving footprints in the dust and in his own blood. He suffered for us before he suffered as an example to us, and so the steps we follow lead not to death but through it to glory. Patient Teacher, he writes the letters again every morning, and he guides the trembling hands of his children until, at last, their lives spell out his name.

verseByVerse.quote: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.

He committed no sin. What follows is one of the most sustained meditations on Isaiah 53 in the New Testament, and Peter applies it, astonishingly, as workplace instruction for slaves. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth, is Isaiah 53:9 almost verbatim. And Peter is not repeating a doctrine he has read. He knew Jesus personally for three years, ate with him, slept beside him on the hills, saw him tired, hungry, angry and grieved, and testifies that in all of it he found no sin (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 John 3:5). His suffering was entirely unjust.

Neither was deceit found in his mouth. Deceit, dolos, guile, is the same word as verse 1. And the relevance to the readers is exact: a slave suffering unjustly is tempted above all to the two things named here, retaliation and the small deceits by which the powerless survive. Even under interrogation and torture, Jesus spoke only truth. He did not lie his way out of a trial that would kill him.

When he was reviled, he did not revile in return. Then verse 23, and Peter is describing something he watched. Reviled, loidoroumenos, is insulted, verbally abused. At his trial and on the cross he was mocked, spat on, blindfolded and struck, and told to prophesy who hit him (Matthew 26:67–68; 27:39–44). He did not answer insult with insult. Peter was in the courtyard that night, close enough for the Lord to turn and look at him (Luke 22:61). The imperfect tenses in Greek suggest sustained action: it kept coming, and the silence kept holding.

When he suffered, he did not threaten. Threaten, ēpeilei, is to warn of vengeance. That is the telling one, because a threat is the last weapon of somebody who has run out of others. And Christ, uniquely, was not out of options. He could have called twelve legions of angels and said so (Matthew 26:53). Instead he prayed for his executioners: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Peter had drawn a sword in the garden. He learned from his Master’s silence what courage really was.

But continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Then the positive, and this is the hinge of the whole passage. The verb, paredidou, means to hand over, to deposit, and it is imperfect: kept handing over, again and again, through the trial and the flogging and the nails. His last words were the same act: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46). And that is the mechanism, which the passage would be cruel without. He was not suppressing the desire for justice; he was transferring it. The case was not dropped; it was handed to a Judge who would hear it properly. Which is precisely what a slave with no court can do, and it is why Peter can ask this of people with no other recourse. Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus never spoke out against evil. He denounced hypocrisy (Matthew 23) and challenged an unjust blow (John 18:23). But he did not retaliate personally or seek revenge.

Does entrusting myself to God mean I must not want justice? No. Wanting justice is right; God wants it more than you do. What Peter forbids is taking vengeance into your own hands. Entrusting means placing the case, with all its pain, in the hands of the Judge who sees everything and will put every wrong right, either at the cross for those who repent or at the judgement for those who do not. That is what frees you from bitterness. You do not have to carry the grievance, nurse it or settle it. You hand it over, and when it comes back to your mind, you hand it over again.

Can I still speak up or report wrongdoing? Yes. Jesus himself asked the officer why he struck him (John 18:23), and Paul appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). Speaking the truth, reporting a crime, seeking protection, or using lawful complaint procedures is not revenge. The difference is in the heart and the method: justice sought through proper means, without hatred, and willing to leave the outcome with God, rather than insult answered with insult and harm answered with harm.

In a sentence. He never sinned, and no lie was ever found on his lips. When they hurled insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly.

On a Tuesday. When someone insults or wrongs you this week, do not retaliate. Hand your case to God, who judges justly. Say it in words if it helps: Father, I give you this. You saw it. You will judge rightly. Then, if the thought returns at three in the morning, do it again. Christ handed over his case continually. So may you.

For worship. They spat in his face, and he did not curse them. They hammered nails through his hands, and he prayed for them. The one who could have ended the world with a word kept silence, and kept trusting his Father, all the way to the last breath. There has never been strength like that: perfect power under perfect control, for love. And the Father who judges justly did not fail him. On the third day the verdict came, and the silent Lamb was declared the Son of God with power. We hand our small wrongs to the same Judge, and he will not fail us either.

verseByVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

He himself bore our sins. And here Peter steps decisively past example. Christ has been the pattern for four verses; now he does something no follower can imitate. He himself, autos, is emphatic: no one else. Bore, anēnenken, means carried up, took up, offered up, echoing Isaiah 53:4, 11–12, and it is the verb used in the Greek Old Testament for carrying a sacrifice up to the altar. He carried our sins and their penalty (Hebrews 9:28). This is substitutionary atonement: our sins were laid on him, and he bore the punishment we deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6).

In his body on the tree. In his body anchors it. Not a spiritual transaction conducted elsewhere but sins carried in a physical body, up a hill, on a specific afternoon. Tree, xylon, wood, is the cross, and it is not a poetic word for it. It is the term from Deuteronomy 21:23: a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God. Peter used the same phrase preaching in Acts (5:30; 10:39), and it is his settled way of saying that Christ went under the curse. Paul draws the same line from the same verse of Deuteronomy: the one hanged on the tree became a curse in our place, to buy us out from under the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13).

That we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Then the purpose. Die to sin, tais hamartiais apogenomenoi, is literally having ceased to exist with respect to sins, having departed from them. Christ’s death breaks sin’s power over us; we are united with him in his death (Romans 6:2–11). Live to righteousness: a new life of obedience. The substitution has a moral aim. He did not bear sins so that we could continue in them, and Peter has been arguing for two chapters that the atonement produces holiness rather than excusing its absence. The purpose of the cross is not only forgiveness but transformation.

By his wounds you have been healed. This is Isaiah 53:5, and the word for wounds, mōlōps, is singular in Greek: the welt, the bruise, the swollen mark left by a lash. Peter is writing to household slaves. Many of them had such marks on their own backs, and he tells them that the marks on his are what healed them. Healed, iathēte, in context means spiritual healing from sin: verse 25 goes straight on to straying sheep returning. For a beaten slave the image would have gone in like a nail: he has been where you are, and his stripes did what yours never could.

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise physical healing now? Some teach that physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement, so that believers can claim it now by faith. Verdict: In context, Peter speaks of healing from sin: we were straying, now we have returned; we have died to sin. Christ’s atonement does secure the ultimate healing of our bodies at the resurrection (Romans 8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and God may heal in answer to prayer now (James 5:14–15). But physical healing is not guaranteed in this life; believers still get sick and die. The healing promised now is the healing of the soul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s death merely shows us how to suffer. It actually removed our sins by bearing their penalty. Penal substitution is at the heart of this verse.

How can one man bear the sins of millions? Because of who he is. A mere man could at best die for his own sins. But Christ is the eternal Son of God made man, of infinite worth and dignity, so that his one sacrifice is of infinite value (1:19). And he was sinless, so he had no debt of his own to pay. The Father laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6), and he bore it fully, so that God is just in forgiving everyone who trusts him (Romans 3:26). The question is not whether his death is enough, but whether you are resting on it.

If Christ bore my sins, why do I still feel guilty? Sometimes because there is a sin you have not yet confessed; then confess it, and you will be forgiven (1 John 1:9). But often believers feel guilty over sins Christ has already carried, because the conscience is slow to believe the gospel. Then the answer is not to do penance, but to look at the cross. Your sins were really borne, in his body, on the tree. God does not punish the same sin twice. When guilt returns over forgiven sin, answer it with this verse, out loud if necessary: he himself bore my sins.

In a sentence. He himself carried our sins in his body on the cross, so that we might die to sins and live for righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

On a Tuesday. Name one sin you are still carrying, either as guilt or as habit. If it is guilt, lay it at the cross: he bore it, it is gone. If it is habit, remember the purpose clause: he bore it so that you might die to it. Do not try to fight it as a man still under its curse, but as a man already freed, who is learning to live the new life he was bought for.

For worship. He himself. Not an angel, not a lamb from the flock, not a better man than us, but the Son of God himself, in his own body, on a cursed tree, carrying up to the altar the whole weight of our sins. The welts on his back were for the welts on ours; the curse he bore was the curse we earned. And from that tree flows healing for every soul that comes. We were dead in sin, and now we live to righteousness, and we will spend eternity looking at the scars by which we were healed.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

For you were straying like sheep. Isaiah 53:6 again, and Peter keeps the prophet’s picture: all we like sheep have gone astray, each turning to his own way. Straying, planōmenoi, is wandering, lost, and the tense describes a settled condition rather than an incident. Straying was what they were doing, continuously. And sheep do not run away deliberately. They drift, head down, one mouthful at a time, until they look up and the flock is gone. They wander without realising the danger: helpless, defenceless, lost, and with no sense of direction to get them home.

But have now returned. Returned, epestraphēte, can be read as passive: you were turned back. That fits everything Peter has said about being caused to be born again (1:3) and called out of darkness (2:9). Sheep are not famous for finding their own way home. They returned because they were turned, by the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost until he finds it, and lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:3–7). I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed (Ezekiel 34:16).

To the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. Two titles, and both are chosen with care for these readers. Shepherd, poimēn, is the tender one, and it carries Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 and John 10 with it: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Peter will call him the Chief Shepherd (5:4). Overseer is episkopos, the guardian, the one who watches over and cares for; the same word translated bishop when it names a church officer. Peter gives the title first to Christ, and he will call himself merely a fellow elder in chapter 5. Jesus is the true Overseer of his people, over all human overseers (5:2–4).

Peter had strayed. And of everyone in the New Testament, Peter had the most reason to write this sentence. He had strayed himself, spectacularly and in public, and he had been turned back, by a look across a courtyard and a charcoal fire on a beach, where he was asked three times whether he loved his Lord and then told three times to feed the sheep (John 21:15–17). So the chapter that began with newborn infants craving milk ends with a shepherd who goes after strays. Both images are about being kept alive by someone else’s care, which is the only thing Peter has offered these people from the start.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the sheep returned by their own initiative. The passive voice shows that they were brought back. Yet they truly returned, by faith and repentance.

What if I have wandered since I became a Christian? Then this verse is for you too. The Shepherd does not only fetch sheep once; he goes on watching over their souls, and he brings back his own when they stray. Peter wandered after three years at Jesus’ side, and was restored. Do not stay away out of shame, as if you had to clean yourself up before coming home. Sheep are carried back, not marched. Confess where you have gone, turn back to him today, and find a faithful church where you can be shepherded. He has not stopped being the Overseer of your soul.

In a sentence. For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have been brought back to the Shepherd and Guardian of your souls.

On a Tuesday. Think of the direction your heart has drifted this year, one mouthful at a time: a habit, a coldness, a distraction. Look up. Where is the flock? Then turn, today, towards the Shepherd. And think of someone you know who has wandered from Christ. Pray for them by name, and ask whether the Shepherd might want to use your voice to call them home.

For worship. We were lost, and did not even know it, grazing our way towards the cliff edge. And he came: the Shepherd who is also the Lamb, who laid down his life for the sheep and took it up again. He found us, and carried us home on his shoulders, and called his friends to rejoice. Now he watches over our souls by day and night; he never sleeps, never loses count, never gives up on a straying one. We are safe because we are his, and we are his because he came looking.

3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview: Chapter 3 completes the household instructions for wives and husbands (vv. 1–7), calls the whole church to repay evil with blessing and to give a gentle reason for its hope (vv. 8–17), and grounds everything in Christ (vv. 18–22): his once-for-all death, his proclamation to the spirits in prison, his resurrection and his ascension to God’s right hand, with every power subject to him. The movement is from the household to the cosmos. Christ’s victory over every power is the ground for enduring any unjust suffering.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wives are to submit to their own husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their lives. Their beauty should be inward, a gentle and quiet spirit, precious to God, like the holy women of old who hoped in God and did not give way to fear. Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding, honouring them as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that their prayers are not hindered.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading This Passage Rightly

The Christ-pattern applies to wives and husbands alike. A believing wife may win an unbelieving husband by her conduct; a husband must honour his wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A woman converted without her husband was in a precarious position.

Now: This is a text about witness in marriage, never about tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 3 continues the theme of godly submission and suffering. Wives are to submit to their husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their lives rather than by words, adorned with the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, like Sarah (vv. 1–6). Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding and honour, as co-heirs of grace (v. 7). All are to be united and tender, repaying evil with blessing (vv. 8–12). If they suffer for doing right, they are blessed; they honour Christ as Lord and are ready to explain their hope gently (vv. 13–17). For Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God; made alive in the Spirit, he proclaimed to the spirits in prison from Noah’s day (vv. 18–20). Baptism now saves, not by washing the body, but as the appeal of a good conscience to God, through the resurrection of Christ, who reigns over all powers (vv. 21–22).

Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands. Likewise, homoiōs, in the same way, ties this to what precedes, and that matters for reading it rightly. Peter has just described Christ, who did not revile in return and kept entrusting himself to the just Judge (2:23). What follows is that pattern applied: first to citizens (2:13), then to slaves (2:18), now to wives, and in verse 7 to husbands. Nobody in the household is exempt. Be subject, hypotassomenai, is the ordering word Peter used of citizens and the state, and will use of the whole congregation towards its elders and one another (5:5). It describes a voluntary, respectful following of a husband’s lead (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18; Titus 2:5). It is not a claim about worth; verse 7 will call her a fellow heir. And it is not submission to men in general. Your own husbands, tois idiois andrasin: one’s own husband, and no one else.

So that even if some do not obey the word. The situation is specific, and Peter addresses the hard case. Do not obey the word, apeithousin tō logō, means they disbelieve the gospel. In that world a wife was expected to take her husband’s gods; Plutarch advised that a wife should worship only the gods her husband believed in and shut the door to strange rites. A woman who had become a Christian alone had done something socially outrageous and was in a genuinely precarious position, with little legal recourse and often no way out.

They may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives. Then the purpose, and it is evangelistic. Won, kerdēthēsontai, means gained, won over, the term Paul uses for winning converts (1 Corinthians 9:19–22). The aim is her husband’s conversion. Peter is giving a woman with little power a strategy that might actually save the man she is married to. Without a word, aneu logou, is the striking phrase, and it is realistic. The gospel word has probably already been heard and rejected; she has said it, and saying it again will not help. Nagging, preaching at the dinner table and leaving tracts on his pillow will only harden him. What is left is the silent sermon of a godly life: the thing he cannot argue with. And this is the likewise at work. The Lord who won these women was the one who, when reviled, did not revile in return (2:23), and who stood silent before his accusers like a sheep before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). A wife’s patient conduct in a hostile home is a copy of his, traced in a kitchen.

When they see your respectful and pure conduct. See, epopteusantes, is the word from 2:12: observe closely, watch over time. A life observed daily at close quarters over years. Respectful, en phobō, is literally in fear: reverence towards God, which shows itself in respect for her husband. Pure, hagnēn, is chaste, holy. A husband who is watching for hypocrisy finds a wife who is kinder than before, more honest, more faithful, more joyful, and who does not despise him. Over time that is very hard to resist. Augustine’s mother Monica, married to a hot-tempered pagan, Patricius, won him to Christ before his death by exactly this, as her son records in his Confessions.

Where Christians differ: does wifely submission belong only to ancient culture? Egalitarians argue that Peter is giving missionary advice suited to a patriarchal culture, and that mutual submission without distinct roles is the Christian ideal today. Verdict: Peter’s concern is indeed partly missional, but he grounds the instruction in the example of holy women of the Old Testament (v. 5), and Paul grounds it in Christ and the church and in creation (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). The complementarian view holds that husband and wife are equal in worth and co-heirs of grace (v. 7), with distinct roles: the husband leads with sacrificial love, the wife follows with respect and strength. Submission never requires sin (Acts 5:29), never means enduring abuse, and never makes the wife inferior.

Does this apply to all Christian wives, or only those with unbelieving husbands? It is the pattern for all wives, as Paul also teaches (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18), and Peter points to the holy women of old (v. 5); here he applies it to the hard case of an unbelieving husband. Submission is given to a husband in his rightful role, as to the Lord. It never means obeying a command to sin (Acts 5:29), and it never requires a wife to endure abuse; she may seek safety and help from the church and the law.

This is not a text about tolerating abuse. It should be said plainly. Peter is describing witness within a marriage, not endurance of violence; the same letter tells husbands their prayers will be blocked if they mistreat their wives, and Scripture everywhere sets God against those who oppress the vulnerable. Anyone using verse 1 to keep a woman in danger is using it against its own author. Headship in Scripture is never a licence to dominate; it is the call to lay down one’s life, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). A man who uses his wife’s submission as a weapon has abandoned the very pattern that makes her submission possible.

What does submission actually look like in an ordinary Christian marriage? It looks like a wife who respects her husband in what she says to him and about him, supports his leadership rather than undermining it, and is willing to let him make the final decision when the two of them, having talked and prayed, still disagree. It does not mean she has no opinions, no voice or no gifts; the wife of Proverbs 31 runs a business and speaks with wisdom. It does not mean she obeys every man, or that she must stay silent about sin. And it is never one-sided: her husband is called to love her as Christ loved the church, which is a far heavier burden. Submission is a free gift, given to the Lord, through a husband.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a wife must abandon her faith to please her husband. She is to remain a Christian, which itself was a form of non-submission in that culture. Nor does it mean wives must never speak about Christ; it means their lives should do most of the speaking.

I am married to an unbeliever and it has been many years. Should I give up hope? No. Peter gives this word precisely because the wait can be long. Keep praying; keep loving; keep living the gospel in front of him. You are not responsible for his conversion, which is God’s work, but you may be the means God uses, and many husbands have come to Christ after decades. Find support in your church; you were never meant to carry this alone. And remember that your faithfulness is precious in God’s sight now, whether or not you see the outcome. Paul says the unbelieving husband is in some sense made holy because of his wife (1 Corinthians 7:14), and that you do not know whether you will save him (7:16): there is room for hope.

In a sentence. In the same way, wives, follow your own husbands’ lead, so that if any of them do not believe the word, they may be won over without words by the behaviour of their wives, when they see the purity and reverence of your lives.

On a Tuesday. Wives with unbelieving husbands: pray daily for your husband, and let your love, respect and joy be your strongest witness. Notice when you are tempted to win the argument rather than the man, and let the argument go. All wives: think of one way this week to show your husband respect in front of others, and one area where you have been resisting his lead out of pride rather than conscience.

For worship. He is the one who submitted first. The eternal Son, equal with the Father in glory, came not to do his own will but the will of him who sent him, and was not made less by it. He did not win us with arguments, but with a life lived before our eyes and a death we could not explain away. And he still wins the hardest hearts by the quiet witness of his people. In the homes where his name is mocked and his daughters live faithfully for years, he is at work, unseen, and the day is coming when many a husband will stand before him with a wife who prayed him there.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious.

Do not let your adorning be external. Adorning, kosmos, means ornament, decoration, arrangement, and our word cosmetic comes from it. External, exōthen, means outward. Peter is not saying a woman should not care how she looks. He is speaking of where a woman’s adorning is located: what she is counting on to make her worth looking at.

The braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear. Three items are named, and they were the recognised display of a wealthy Roman woman. Fashionable women wore towering, elaborate hairstyles, woven with gold threads and pearls; it took hours and a slave to do it, and the portrait busts of empresses show it. Jewellery and expensive clothing displayed status, as in 1 Timothy 2:9. Peter is not forbidding clothes, since the sentence would then forbid the third item absolutely. He is warning against making appearance the main thing.

But let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart. The hidden person of the heart, ho kryptos tēs kardias anthrōpos, is the inner self, character, who you really are when no one is looking. The contrast is outer and visible against inner and hidden, and note that Peter does not tell her to stop adorning herself. He tells her to move the adornment.

With the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit. That word imperishable, aphthartos, again: the inheritance (1:4), the seed (1:23), and now this. Peter keeps setting one thing beside everything that decays, and hair and gold and cloth all belong to the perishing side. Outward beauty fades; inner beauty lasts for ever. Gentle and quiet needs rescuing from a caricature. Gentle is praus: the word for strength under control, used of a broken-in horse, and the word the Lord uses of himself: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). It means meek, not self-assertive, not grasping. Quiet, hēsychios, means settled, tranquil, not agitated or anxious. Neither word means timid, silent or without opinions. Not a personality type, quiet versus loud, but a heart at rest in God. A noisy, laughing, talkative woman can have a quiet spirit; a silent one can be seething.

A composure that does not depend on circumstances. And it is a description of exactly what such a woman most needed. A Christian wife in a hostile household, unable to argue and unable to leave, is offered composure that does not depend on her circumstances improving. Gentleness and quietness are not weakness; they are what fear and anger look like when they have been handed over to God.

Which in God’s sight is very precious. There is the point of the whole paragraph. Very precious, polytelēs, very costly, is the word used of the expensive perfume poured on Jesus’ head (Mark 14:3). She is in a house where she is not valued and a society that valued the braided hair; Peter tells her what she looks like from the one perspective that will still be there in a thousand years. And precious is what Christ himself is called in 2:4. God values inner beauty more than all the jewellery in the world.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid braided hair, jewellery or nice clothes entirely; otherwise it would forbid the clothing you wear too. It forbids making outward appearance the main focus. Nor does it apply only to women; men too should be adorned with gentleness.

Is it wrong to care about how I look? No. God made beauty, and caring for your appearance in a way that is modest, appropriate and not extravagant honours him. The danger is when appearance becomes the place you look for your worth, the thing that consumes your time, money and thoughts, or a way of competing with others. Ask: how much of my time and money goes on the outside, and how much on the hidden person of the heart? Am I more anxious about a bad hair day than about an unkind word I spoke? The aim is not to neglect the body but to put it in its place.

How does someone become gentle and quiet in spirit? Not by suppressing your personality, but by bringing your fears and frustrations to God until they lose their grip. A quiet spirit grows from trust: the more you are convinced that God is in control and loves you, the less you need to fight, control or worry. Spend time in his presence. Bring him your anxieties specifically (5:7). Learn from Christ, who called himself gentle and lowly. And when you notice agitation rising, a sharp word, a need to have the last word, take it as a signal to pray rather than to push.

In a sentence. Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles, gold jewellery or fine clothes. Instead, it should be the beauty of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight.

On a Tuesday. Before you look in the mirror tomorrow morning, look at your heart: what is agitating it, what fear is loudest. Give that to God first. Then, when you get dressed, do it gladly but briefly, and spend at least as long on the hidden person as on the visible one. And notice who in your church has the beauty Peter describes. Often it is an elderly woman nobody would put on a magazine cover. Tell her.

For worship. The most beautiful person who ever lived had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isaiah 53:2). His beauty was all within: gentle and lowly in heart, strong enough to be silent, secure enough to serve. And on the cross that hidden beauty was poured out like costly perfume. The God who sees in secret prizes the hidden heart, and he is making his people beautiful from the inside out, with a beauty that will not wrinkle or fade, until they shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.

For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves. Peter appeals to precedent. Holy women: the godly women of the Old Testament, like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, Hannah, Ruth. And note the phrase he uses of them: they hoped in God. That is the source of the composure just described. These were not naturally placid women; they were women whose expectation was fixed somewhere secure. Their hope was not in their husbands or their beauty but in God, and that gave them the security to submit.

By submitting to their own husbands. Their adornment was a godly submission flowing from hope in God. It was not resignation, and it was not fear; it was the confident trust of women who knew who was really in charge of their lives.

As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. The reference is to Genesis 18:12, where Sarah, told she will have a son at ninety, laughs to herself and refers to her husband as my lord. Lord, kyrios, master, sir, was the ordinary courteous term of that world. Even in her private thoughts, she spoke of him with respect. And be honest that Sarah is a slightly surprising example, and the honesty helps rather than hurts. She laughed at God’s promise; she gave Hagar to Abraham and then dealt harshly with her (Genesis 16:5–6; 21:10); she was not a model of quiet submission throughout. She was strong-willed and spoke frankly, and on one occasion God told Abraham to listen to her: whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you (Genesis 21:12). She was no doormat. Peter is not holding up a flawless woman but pointing to one whose hope was in God despite everything, which is precisely the encouragement a struggling wife needs.

Sarah’s journey. Think what Sarah’s hope cost her. She left her home in Ur and then Haran with a husband following a God she could not see, to a land she did not know. She lived in tents for decades. Twice Abraham passed her off as his sister to save his own skin, and twice God protected her (Genesis 12; 20). She waited twenty-five years for a promised son. Her submission was not to a perfect man; it was to an imperfect one, trusting a perfect God. And God honoured her: she is named in Hebrews 11 among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:11), the mother of the promised line.

And you are her children. Children, tekna, here daughters. The same move Peter has made all through the letter: Gentile believers are given Israel’s ancestry. As believers are Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7), Christian women become Sarah’s daughters by following her example of faith. A former pagan wife in Cappadocia, with no Jewish blood at all, is told she belongs in the family of the mother of Israel.

Children of the free woman. Sarah matters because of the son she bore. Isaac, whose name means laughter, was born when it was impossible, by God’s promise alone, and through his line came the Christ. Paul reads Sarah the same way: believers are children of the free woman, children of promise like Isaac, not children of the slave (Galatians 4:28–31). So to be Sarah’s daughter is more than to copy her manners. It is to share her son’s kind of birth, by promise and not by human strength, which is exactly what Peter said of his readers at the start: born again of imperishable seed (1:23). Every one of Sarah’s daughters is a miracle child of the Messiah who came from her line.

If you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening. Then the condition, and the second half of it is the surprise. Do good, agathopoiousai; fear, phoboumenai, be afraid; frightening, ptoēsis, terror, intimidation, alarm. That is not what we expect after a paragraph on gentleness and quietness. Peter’s picture of a godly wife ends in courage. The Greek echoes Proverbs 3:25: do not be afraid of sudden terror. Christian wives with pagan husbands faced real threats. Submission is not fear-driven. Her composure is not fragility; she is not gentle because she is afraid. A woman who has hoped in God can be quiet in a hostile house precisely because there is nothing left in it that frightens her, including her husband’s anger.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wives must use the word lord for their husbands today. The principle is respect, not a particular form of words. Nor does it mean Sarah was perfect; she also laughed in unbelief and mistreated Hagar.

What if my husband frightens me? Then Peter’s words, do not fear anything that is frightening, are a call to trust God, not to stay in danger. If your husband threatens, hits, controls or terrifies you, that is abuse, and God hates it. Submission never requires you to endure it, and you should not keep it secret. Tell a trusted friend and your pastor or elders, and if you are in danger, contact the police or an abuse helpline and get to a safe place. A godly church will support and protect you, and will call your husband to repentance. Seeking safety is not a failure of faith or of submission; it is what the courage Peter describes may look like.

In a sentence. This is how the holy women of the past who put their hope in God used to make themselves beautiful: by following their own husbands’ lead, like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him her lord. You are her daughters if you do what is right and do not give way to fear.

On a Tuesday. What fear is controlling you? Bring it to God, put your hope in him, and do what is right. Ask where your hope is really placed: in your husband changing, in your children turning out well, in your health holding, or in God. Then do the next right thing in front of you, gently and unafraid, as a daughter of Sarah.

For worship. The God of Sarah keeps his promises to women who laugh in disbelief. At her tent door he asked, is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14), and two thousand years later his angel gave the answer to a girl in Nazareth: nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). He has never failed a woman who hoped in him. He sees the wife in the hostile home, the widow, the woman waiting for decades; he counts her tears and names her among his heroes. And the Son of his impossible promises has overcome the world, so his daughters need fear nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

Likewise, husbands. The same word that opened the paragraph to wives, homoiōs, and it puts the man under the same Christ-pattern. In a culture where a husband’s authority was essentially unquestioned, the mere existence of a command to him is remarkable. Peter gives him one verse to the wives’ six, which is not a measure of importance but of who most needed the encouragement, perhaps because fewer husbands in these congregations were believers, or because the wives were in the harder place. But the one verse is very heavy.

Live with your wives in an understanding way. Live with, synoikountes, means dwell together, share a home, and it includes the whole of married life, the sexual relationship among it. In an understanding way is literally according to knowledge, kata gnōsin. It requires him to know her: to have studied this particular woman well enough to live with her intelligently, her needs, her feelings, her fears and concerns, her gifts and her burdens. That is a lifetime’s work and it cannot be done at a distance, which rules out the husband who is present in the house and absent from the marriage.

Showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel. Showing honour, aponemontes timēn, means assigning honour, paying respect, giving her what is her due. The phrase weaker vessel, asthenesterō skeuei, has been misused and needs stating carefully. Vessel is used of both of them, God’s containers (2 Timothy 2:21): she is the weaker of two vessels, so he is a vessel too. Weaker most likely refers to physical strength, and perhaps to social vulnerability in a world where women had few rights. Not weaker morally, intellectually or spiritually. And see what Peter does with it. The weakness is given as the reason for honour, not for contempt or command. Precisely because she is more vulnerable to him, he owes her more deference. That inverts the ordinary logic of power completely. Husbands must not exploit their greater strength, but use it to protect and honour, as a man handles fine porcelain with care, not because it is worth less than an iron pot but because it is worth more.

Since they are heirs with you of the grace of life. Fellow heirs, synklēronomois, co-heirs, joint heirs: equal standing, equal inheritance, the same imperishable estate of 1:4. Spiritually, husband and wife are completely equal before God, inheriting the same eternal life (Galatians 3:28). Whatever verse 1 means, it cannot mean she is worth less, and Peter has settled that inside the same paragraph. Distinction of roles does not mean distinction of worth. One day he will stand beside her before the throne, and the King will not ask which of them was the head of the house.

A bruised reed he will not break. The husband’s likewise points him to the same Christ the wives were given (2:21–24), and it is the Christ of strength used for the weak. Matthew applies Isaiah’s words to him: a bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench (Matthew 12:20). He had all power, and he spent it touching lepers, lifting a woman bent double for eighteen years, defending a weeping woman at a Pharisee’s table, and speaking to his own mother from the cross to see her cared for. A husband who uses his strength to honour the more vulnerable is not being soft. He is tracing his Lord.

So that your prayers may not be hindered. One of the most sobering sentences in the New Testament. Hindered, enkoptesthai, means cut in on, blocked, obstructed, as a road is blocked by a fallen tree or a trench dug across it. A man who treats his wife badly will find his prayer life obstructed. God takes her side against him, and will not carry on ordinary dealings with a man who is mistreating a fellow heir (Malachi 2:13–16). Relationship with God and relationship with one’s wife are bound together. A husband cannot be a lion of prayer in the church and a bully in the kitchen.

What it does not mean. Weaker vessel does not mean inferior. Peter immediately calls wives co-heirs. Nor does it give husbands authority to dominate; it requires them to honour.

What does it mean for a husband to lead? To go first in love, in sacrifice and in serving. Christ’s headship over the church is the pattern, and he led by washing feet and dying (Ephesians 5:25–29). A Christian husband leads by praying with and for his wife, by taking responsibility for the spiritual health of the home, by listening carefully before deciding, by protecting her, and by putting her good before his own comfort. He does not make every decision, does not demand his way, and never uses his strength to frighten her. Do not be harsh with them (Colossians 3:19). Leadership that does not look like Christ is not biblical headship, whatever it calls itself.

How do I live with my wife in an understanding way if I do not understand her? Start by admitting it, and asking. Ask her what she needs from you, what burdens her, what makes her feel loved and what makes her feel dismissed, and then listen without defending yourself. Notice her moods and ask about them. Learn what her days are really like. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Understanding is not a gift some men have and others lack; it is knowledge gained by attention over years. The husband who keeps asking, keeps listening and keeps adjusting is obeying this verse, even if he still finds her a mystery.

In a sentence. Husbands, in the same way, be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the physically weaker partner and as co-heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

On a Tuesday. Husbands: what does your wife need from you this week? Ask her, listen, and honour her in a specific way: take a burden off her, praise her in front of others, give her an hour of your full attention without the phone. And if your prayers feel blocked, ask honestly whether there is something between you and your wife that needs putting right first. Apologise without excuses.

For worship. He is the Bridegroom who loved his bride when she was unlovely, who knew her completely and was not repelled, who gave himself up for her to make her holy and beautiful. He never once used his strength against her; he used it to carry her sins. He prays for her without ceasing, and his prayers are never hindered. And he has made husband and wife fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that the humblest Christian marriage is a small picture of the great marriage to come, when the Lamb takes his bride and she is radiant with his glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All of you: be like-minded, sympathetic, loving, tender-hearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, as Psalm 34 teaches: the Lord sees the righteous and hears their prayers. If you suffer for doing right, you are blessed. Do not fear your opponents, but honour Christ as Lord in your hearts, and be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Forgotten Half of Verse 15

Repay evil with blessing. Be ready to give a reason for your hope — with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Slandered believers were told to fear the Lord, not their accusers.

Now: A life that raises questions, and answers them courteously, is the best reply to slander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.

Finally, all of you. Finally, to telos, in summary. The household instructions end and the whole congregation is addressed: citizens, slaves, wives, husbands, everyone. Five qualities follow, and they are all relational. Peter has been speaking about how believers live under pressure from outside; now he turns to how they live with one another, because a church under fire that turns on itself has already lost.

Have unity of mind. Unity of mind, homophrones, is like-mindedness, thinking together. Not uniformity of opinion on every question but a shared outlook on what matters most (Philippians 2:2): the same Lord, the same gospel, the same hope, the same direction.

Sympathy. Sympathy, sympatheis, is literally suffering-with, and it is the root of our word: feeling what the other feels. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). In a persecuted network of congregations that was not sentiment but survival. When one member was fined or beaten, the others felt it.

Brotherly love. Brotherly love, philadelphoi: loving as family. Peter has used the word before (1:22). The church is not a club of the like-minded but a family of the born-again, and families are where you learn to love people you did not choose.

A tender heart. A tender heart, eusplanchnoi, is literally having good inner parts. It is the gut-word, the visceral term for compassion that the Gospels use when Jesus saw the crowds and was moved with compassion (Matthew 9:36). Deep, felt kindness (Ephesians 4:32), not a professional politeness.

And a humble mind. Humble, tapeinophrones, lowly-minded: not thinking too highly of oneself (Philippians 2:3). It is the word Christianity effectively invented as a virtue, since in classical Greek the root was mostly an insult; it meant mean, abject, servile. It took the Son of God washing feet to make humility beautiful.

Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling. Then the command that everything has been building towards. Repay, apodidontes, means give back. Note the second half. It is not only violence that is forbidden but the returned insult, which is the retaliation actually available to people with no power, and therefore the one they would actually use. Do not retaliate in deed or word, as Christ did not (2:23; Romans 12:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:15).

But on the contrary, bless. Not merely refrain. Bless, eulogountes, means speak well of, and ask God’s good on. The instruction is not neutrality but active good: speaking well of, and asking God’s favour on, the people slandering you. It is the Lord’s own command: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14). And Peter had heard it.

For to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing. The called-to language again from 2:21, eklēthēte. Obtain, klēronomēsēte, means inherit: the same family as the inheritance of 1:4. And the last clause is not a bargain, bless in order to be paid, but a description of the economy they are now in. They were called to inherit blessing, and blessing is therefore what they have to give away. You hand on what you were given. God’s blessing comes to those who bless, and those who bless show they have been blessed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring wrong or never seeking justice. It means personal retaliation is forbidden; we leave vengeance to God and civil authorities (Romans 12:19; 13:4).

How can I bless someone who has hurt me badly? Begin with prayer, not feeling. Ask God to do them good: to bring them to repentance, to save them, to give them what they truly need. You can pray that honestly long before you feel warmly. Then refuse to curse them in your speech: no mocking, no running them down to others. When an opportunity comes to do them a kindness, take it, if it is safe. Blessing does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, restoring trust that has not been earned, or putting yourself back in harm’s way. It means refusing to return the poison, and handing the case to God.

What about the person in church I simply do not get on with? Then the five words of verse 8 are your homework. Like-minded: focus on the gospel you share, not the preferences you do not. Sympathetic: find out what they are carrying. Brotherly: remember they are family by God’s choice. Tender: ask God to give you compassion for them. Humble: consider that they may find you hard work too. You do not have to become best friends. You do have to love them, speak well of them, and refuse to build a faction against them.

In a sentence. Finally, all of you, be like-minded, be sympathetic, love one another as family, be compassionate and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult. On the contrary, repay evil with blessing, because to this you were called, so that you may inherit a blessing.

On a Tuesday. Who has wronged or insulted you recently? Bless them this week: pray for them by name and speak well of them, at least once, to someone else. And look around your congregation for one person who is suffering and needs someone to feel it with them. Send the message. Make the call.

For worship. When we cursed him, he blessed us. When we reviled him, he prayed for us. When we drove nails into his hands, he asked his Father to forgive us. That is the God we worship: not one who returns evil for evil, but one who overcame our evil with his good, and called us not to wrath but to inherit a blessing. Every blessing we speak over an enemy is an echo of his voice from the cross, and his church is meant to be a whole choir of such echoes.

verseByVerse.quote: For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

For Whoever desires to love life and see good days. Peter supports the command with Psalm 34:12–16, and the choice is not accidental. He has already quoted this psalm in 2:3, and it is the psalm David wrote after escaping from Achish, king of Gath (called Abimelech in the psalm’s title), by pretending to be insane, scrabbling at the doors and letting spit run down his beard (Psalm 34 title; 1 Samuel 21:10–15). A man in real danger, with no power, getting out alive. It is a psalm of God’s protection of the persecuted righteous, and the right psalm for these readers. Love life and good days mean a blessed life, now and for ever. The offer is put as an invitation to ordinary human longing. Peter is not sneering at the wish for a good life; he is telling them where it is found.

Let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. And the first instruction is about the mouth. Which is exactly the point at issue. He has just forbidden reviling in return (v. 9), and the psalm’s first counsel to a man in danger is the same: control what you say when they come at you. No reviling, no lies. Most of the damage we do to others, and to ourselves, comes out through the lips.

Let him turn away from evil and do good. Both halves, and in that order. Avoidance and then action, which is the pattern the New Testament keeps: put off, and put on. A life of mere avoidance is empty; a life of good deeds that never turns from evil is hypocrisy.

Let him seek peace and pursue it. The second verb is the hunting word: chase it down. Peace here is not passivity; it is something you go after, and it will not be found by waiting for it to arrive (Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:14). Peacemakers are not people who avoid conflict, but people who run towards broken relationships to mend them.

For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. Then the ground, and it is the reason any of this is possible. Two organs of attention. He is watching, and he is listening, which is precisely what a slandered congregation could not be sure of. God watches over the righteous with care, and hears their prayers. The persecuted are not forgotten.

But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. Peter includes the hard half, and it belongs. God opposes evildoers. The reason a Christian can decline to return the insult is not that the insult does not matter. It is that it has been noticed by someone better placed to deal with it: the same argument as 2:23, where Christ handed the case to the one who judges justly. And Peter stops the quotation before the psalm’s next line, which speaks of cutting off the memory of them from the earth, perhaps leaving room for persecutors to repent.

The righteous man of Psalm 34. The psalm Peter quotes goes on: many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken (Psalm 34:19–20). John saw that promise kept at Golgotha, when the soldiers broke the legs of the two criminals and did not break Jesus’ legs: these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled, not one of his bones will be broken (John 19:33–36), echoing the Passover lamb and this psalm together. So the righteous one on whom the Lord’s eyes rested most of all was the one whose afflictions were greatest, and his deliverance came through death to resurrection. That is the road by which the good days of verse 10 reach his people.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that the righteous will never suffer. The next verses deal with suffering for righteousness. It means God sees, hears and cares, and that ultimately the righteous will see good days.

Does this mean that if I live well, life will go well? Generally, yes, and Scripture is not ashamed to say so: honest, peaceable, kind people usually have better lives than liars and brawlers. But it is not a guarantee of comfort in this life, as the very next verses show. Christ lived perfectly and was crucified. The good days promised are finally the days of the age to come, though many are tasted now. So the psalm gives both a practical wisdom and a final hope. Live this way because it is right, because it usually goes better, and because God is watching, and leave the timing of the good days to him.

In a sentence. For, “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep their tongue from evil and their lips from deceitful speech. They must turn from evil and do good; they must seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears are attentive to their prayer, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

On a Tuesday. Pick one relationship that is broken or strained, at home, at work, in church, and pursue peace in it this week: an apology, a message, an invitation, a conversation you have been avoiding. And set a guard on your mouth. Before you speak in a tense moment, ask: is this evil, is this deceit, will this pursue peace?

For worship. The eyes of the Lord are on his people. Not one of them is out of his sight: not the slave in the harsh household, not the wife in the hostile home, not the believer facing the magistrate, not you. His ears are open to their cry; no prayer is too faint for him to hear. And the face that is set against evildoers is the face that shone on Moses and was struck for us, and will be turned on his people in perfect kindness for ever. The Father who forsook his Son on the cross, so that his people would never be forsaken, now looks on them with the very delight with which he looks on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,

Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? Harm, kakōsōn, means do evil to, injure. Zealous, zēlōtai, means eager, passionate: the word that gave its name to the Zealots, and one of Peter’s fellow disciples had been one of them (Luke 6:15). Peter wants a zeal for good as hot as theirs was for revolution. The question expects the answer nobody, and then verse 14 immediately concedes that somebody might. That is not a contradiction; it is a distinction between two kinds of harm. Ordinarily, a life of conspicuous good does disarm hostility, and Peter has already made that his strategy (2:12, 15). And ultimately no one can harm the believer’s soul (Matthew 10:28; Romans 8:31).

But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed. Even if, ei kai, with the rare Greek optative, suggests a real but not constant possibility: it may happen. Peter is a realist, and he knows what happened to his Lord. For righteousness’ sake, dia dikaiosynēn, means because of doing right, because of loyalty to Christ. And blessed, makarioi, is the Beatitude word: blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:10–12). Peter is quoting his Lord almost directly, and he had been on the hillside when it was said. So the answer to who can harm you? is that they can hurt you and cannot harm you. The worst they can do lands on a man who is thereby called blessed, which means the injury does not reach the part of him that matters.

Have no fear of them, nor be troubled. The words are from Isaiah 8:12, and the context there is worth knowing. Judah was terrified of an alliance of Syria and Israel forming against it, and of the might of Assyria behind them, and Isaiah was told not to fear what the people feared, but to regard the LORD of hosts as holy and let him be their fear (Isaiah 8:12–13), which is the next verse Peter quotes. Fear of them, ton phobon autōn, can mean their fear, what they fear, or fear of them, and all three fit. Troubled, tarachthēte, means shaken, agitated, stirred up like water. Two commands, and they are different. Do not fear them deals with the object; do not be troubled deals with the inner state, the agitation that persists after the threat has passed. Peter addresses both, and neither is a demand to feel nothing. Isaiah’s word to a frightened nation was not that the danger was imaginary. It was that God was bigger.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never feel fear. It means fear does not govern them. They honour Christ above their fear (v. 15).

What kind of suffering counts as for righteousness’ sake? Suffering that comes because you belong to Christ or because you did what was right: losing a promotion because you would not lie, being mocked for your faith, rejected by family for following Christ, punished for refusing to sin. It does not include suffering that comes from your own foolishness, rudeness or wrongdoing (2:20; 4:15), nor ordinary troubles that come to everyone, though God uses those too. Be careful not to call every criticism persecution. But when the suffering really is for Christ, do not be ashamed. You are in the line of the prophets, and Christ calls you blessed.

In a sentence. Who is going to harm you if you are eager to do good? But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. Do not fear their threats; do not be frightened.

On a Tuesday. What are you afraid of losing if you stand for Christ? A friendship, a job, your reputation, peace at family gatherings? Name it, and bring that fear to him. Then choose to honour him above it. And notice the difference between the fear and the agitation: even when you have decided to obey, the stomach may still churn. Give that to God too, as often as it comes back.

For worship. No one can harm those whom God has blessed. Kings may rage and crowds may jeer, but the one who calls his people blessed is the one who holds the keys of death and Hades. He was persecuted for righteousness’ sake as no one ever was, and the kingdom of heaven is his. And he shares it with every one of his persecuted people, so that the prison cell, the empty desk and the family table where they sit alone become places where heaven’s blessing rests.

verseByVerse.quote: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,
verseByVerse.commentary:
but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,

But in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy. This is the positive replacement for the fear just forbidden, and the logic is displacement: one fear drives out another. It is from Isaiah 8:13, where Judah was told to regard the LORD of hosts as holy and make him their fear and their dread, instead of the coalition. Peter does the same, with one change he clearly intends. Isaiah’s the LORD of hosts becomes Christ the Lord. In Isaiah the LORD is Yahweh, the covenant God of Israel; Peter applies the verse directly to Christ, without a word of explanation. Christ is the LORD. It is a strong, almost casual, statement of his deity. Honour as holy, hagiasate, means sanctify, set apart, revere: enthrone Christ in your heart as Lord. The heart that has Christ on its throne has no room left there for the magistrate.

Always being prepared to make a defense. Prepared, hetoimoi, ready. Defence, apologia, is a reasoned answer, the speech for the defence in a courtroom, and our word apologetics comes from it. For these readers that was not always metaphorical. Christians should be able to explain why they believe, whether in a courtroom or a conversation, and always means at any moment, without notice.

To anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you. Asks, aitounti, can mean demands as well as requests. Reason, logos, is an account, an explanation. Hope is the living hope of 1:3. Note the shape of the situation Peter assumes. They are not going out to argue; they are being asked. Somebody has noticed something and enquired. Which means the hope that is in you must have been visible enough to prompt a question, and a Christian whose life raises no questions will not need this verse. Christian hope in suffering is so striking that people will ask about it. And observe what they are asked to explain. Not the doctrine of the atonement in general, but the hope in you: why you are like this, under these conditions. It is personal testimony grounded in reasons, which is why always being prepared means having thought about it in advance.

Yet do it with gentleness and respect. Then the manner, and it is half the verse though it is usually the forgotten half. Gentleness, prautēs, is the same word used of the wife in verse 4: strength under control, towards the person asking. Respect is literally fear, phobos, most likely reverence towards God, though it certainly rules out contempt for the questioner. Either way the point stands: an answer given harshly has not obeyed this verse, however correct its content. How we answer matters as much as what we say. Peter is describing a man who honours Christ in his heart, and it comes out as courtesy to the person interrogating him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be a trained philosopher. It means every Christian should know the gospel and why they believe it well enough to explain it simply, and be ready to do so.

What should I actually say if someone asks why I believe? Keep it simple, honest and centred on Christ. Say who Jesus is: God the Son who became man. What he did: lived a perfect life, died in the place of sinners, rose again. Why you trust him: perhaps the evidence of the resurrection, the way Scripture has proved true in your life, the change he has made in you, the forgiveness you have found. And what your hope is: that because of him you are forgiven, and death is not the end. You do not need to answer every objection on the spot. It is fine to say, that is a good question; let me think about it and come back to you, and then do.

What if I am shy or afraid I will say it badly? Then remember that Peter, who once could not say I know him to a servant girl, wrote this verse. God uses ordinary words from ordinary people. Prepare a little: write down in a few sentences why you are a Christian, and read it over until it is your own. Pray for opportunities and for courage. And remember that gentleness and respect, which shy people often have in abundance, are half the command. A quiet, kind, honest answer often does more than a brilliant argument.

In a sentence. But in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you to explain the hope you have. But do it with gentleness and respect,

On a Tuesday. Could you explain your hope in Christ in two minutes? Practise it this week, out loud, and pray for an opportunity to share it. Then ask the harder question: is there anything about my life that would make someone ask? If not, the problem may not be that I lack answers, but that my hope is not visible.

For worship. He is the LORD of hosts, before whom Isaiah trembled, and he is Jesus, who sat by a well and answered a Samaritan woman’s questions with gentleness. The same Lord. Enthroned in the hearts of his people, he drives out the fear of man and gives them a hope so bright that strangers stop to ask about it. And when they answer, haltingly, in kitchens and offices and prison cells, he speaks through them, so that the hope in one heart is carried to another, and his kingdom grows one question at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil.

Having a good conscience. Good conscience, syneidēsis agathē, is a conscience that does not accuse, because one has lived rightly: Paul could say, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day (Acts 23:1; 1 Timothy 1:5, 19). Not sinlessness, but integrity: sins confessed, wrongs put right, nothing hidden. The defence of verse 15 requires a life to stand on. A man with something to hide cannot give a straight answer about his hope, because he knows the follow-up question.

So that, when you are slandered. Slandered, katalaleisthe, spoken against, as in 2:12. Note again that Peter says when. He has assumed the slander throughout the letter, and here he describes precisely how it is defeated.

Those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. Revile, epēreazontes, means insult, mistreat, abuse. Good behaviour in Christ, agathēn en Christō anastrophēn, is good conduct flowing from union with Christ. Put to shame, kataischynthōsin, means be embarrassed, exposed as wrong. The mechanism is exposure. The accusation is made publicly; the life is then observed publicly; and the gap between them shames the accuser. Peter is not promising the slander will stop, and he is not recommending a rebuttal. He is saying that a sufficiently clean life eventually embarrasses the people describing it falsely. And there is a sharp phrase inside it: they revile your good behaviour in Christ. What is actually being attacked is not the Christians but Christ in them, which is why the conduct matters so much and why the vindication is finally his.

For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil. The most carefully worded sentence in the paragraph, and two things in it matter. First, the comparison assumes suffering either way and simply asks which kind. That is bleak and it is honest: Peter never suggests the alternative to suffering for righteousness is no suffering at all. If we must suffer, let it be for doing good, not for wrongdoing (2:20; 4:15). Second, and most important: if that should be God’s will, ei theloi to thelēma tou theou. Suffering comes only within God’s will (4:19); he is sovereign over it. Peter will not let unjust suffering be described as an accident, an oversight, or the devil’s victory. It falls inside the will of God, which is either intolerable or the only thing that makes it bearable, and this letter has been arguing for the second since chapter 1.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in our suffering. It means he permits and uses it for good, and that suffering for righteousness is honourable, while suffering for sin is not.

My conscience still troubles me about past sins. Can I have a good conscience? Yes, through the blood of Christ, which purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). A good conscience is not one that has never sinned, but one that has been cleansed and is kept clean by confession and repentance. If there is something you can still put right, a debt, an apology, a lie to correct, do it. Then rest on Christ’s forgiveness. If your conscience goes on accusing you over sins already confessed and forgiven, it is no longer telling the truth; answer it with the gospel, and if it persists, talk to a pastor.

In a sentence. keeping a clear conscience, so that those who speak maliciously against your good behaviour in Christ may be ashamed of their slander. For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything in your life you would not want a hostile neighbour to find out? Deal with it this week: confess it, put it right, bring it into the light. Then, when the accusation comes, you will have nothing to fear from the follow-up question. And if you are suffering now, ask honestly which kind it is. If for doing evil, repent. If for doing good, take heart: it is within God’s will, and he is watching.

For worship. He is the Righteous One who had a perfect conscience, and suffered not once for any evil of his own, but always and only for doing good. His enemies reviled his good behaviour, and on the third day God put them to shame. Now his blood washes guilty consciences clean, so that people who once had everything to hide can stand in the open, slandered but unafraid. Even our sufferings are held within his will. Nothing touches his people that has not first passed through the hands that were pierced for them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter grounds his call to suffer well in Christ’s own suffering. Christ died once for all for sins, the innocent for the guilty, to bring us to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive by the Spirit, and in that state he went and made a proclamation to the imprisoned spirits who had disobeyed long ago in Noah’s day, while God waited patiently as the ark was built and a few people, eight in all, were brought safely through the water. That water foreshadows baptism, which saves now, not by washing dirt from the body, but as a pledge or appeal to God from a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. He has gone into heaven and is at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers made subject to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ’s Victory
