Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Verses 19–20 are disputed, but no reading offers a second chance after death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Noah's household of eight was a small minority brought safely through.

Now: Every power believers fear has already been made subject to the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,

For Christ also suffered once for sins. The for connects it to verse 17: if unjust suffering can be God’s will, here is the supreme case of it. And also: Christ is the supreme example of suffering for doing good. But at once Peter moves beyond example. Once, hapax, means once for all, never to be repeated. It is the word Hebrews builds its argument on (Hebrews 9:26–28), and it rules out any notion of a sacrifice that must be topped up, repeated or re-presented. His suffering was unique and complete. For sins, peri hamartiōn, is the phrase used in the Greek Old Testament for the sin offering. His death was a sacrifice for sin.

The righteous for the unrighteous. Five words in English, and they are as compact a statement of substitution as the New Testament contains. Righteous, dikaios: Christ, the sinless one, the Holy and Righteous One whom Peter had preached to the crowds in the temple (Acts 3:14). For, hyper, on behalf of, in place of. Unrighteous, adikōn: us, sinners. Singular and plural: one righteous man in the place of many unrighteous ones. And note the exchange is not a transaction between equals: it is the innocent standing where the guilty were (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:6–8). This is penal substitution in a single phrase. Barabbas, released while Jesus was led away, is its picture.

That he might bring us to God. Bring, prosagagē, means lead to, usher into the presence of, as a courtier introduces someone to the king; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of bringing a sacrifice to the altar and of presenting priests for consecration. The purpose of the cross is stated as access (Ephesians 2:18; 3:12). Not primarily to make us safe or happy but to bring us into a presence we had no business entering. Sit with that, because it names what salvation is finally for. The end is not an improved life or even an escaped hell. It is God himself, and everything else is arrangements for getting there.

Being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. Put to death in the flesh, thanatōtheis sarki: he truly died, physically, in his human body. Made alive in the spirit, zōopoiētheis pneumati: either in the Spirit, by the Holy Spirit who raised him (Romans 8:11), or in the spiritual realm, the realm of the Spirit and of his resurrection life. The two datives are parallel and describe two spheres: killed as far as earthly, mortal human life goes; made alive in the realm of the Spirit, the new creation. It refers to his resurrection, in which he was raised in a glorified body empowered by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45; Romans 1:4; 1 Timothy 3:16). And it sets up the notoriously difficult verse that follows.

What does made alive in the spirit mean? Some take it as Christ’s human spirit living on after death; others as the Holy Spirit by whom he was raised (Romans 8:11). The more likely reading is that Peter contrasts two spheres: put to death in the realm of the flesh, raised to life in the realm of the Spirit, the new resurrection life.

What it does not mean. Made alive in the spirit does not mean Jesus’ body stayed dead and only his spirit lived on. He rose bodily (Luke 24:39). Nor does it mean his human spirit died; at death, his spirit went to the Father (Luke 23:46).

If Christ suffered once for all, why do Christians still suffer? Because his suffering for sins and our suffering for righteousness are different things. He suffered to pay for sin, and that is finished; nothing we suffer adds to it or pays for anything. Our sufferings are not punishment for sin, which has been fully borne, but the path of a disciple following his Master to glory (2:21; 4:13). Christ’s once-for-all suffering means your suffering can never be God’s condemnation. It can only be his discipline, his refining, and the fellowship of the cross. That changes how you bear it. You suffer as one already brought to God.

How do I come to God through Christ? By trusting him. Peter says Christ died to bring us to God, and the way in is not by improving yourself first, or by any ceremony, but by faith: admitting you are among the unrighteous, believing that the Righteous One died in your place and rose again, and coming to God on that basis alone. If you have never done that, you can do it now, in your own words, in prayer. And if you are a believer who feels far from God, the same verse applies. The door Christ opened is still open. Come in again.

In a sentence. For Christ also suffered once for all for sins, the righteous one for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive by the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. When you pray today, notice how you approach God. Do you come hesitantly, as one not sure of welcome, or on the basis of your good week? Come instead as one brought in by Christ: the Righteous One for the unrighteous. And when you suffer unjustly this week, remember that Christ also suffered, and that the road he walked ended at an empty tomb.

For worship. Once for all: never again will a sacrifice for sin be needed, because the one sacrifice was enough. The Righteous One stood in the place of the unrighteous; the Holy One took the sinner’s death; and the curtain was torn from top to bottom. He was put to death, and the Spirit raised him, and now he takes us by the hand and brings us into the presence of the King, and introduces us as his own. We were far off, and now we are brought near, the unrighteous welcomed by the Righteous, and he will never let go of the hand he has taken.

verseByVerse.quote: in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.

In which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison. These are among the most disputed verses in the New Testament, and honesty about that serves better than confidence. Godly readers have differed for centuries, and Luther confessed that he did not know for certain what Peter meant. The passage should be handled with the humility it demands. The main views: (1) between his death and resurrection, Christ went to the realm of the dead and preached the gospel to the souls of those who died in Noah’s flood, giving them a second chance; (2) between his death and resurrection, Christ descended to the place of the dead and announced his victory to the dead, without offering a second chance; (3) after his resurrection, in his ascension, Christ proclaimed his victory to fallen angels (spirits) imprisoned for their sin in Noah’s day (2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6; Genesis 6:1–4); (4) Christ, by the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who rejected the message and are now spirits in prison (in hell).

The words themselves. In which, en hō: in the Spirit, or in the spiritual realm, the sphere just named. Proclaimed, ekēryxen, means heralded, announced: it is the herald’s word, not necessarily the gospel, for a herald may announce victory or judgement. Peter does not use the word for preaching good news here. Spirits, pneumasin: in the New Testament, used alone, this word usually means angelic beings, not human souls (Hebrews 1:14; Matthew 8:16). In prison, en phylakē, means under guard. And went, poreutheis, is the same participle as in verse 22, he has gone into heaven, which suggests that the going in both verses may be one journey: the risen Christ on his way to the Father’s right hand.

Because they formerly did not obey, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah. Did not obey, apeithēsasin, disobeyed. God’s patience waited, apexedecheto hē tou theou makrothymia: God waited, perhaps 120 years (Genesis 6:3), while Noah built and preached, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). Jewish writings of Peter’s day, especially the book of 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes (Jude 14–15), told at length of the angels who sinned before the flood and were bound in darkness until the judgement, and Peter’s readers would very likely have heard of them. Whatever else the verse means, it shows God’s patience: he waited a long time before the waters came.

While the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water. Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives (Genesis 7:13). Brought safely through, diesōthēsan, were saved through. The water that destroyed the world carried the ark to safety: the same water was judgement to some and rescue to others. And the pastoral point survives every reading, which is presumably why Peter included it. Noah was a tiny minority, a few, that is, eight persons, in a world entirely against him, and God’s patience waited while he built. That is the situation of the people receiving this letter, a small, persecuted minority in Pontus and Bithynia, and the eight were not lost.

Where Christians differ: did Christ offer the dead a second chance? Verdict: The view that Christ offered salvation to the dead contradicts Scripture’s clear teaching that destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27), and it would be strange to offer it only to Noah’s generation. The two strongest views are the third (Christ, in his resurrection and ascension, proclaimed his triumph over the fallen angels imprisoned since Noah’s day, as 2 Peter 2:4–5 and Jude 6 describe) and the fourth (Christ by his Spirit preached through Noah to those who are now in prison). The third fits the word spirits, the link with verse 22 (angels subjected to him), and the context of Christ’s victory. Either way, the point is clear: Christ suffered and was vindicated; he triumphed over every evil power; and his people, though few and persecuted like Noah’s family, will be saved. There is no second chance after death, and no purgatory.

Why the third view is preferred. Unqualified spirits in the New Testament nearly always means spiritual beings, and the paragraph ends with angels, authorities and powers subjected to the risen Christ (v. 22). The herald’s word suits an announcement of triumph rather than an offer of mercy. The same participle, went, links the proclamation to the ascension. And it fits the picture Paul gives: he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:15). The fourth view has real strength in the immediate mention of Noah’s preaching, and many good Reformed interpreters have held it. What no reading may do is turn this into a promise of a second opportunity after death, since the announcement is a proclamation of triumph rather than an offer.

What it does not mean. It does not teach that Christ went to hell to suffer further for sins. His suffering was finished on the cross (John 19:30). The phrase he descended into hell in the Apostles’ Creed is understood by Reformed churches to mean that he truly died and remained under death’s power for a time, bearing the full weight of God’s wrath on the cross.

Does this teach that Christ descended into hell, as the Apostles’ Creed says? The creed’s phrase has been read in several ways. Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) understand it of the hellish anguish Christ suffered in his soul on the cross; the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) of his continuing in the state of the dead, under the power of death, until the third day. This verse is often linked to it, but Peter speaks of Christ proclaiming in which, in the Spirit, to the spirits in prison, and the more likely reading, as the verdict above holds, is the risen Christ announcing his victory to rebellious spirits; others take it of Christ preaching through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who are now in prison. Either way, it is not a second chance for the dead, and it is not a further suffering.

What about people who never heard the gospel? This verse does not teach that they will get a chance after death, and Scripture gives no such hope (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church is sent to the ends of the earth with urgency. We can trust that the Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25), that no one will be condemned for anything but their own sin against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12), and that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit. But the right response to the question is not speculation; it is mission. Peter’s point is that God waited patiently in Noah’s day, and he is waiting patiently now, while the gospel goes out (2 Peter 3:9).

In a sentence. After being made alive, he went and made a proclamation to the imprisoned spirits, who had disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In it only a few people, eight in all, were saved through water.

On a Tuesday. If you feel outnumbered as a Christian, at work, at school, in your family, remember Noah’s eight, and remember that numbers did not decide who was safe. The ark did. Keep building, keep obeying, keep speaking, and trust the God who waits patiently and then acts. And give thanks that the powers behind the hostility you face have already heard their sentence announced by the risen Christ.

For worship. While the whole world mocked, God shut eight people safely into the ark, and the waters that drowned the world lifted them up. Now the risen Christ has gone up through every realm of darkness, a herald of his own victory, and the rebel spirits in their prison have heard that they are defeated. There is no power left that can claim his people. The God who waited in Noah’s day is waiting still, with long patience, and when the door is shut, every one of his own will be inside, carried through the judgement by the one who bore it for them.
verseByVerse.note: One of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Main views: Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day; or after his death he proclaimed victory to fallen angels imprisoned for the sins of Noah’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.

Baptism, which corresponds to this. Another sentence that needs careful reading rather than either alarm or overstatement. Corresponds, antitypon, means antitype, counterpart, the fulfilment of a pattern: the thing the earlier pattern pointed to. The flood was a type or picture; baptism is its counterpart. The flood pattern is: judgement falls, water is the instrument, and a few are brought safely through it in the ark into a new world. As Noah’s family passed through the waters of judgement in the ark and were saved, so believers pass through the waters of baptism in Christ. The water of baptism pictures the judgement that fell on Christ, the ark of his people, and our coming through it with him into new creation.

Now saves you. Saves, sōzei. A surprising statement, and Peter immediately qualifies it, which settles the matter. He raises the strongest way of putting it, and in the same breath rules out the mechanical reading.

Not as a removal of dirt from the body. Peter explains what he does not mean: the water itself does not save. It is not an external washing that has power in itself. The water does nothing; a Jew who washed for ritual purity, or a pagan bathed in an initiation rite, would gain nothing from it before God, and neither would a baptised man without faith.

But as an appeal to God for a good conscience. Appeal, eperōtēma, can mean a request, a pledge, or the answer to a question. Either it is the cry of a man asking God to give him a clear conscience, or it is the pledge of a good conscience given to God, the response made at baptism to the question, do you believe? The word was used in the commercial world of the formal question and answer that sealed a contract. Either way it locates the saving power in what is happening between the person and God, not in the liquid. Baptism saves as the outward expression of inward faith, the believer’s commitment to God and request for cleansing, based on Christ’s work.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. And there is the final safeguard. The saving power is not in the water but in Christ’s resurrection (1:3). Baptism saves the way a wedding ring marries you: it is the sign and pledge of a union whose power lies entirely elsewhere. What saves is the risen Christ; baptism is how a person is joined to him publicly and says so. It unites us symbolically with Christ in his death and resurrection: we were buried therefore with him by baptism into death (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12), and faith receives the reality.

Who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God. His ascension and enthronement (Acts 1:9–11; Hebrews 1:3). Peter had stood on the Mount of Olives and watched him go, and had preached at Pentecost that God had exalted him at his right hand (Acts 2:33). The right hand is the place of authority, honour and rule. The man who was put to death in the flesh is now seated on the throne of the universe.

With angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him. Subjected, hypotagentōn, placed under: the same family as the be subject that has run through the letter (2:13, 18; 3:1). The Christian who submits to the emperor for the Lord’s sake serves a Lord to whom every power in heaven and earth has already been made subject. All spiritual powers, good and evil, are under Christ’s authority, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion (Ephesians 1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). This is the letter’s whole answer to intimidation. Every power these readers were afraid of, the magistrate, the mob, the emperor, and whatever stood behind them, is named and placed. Subjected, past tense, already done. The man they follow was rejected by men (2:4), suffered unjustly (2:23), and is now seated with the authorities under his feet; and that is the sequence Peter has been asking them to trust for their own lives since the first verse.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some others hold that baptism conveys regeneration and forgiveness. Verdict: Peter explicitly denies that the water itself saves (not as a removal of dirt from the body). Baptism saves as the appeal or pledge of a good conscience, that is, as the expression of faith, through Christ’s resurrection. The sign is so closely tied to the reality it signifies that Scripture can speak of the sign as doing what the reality does, as when the Lord’s Supper is called the body of Christ. Salvation comes through faith in the risen Christ; baptism is the outward sign and seal of that faith, rightly given to those who profess it.

Does Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you mean that baptism gives new birth? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it so. But Peter explains immediately: not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. What saves is not the water but what baptism expresses, a heart turning to God and trusting the risen Christ. That is why baptism belongs to those who can make that appeal. This is the conviction of the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), that those who actually profess repentance towards God and faith in Christ are the proper subjects of baptism. Our paedobaptist brothers in the Reformed churches, who baptise the children of believers as a sign of the covenant, agree with us that the water does not regenerate; we differ in love on who should receive the sign, and gladly share the same Saviour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism is unimportant or optional. Christ commanded it (Matthew 28:19), and it is the normal public mark of entering his people. But it is not the cause of salvation.

I am a believer but have never been baptised. Should I be? Yes. Baptism is Christ’s command to every disciple (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38), and it is the way he appointed for you to confess him publicly and be joined visibly to his people. You are not saved by it, but you are called to it, and holding back disobeys the Lord you love. If fear, embarrassment or uncertainty is stopping you, talk to your pastor. And remember the thief on the cross: those who truly believe but die before they can be baptised are not lost. The command is for those who have the opportunity, and you do.

Why is Christ’s reign over the powers good news for me today? Because whatever is pressing on you, a hostile boss, a government that opposes Christians, an addiction, fear of the dark spiritual forces Scripture speaks of, is already under his feet. Nothing has authority over you that he does not allow, and nothing can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39). You do not have to defeat the powers; he already has. Your task is to stand firm in him, resist the devil (5:9), and trust that the one at God’s right hand is ruling all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:22).

In a sentence. And this water symbolises baptism, which now saves you also, not by washing dirt from the body, but as the pledge of a clear conscience toward God. It saves you by the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers placed under him.

On a Tuesday. Remember your baptism today, not as a ceremony in the past but as a pledge you made to God and he sealed: I belong to the risen Christ. When temptation comes, say it. When fear comes, say it. And when you are tempted to think the powers of this world are in charge, look up. There is a man on the throne of heaven, and every authority is under him.

For worship. He went down into death, and rose, and went up through the heavens, and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Angels bow before him; principalities and powers tremble; the emperor who would soon kill his servants is under his feet. And we are joined to him: buried with him in the waters, raised with him to new life, carried through the judgement in him as Noah was carried in the ark. Our baptism points to him, our conscience is cleansed by him, our hope rests on him. Jesus Christ is Lord over all, and he is ours.

4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to suffering in the light of the end: “The end of all things is at hand” (v. 7). The first half (vv. 1–11) shows how suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and how a church facing the end should live: clear-headed for prayer, loving earnestly, hospitable, and using every gift for others. The second half (vv. 12–19) speaks directly to the fiery trial: do not be surprised; rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings; do not be ashamed to suffer as a Christian; and entrust your soul to a faithful Creator.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since Christ suffered, arm yourselves with the same mind: suffering for him settles our break with sin. You have spent enough time living as pagans do; your old friends are puzzled and slander you, but they will answer to God. The end is near, so be clear-headed for prayer, love one another deeply, show hospitality without grumbling, and use each gift to serve others, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
