Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 4 prepares believers to live for God in a world that will mock and persecute them. Christ suffered in the flesh; so they must arm themselves with the same mindset, finished with living for sinful desires and now living for God’s will (vv. 1–2). Their former pagan life of indulgence is over; former friends are surprised and slander them, but those friends will give account to the Judge of the living and the dead, which is why the gospel was preached to believers who have since died, so that though condemned by people they live with God (vv. 3–6). Because the end is near, they should pray with clear minds, love one another deeply, since love covers many sins, show hospitality without grumbling, and use every gift as faithful stewards of God’s grace, speaking God’s words and serving in God’s strength, so that God is glorified through Christ (vv. 7–11). They should not be surprised at the fiery trial, but rejoice as they share Christ’s sufferings, knowing they will rejoice even more when his glory is revealed; if insulted for Christ’s name, they are blessed, for the Spirit of glory rests on them (vv. 12–14). They must not suffer as wrongdoers, but if they suffer as Christians, they should not be ashamed but glorify God (vv. 15–16). Judgement begins with God’s household; if the righteous are saved only with difficulty, how terrible will be the end of the ungodly. So those who suffer by God’s will should entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and keep doing good (vv. 17–19). The chapter is a soldier’s briefing, a family meeting and a deathbed prayer in one, and at its centre Peter cannot help breaking into praise: to him belong glory and dominion for ever and ever.

Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh. Therefore picks up 3:18: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous. In the flesh, sarki: in his body, physically, to death. Peter has just shown Christ enthroned above all powers (3:22). Now he turns back to the road that led there, and tells his readers that it is their road too.

Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking. Arm yourselves, hoplisasthe, is a soldier’s word: put on armour, take up your weapons, the word behind the Greek hoplite, the heavy infantryman. And what Peter hands them is not a shield but a thought. Way of thinking, ennoia, is mindset, attitude, settled resolve. The armament is mental: the settled conviction that suffering is the road Christ took. Christ’s attitude was willingness to suffer rather than sin, and to do God’s will at any cost. The Christian life is warfare, and the right mindset is armour. That is a realistic piece of pastoral care. A Christian ambushed by suffering he did not expect is far more likely to collapse than one who decided in advance what it means. Peter is telling them to make the decision before the trial rather than during it. Soldiers do not put their armour on after the arrows start flying.

For whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin. Then the difficult clause. Read flatly it seems to say that suffering makes a person sinless, which is plainly untrue and contradicts the commands that follow. Two readings carry weight. It may refer to Christ himself: he suffered and is now done with sin, having dealt with it once for all (3:18). Or, more likely given the whoever, it describes what suffering does to a believer’s relationship with sin. The person who has made a decisive break with sin, embracing suffering for Christ rather than compromise, has thereby shown that sin no longer rules him (Romans 6:7). He has already chosen, under pressure, and the choosing settles something. It may also allude to union with Christ’s death: having died with him, we are finished with sin as a master.

So as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God. Verse 2 supports the second reading by stating the result. The rest of the time is the remainder of earthly life. Human passions, anthrōpōn epithymiais, are the desires of people, what everyone around you wants. Will of God, thelēmati theou. The great reorientation: from living for desires to living for God. The break is about direction, not perfection. Something has been finished with. And anyone who has suffered for a conviction knows the effect. Once you have lost something real for Christ, the appeal of what you gave up is permanently reduced: you have already found out what it was worth. That is not sinlessness. It is a man who has stopped negotiating.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering makes us sinless or that physical suffering itself removes sin. Only Christ’s suffering atones. It means willingness to suffer for righteousness shows that sin’s dominion is broken.

What does arming myself look like in practice? It means settling now, in a calm hour, what you will do when obedience becomes costly, so that you are not deciding in the heat of the moment. Decide in advance that you will not lie for your employer, that you will not join the mockery of the colleague, that you will tell your family you are a Christian, that you would rather lose the deal than cut the corner. Think through what it might cost, and pray it through. Read the accounts of Christ’s passion until his mindset becomes familiar. Then, when the moment comes, you will find that the armour is already on.

In a sentence. Therefore, since Christ suffered in his body, arm yourselves also with the same attitude, because whoever suffers in the body is done with sin. As a result, they do not live the rest of their earthly lives for evil human desires, but for the will of God.

On a Tuesday. What would it look like to arm yourself with Christ’s mindset this week, choosing God’s will even when it costs you? Name one situation coming up where obedience may be expensive, and decide now, before you get there. And think of the rest of the time Peter speaks of: however many years you have left, they are not for your passions but for his will. Begin today.

For worship. He armed himself with this mind first. He set his face like flint towards Jerusalem, knowing what waited there; in Gethsemane he said, not my will, but yours, be done; and he went to the cross with his eyes open. He did not drift into suffering; he chose it, for us. And now he arms his soldiers with his own mind, so that people who once lived for whatever they wanted can stand in the fire and say, his will, not mine. The captain went first, and the war is already won.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;

For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do. Suffices, arketos: is enough. The understatement is almost dry: you have given that quite enough of your life already. There is a touch of irony in it: you have had more than enough time for that. Peter does not argue them out of their old habits; he simply says the account is closed. Gentiles here means pagans, unbelievers (2:12), and Peter’s readers were mostly former pagans. What the Gentiles want to do is the will of the culture, set against the will of God of verse 2.

Living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. Then six words for what they had left, and the list is unsparing. Sensuality, aselgeiai: unrestrained immorality, shameless excess. Passions, epithymiai: lusts. Drunkenness, oinophlygiai: literally overflowing with wine. Orgies, kōmoi: carousing, wild revelry, the drunken processions that wound through the streets at night, often linked to the cult of Dionysus. Drinking parties, potoi: drinking bouts. Lawless idolatry, athemitoi eidōlolatriai: abominable, forbidden idolatry. These were not abstractions. Much of it was religious: the temple feasts of a Greek city and the banquets of the trade guilds, held in temple dining rooms in honour of the guild’s patron god, ran on exactly this, and the last item names what held the rest together. Note that the whole list is social. Every item is something done in company, which is precisely why leaving it cost these people their friends, and often their livelihoods.

With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them. Surprised, xenizontai, means to be taken aback, to think something strange, thrown by something unaccountable. The word is related to xenos, stranger: the Christians have become strangers in their own town. Their neighbours are genuinely puzzled: not offended on principle but bewildered that anyone would opt out. Former friends could not understand why converts no longer joined in, and Christians were seen as antisocial, odd, and disloyal to civic religion.

In the same flood of debauchery. Join, syntrechontōn, means run together with, rush along with. Flood, anachysis, is a vivid word: an outpouring, a torrent, something running out of its channel like a drain overflowing. Debauchery, asōtia, is wild living, dissipation, the word used of the prodigal son, who squandered his property in reckless living (Luke 15:13). A crowd rushing headlong into a torrent of excess. And the picture explains the reaction. When everyone is being carried along by a current, the person standing still is not merely different; he is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him.

And they malign you. Malign, blasphēmountes: slander, abuse, speak evil of. They mocked and slandered the Christians, perhaps as killjoys, haters of humanity, or atheists; the Roman historian Tacitus could describe the Christians as hated for their abominations and convicted of hatred of the human race. That is the mechanism of the slander this whole letter addresses. It does not begin in theological objection. It begins in social withdrawal: you stopped coming, and the people you stopped coming to have drawn their own conclusions about why.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be joyless or avoid all social occasions. Jesus attended feasts (John 2:1–11). It means they must not join in sinful excess.

Does this mean Christians should avoid social occasions with unbelievers altogether? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul says we cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Peter warns against joining in the excesses: drunkenness, orgies, idolatry. A Christian may be at the party; he should not be part of what the party becomes.

How do I handle friends who mock me for not joining in? With good humour, honesty and kindness. You do not need to preach at them or explain yourself at length; a simple, cheerful I would rather not is often enough. Keep up the friendship in other ways: invite them for a meal, help them move house, be there when life goes wrong for them. They are often more watchful than they seem, and many who mock now will one day come to the one friend who did not join in. Do not be bitter if some drift away. And find Christian friends too, so that you are not standing in the current alone.

In a sentence. For you have spent enough time in the past doing what pagans choose to do: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, wild partying, drinking bouts and detestable idolatry. They are surprised that you no longer join them in their reckless, wild living, and they heap abuse on you.

On a Tuesday. Are you being mocked for not joining in something sinful? Take heart; that is exactly what Peter’s readers faced. Stand firm. And look honestly at your own life: is there a part of the old flood you have quietly gone back to, perhaps in what you watch, or how much you drink, or how you talk? The time that is past suffices. Do not give it any more.

For worship. He has pulled us out of the flood. We were carried along in the current with everyone else, living for passions that promised life and paid out emptiness, and he reached into the torrent and lifted us onto the rock. Now we stand still while the world rushes past, and they think it strange, and they do not know that we are standing on the only ground that will not wash away. The time that is past was wasted; the time that is left is his; and the time that is coming is endless joy.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.

But they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. Give account, apodōsousin logon, means render an account, as a steward does to his master. The answer to being maligned is not vindication now but a court later: the same move as 2:23, where Christ entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. The slanderers will answer to God. Ready, hetoimōs, is the sharp word: prepared, about to. Not eventually, not one day. He is standing by, prepared, and the delay is patience rather than absence. Judge the living and the dead may refer to Christ or to God the Father, and Scripture says both; Peter himself had told Cornelius that Christ is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1). All people, whether alive at his return or already dead, will be judged.

For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead. Then verse 6, another genuinely disputed sentence. Those who are dead, nekrois: most likely Christians who have since died, people who heard the gospel while alive and are now dead, perhaps through martyrdom, perhaps through ordinary death. That was a live pastoral problem: believers had been dying, sometimes under persecution, and the obvious taunt from neighbours was that their faith had done them no good at all. Some in the churches may have wondered the same: what good did the gospel do for those believers who died? (The Thessalonians had worried about exactly this, 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18.) Peter answers that the gospel was preached to them in life for this very purpose.

That though judged in the flesh the way people are. Judged in the flesh, krithōsi sarki: they suffered physical death, the common human judgement for sin (Romans 5:12), or they were condemned by human courts, or both. The way people are, kata anthrōpous: according to human standards, in human eyes. The verdict of death was passed on them as it is on everyone. It was not the last word.

They might live in the spirit the way God does. Live in the spirit, zōsi pneumati: they are alive in God’s presence, in the spiritual realm, awaiting the resurrection, the spirits of the righteous made perfect (Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 6:9–11). The way God does, kata theon: according to God, in God’s estimation. Human verdict: condemned and dead. God’s verdict: alive. So the pastoral force is this. A congregation burying its members under slander is told that death is the judgement everybody receives in the flesh, and that it settles nothing about the verdict that matters.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a second chance after death? Some read this verse, alongside 3:19, as teaching that the gospel is preached to the dead in the afterlife, giving them an opportunity to believe. Verdict: The verb is past tense (was preached), and the most natural reading is that the gospel was preached to people while they were alive, who are now dead. Scripture consistently teaches that death fixes one’s destiny (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no second chance after death. The verse comforts believers: those who died in Christ are not lost but live with God.

Does this offer a second chance after death? Some early writers read it as preaching to the dead in Hades; others link it to 3:19. The more likely reading is that the gospel was preached to believers while they were alive, who have since died; though they suffered judgement in the flesh, they live with God. Scripture offers no second chance after death (Hebrews 9:27). The alternative reading empties the urgency of the New Testament’s own preaching, and it is not needed, because the natural reading is both simpler and more comforting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the departed believers are unconscious or in purgatory. They are alive with God, consciously enjoying his presence.

Where are Christians who have died, and what are they doing? With Christ, consciously, in joy. Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not asleep in the sense of unconscious, nor waiting in purgatory to be purified; Christ’s blood has already done that. They rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13), worship, and wait with longing for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return, when they will come with him and we will be reunited (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17). Grieve for them, but not as those who have no hope.

In a sentence. But they will have to give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is the reason the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that, though judged in the body by human standards, they might live in the spirit by God’s standard.

On a Tuesday. Think of a believer you have known who has died. Thank God for them by name, and remind yourself, in Peter’s words, where they are: alive with God. And when someone sneers that your faith will not help you, remember the Judge who is ready, and the verdict that matters. Let that free you from needing the approval of the people who give account to him.

For worship. Death is the sentence on all flesh, and the world reads it as the end. But God reads it otherwise. The saints we buried, the martyrs of Bithynia and the grandmothers of our own churches, are not lost; they live to God, in his presence, in joy, because the gospel reached them while they lived and Christ died and rose for them. The Judge of the living and the dead is the Saviour of his people, and on the last day he will raise the bodies we laid in the ground and give them back to us, glorious, and death will be swallowed up for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.

The end of all things is at hand. The word for end is telos: not merely the stopping but the goal, the completion, the point everything has been heading for. Peter is not announcing that things will run out; he is saying they will arrive. All things means the present age, history itself. At hand, ēngiken, has drawn near, as in James 5:8. The death and resurrection of Christ have brought the end near. The next great event in God’s plan is Christ’s return, which could come at any time.

Why near? And at hand has drawn a great deal of comment, since two thousand years have passed. The New Testament’s consistent posture is not a calculated date but a nearness that makes everything urgent. The last days began at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and nothing now remains on God’s calendar before the return of Christ except the gathering in of his people. Peter himself writes that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8), so he was not making a prediction he could be caught out by. Near describes the nature of the whole age: we live on the edge of eternity, and the door could open at any moment.

Therefore be self-controlled. What matters is what he draws from it, and it is startling. Given that the end is near, you might expect a call to dramatic action: evangelise harder, wind up your affairs, gather on a hillside. Peter says: be self-controlled and sober-minded, and pray. Self-controlled, sōphronēsate, means be sensible, of sound mind: the word used of the man from whom Jesus drove the demons, found sitting, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Not panicked or carried away by end-time speculation, but clear-headed.

And sober-minded. One of these words has appeared already. Sober-minded, nēpsate, is from 1:13 and will come again in 5:8: clear-headed, alert, unintoxicated, seeing things as they are. It is the opposite of the drunkenness of verse 3. Self-controlled is its companion. Peter’s answer to eschatological urgency is a steady head.

For the sake of your prayers. And there is the purpose, which is the surprising part. Literally for prayers. The clear head is not for its own sake or for better decisions. It is so that they can pray, because a mind that is agitated, frightened or intoxicated cannot. Jesus told his disciples to watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation (Mark 14:38), and Peter had failed to do it in Gethsemane. He had slept while his Lord prayed, and the Lord had asked him, could you not watch with me one hour? (Matthew 26:40). An hour later he was denying him. He has learned what a sleeping mind costs. That is worth taking personally. Most people’s prayer life fails not through unbelief but through mental clutter, and Peter treats the clearing of the head as a discipline undertaken specifically so that prayer becomes possible again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should sell everything, stop working and wait on a hilltop. Nearness of the end calls for clear thinking, prayer, love and service (vv. 8–11), not frenzy. Nor does it mean Peter was mistaken; near describes the nature of the whole age (2 Peter 3:8–9).

Should I try to work out when the end will come? No. Jesus said that concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36), and every generation that has tried to set dates has been embarrassed. Scripture does not teach a secret rapture that takes the church away before the end; it teaches one visible return of Christ, in glory, to raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). The right response is not speculation but readiness: a clear mind, a praying heart, a loving life. Live every day as if he might come today, and plan as if he might not come for a hundred years.

How do I clear my head to pray? Begin by noticing what is clogging it: worry, noise, screens, resentment, too much to do. Pray at a time and place where those can be shut out, even for ten minutes: before the phone is switched on, on a walk, in the car with the radio off. Write down the worries that crowd in, then hand each to God. Pray Scripture, which steadies the mind, especially the Psalms. And keep short accounts with God and with others, because unconfessed sin is the loudest distraction of all. A sober mind is not a blank mind; it is a mind turned towards God.

In a sentence. The end of all things is near. Therefore be alert and of sober mind so that you may pray.

On a Tuesday. Since the end is near, clear your mind of distractions this week, and give yourself to prayer. Choose one distraction to cut for seven days, and give the time to prayer instead. And when the news of the world unsettles you, do not doom-scroll; let it drive you to pray for the world, and to remember who is coming.

For worship. The end is near, and the end is not a catastrophe but a Person. The one who began history will finish it; the one who died at its centre will come at its close; and everything that has been groaning will be set free. He is not slow, he is patient; he is not absent, he is near. So his people do not panic. They pray, with clear eyes and steady hearts, because they know the King is coming, and his coming will be the end of all their sorrow and the beginning of all their joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.

Above all, keep loving one another earnestly. Above all, pro pantōn, before everything. The priority is stated plainly: love is the top priority. And earnestly, ektenē, is the stretched-out word from 1:22: fervent, intense, love at full extension, the effort of a muscle under strain. Under persecution, the church must hold together in strong love. A besieged city whose citizens are fighting one another will not last long.

Since love covers a multitude of sins. The phrase comes from Proverbs 10:12: hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses; James uses it too (James 5:20). And covers, kalyptei, hides, overlooks, must be read rightly. This is not concealment of wrongdoing, and it is not the covering that atones; only Christ’s blood does that. It means love does not spread things. It refuses to publish, to exaggerate, to relitigate, to keep the account open (1 Corinthians 13:5, 7). It forgives and overlooks offences. A congregation of a dozen households under persecution, meeting weekly in someone’s front room, will generate friction constantly; and the difference between a church that survives that and one that tears itself apart is whether small offences get covered or circulated.

Show hospitality to one another without grumbling. Then verse 9, and it follows for a very practical reason. Hospitality, philoxenoi, means love of strangers. And hospitality was not optional in that world. There were no church buildings: the congregation met in a home, and somebody’s floor took the wear. Travelling believers and missionaries needed lodging, since inns were expensive and often little better than brothels. Peter’s word means love-of-strangers, and it was a costly practical burden borne by whoever had the largest room (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). Which is exactly why without grumbling, aneu gongysmou, is attached. Peter knows that the household hosting the church is the household most likely to resent it, and that the resentment will come out as muttering rather than refusal. The command is not to open your door; they were already doing that. It is to stop complaining about the cost of it. Hospitality can be tiring and costly; it is to be given cheerfully.

What it does not mean. Love covers sins does not mean love earns forgiveness from God, or that love ignores serious sin that needs discipline (Matthew 18:15–17). It means love does not keep a record of wrongs and readily forgives.

Does love covers a multitude of sins mean we should keep quiet about serious sin, abuse or crime? No. Love overlooks many small offences and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin is to be confronted (Matthew 18:15–17; Galatians 6:1), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

How do I know whether to overlook something or raise it? Ask a few questions. Is it a small irritation, a thoughtless word, a matter of personality or preference? Then cover it: forgive it, and do not mention it to others. Is it a pattern that is harming the person or others, a serious sin, or something that is damaging your relationship so that you cannot let it go? Then go to the person privately and gently (Matthew 18:15). Is anyone in danger, or has a crime been committed? Then it must be reported, at once. Love overlooks much but never covers what endangers the vulnerable. When in doubt, ask a wise elder.

What if hospitality is genuinely hard for me? Then start small and start honestly. Hospitality is not about a beautiful house or elaborate food; it is about opening your life to others. A cup of tea, soup and bread, an invitation to Sunday lunch with whatever you were already eating. If your home is not suitable, take someone out for coffee, or help someone else host. If you are exhausted, or ill, or caring for someone, God knows your limits; do what you can, gladly. And notice that Peter forbids the grumbling, not the tiredness. Ask God for a cheerful heart, and remember that some have entertained angels unawares.

In a sentence. Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. Offer hospitality to one another without grumbling.

On a Tuesday. Is there an offence you are holding onto? Let love cover it: decide to stop rehearsing it, and do not mention it to anyone else this week. And invite someone for a meal this week, cheerfully: a lonely member, a new family, a student far from home. Notice if you start muttering about the washing-up afterwards, and turn the muttering into thanks.

For worship. Love covers a multitude of sins, and no love has covered more than his. He looked at the whole record of our offences, and did not publish it; he took it to the cross and blotted it out. He has made us welcome in his Father’s house, strangers and enemies as we were, and set a table for us, and never once grumbled at the cost, though the cost was his own blood. Every forgiven grudge and every opened door in his church is a small sign of the hospitality of God, who is preparing a feast for his people that will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

As each has received a gift. Each, hekastos: the word carries the weight. Peter assumes that every member of these scattered congregations has been given something, and there is no category of Christian who has not. Every believer has at least one gift. Gift, charisma, is a grace-gift, as in Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4: given by God’s grace, not earned, and not chosen.

Use it to serve one another. Serve, diakonountes, minister, the word from which deacon comes. The gift is not for the possessor. It arrives already assigned, and the direction is towards other people, which settles the question of what gifts are for before anyone can make them a measure of standing. Gifts are for others, not for self-display.

As good stewards of God’s varied grace. A steward, oikonomos, managed a household that belonged to someone else, often a slave entrusted with the master’s property (Titus 1:7), and he would be asked about it. We do not own our gifts; we manage them for God, and it is required of stewards that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2). And varied, poikilēs, is a lovely word: literally many-coloured, used of an embroidered cloth. It is the same word as the various trials of 1:6. God’s grace is as many-coloured as our trials, and for every shade of trouble there is a matching shade of grace. God’s grace is not issued in one shade; the congregation is a fabric of different colours, and a single-coloured church has lost something God intended to be seen.

Whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God. Then Peter divides all gifts into two: whoever speaks and whoever serves. Word and deed, and both are needed. Oracles, logia, are words, utterances of God (Romans 3:2). That is a weighty standard. Not that every Christian’s words are inspired, but that anyone speaking in the congregation, teaching, preaching, exhorting, should handle the responsibility as though delivering God’s own utterances: faithfully conveying his word, not their own opinions, carefully, and not casually (2 Timothy 4:2).

Whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies. Supplies, chorēgei, is the choregos word: in Athens a wealthy citizen funded a chorus for the great drama festivals and paid lavishly for everything it needed, costumes, training and all. The word came to mean provide abundantly. The servant does not run on his own reserves. Practical service, cooking, visiting, cleaning, giving, administering, depends on God’s strength, not ours, and God is a generous sponsor.

In order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. And the purpose gathers both: in everything, not only in the dramatic gifts. The purpose of all gifts is God’s glory, through Christ.

To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. Which is why Peter breaks into doxology mid-letter. A man thinking about gifts rightly ends up talking about God rather than about gifts. Him may be God or Christ; the grammar allows either, and either way all glory is his. Dominion, kratos, is might, the power to rule. The scattered, powerless congregations are reminded that the one they serve holds all power for ever.

What it does not mean. Speaks oracles of God does not mean preachers today receive new revelation. It means they must speak faithfully what God has already said in Scripture, with the seriousness that befits God’s word. The apostolic gifts of revelation belonged to the foundational era; today God speaks through his completed word.

Does whoever speaks include prophecy and tongues today? Peter divides the gifts into speaking and serving, and the speaking he has in mind is the church’s teaching, preaching and exhortation, handled as God’s word, not new revelation. Continuationists include prophecy here, and they are brothers and sisters whose love for Christ we gladly recognise; the more likely reading is that those who speak in the church today speak as one who speaks oracles of God by faithfully passing on the words God has already given. The revelatory gifts served to lay the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon complete, Scripture is sufficient.

How do I find out what my gift is? Not mainly by taking a test, but by serving. Look at the needs around you in your church and start meeting them. Over time you will find what you do well, what others are blessed by, and what you find yourself drawn to. Ask mature Christians who know you what they see in you. Do not despise ordinary gifts: Peter puts serving beside speaking, and the person who stacks chairs, keeps accounts or visits the sick is as much a steward of God’s grace as the preacher. And remember that your gift is not your identity; it is God’s grace, lent to you, for others.

In a sentence. Each of you should use whatever gift you have received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God’s grace in its many forms. If anyone speaks, they should do so as one who speaks the very words of God. If anyone serves, they should do so with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be praised through Jesus Christ. To him be the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.

On a Tuesday. What gift has God given you? Use it this week to serve someone in your church, in his strength and for his glory. Before you do it, pray: Lord, supply the strength. Afterwards, say: to you be the glory. And if you have been holding back, waiting to be asked or to feel ready, step forward. Stewards who bury what they are given are not praised.

For worship. Every gift in the church is a ray of his many-coloured grace. The teacher’s clear word, the deacon’s quiet labour, the widow’s faithful prayer, the young man’s strong arms on moving day: all of it is grace, given by the ascended Christ to his people, supplied by a Father who funds his servants lavishly. Nothing we have is ours; everything we do is by his strength; and so all the praise flows back to him. To him belong glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not be surprised by the fiery trial, as though something strange were happening. Rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings. If you are insulted for his name, the Spirit of glory rests on you. Do not suffer as a wrongdoer or a meddler; but if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed. Judgment begins with God’s household. So those who suffer by God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: Make sure any suffering is for Christ’s name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.

Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial. Beloved, again: Peter never addresses suffering people coldly. The word for surprised, xenizesthe, think it strange, is the one used in verse 4 of the pagans, who were taken aback that Christians would not join them. Peter turns it round: they are astonished at you; do not you be astonished at this. The fiery trial, pyrōsis, is literally the burning: the word used of smelting metal in a furnace, and it reaches back to 1:7, where faith is refined like gold. Peter has not changed his mind about what the fire is for. Severe persecution is in view, and some think this anticipates Nero’s persecution of AD 64, when Christians in Rome were burned as living torches. Whether or not the flames were yet literal in Asia Minor, they soon would be.

When it comes upon you to test you. When it comes, not if. And to test you, pros peirasmon, names the purpose, which is the whole point of the sentence. God uses the fire to refine faith (1:6–7). A trial with a purpose is a different experience from a trial without one, though the heat is identical.

As though something strange were happening to you. There is the pastoral target. The danger is not only the suffering but the interpretation: the conclusion that this is abnormal, that it means God has withdrawn, that other Christians somewhere are having an easier time and must be doing it better. Peter’s answer is that persecution is not a deviation from the Christian life but a normal feature of it. If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12). Which is a hard word and a strangely freeing one: a great deal of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings. Note the careful measure: insofar as. Peter is not commanding joy in suffering generally, but in the specific portion of it that is genuinely a share in Christ’s. And share, koinōneite, is the fellowship word: participate in, have communion in. This is participation, not imitation. Suffering for Christ is fellowship with him (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24). Not adding to his atonement, which is complete, but sharing in the opposition the world gave him. The hostility aimed at him in Jerusalem is now aimed at his body in Bithynia, and when his people bear it, they are standing with him. Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

That you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed. The joy is not two joys but one, arriving in two instalments. What is begun now under the fire will be completed at the revelation, and the second verb is the exuberant one: be glad, agalliōmenoi, exult, the word for shouting gladness, leaping for joy (1:6, 8). Present joy in suffering leads to overflowing joy at his return. The pattern: suffering, then glory (1:11; Romans 8:17). Peter had seen it once already, on a hillside in Galilee, when the face of his Lord shone like the sun; and he knew the glory that was coming was real.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should enjoy pain itself. They rejoice in what the suffering means and leads to.

How can I rejoice when I am suffering? Not by pretending it does not hurt, but by looking past the pain to what it means and where it leads. You rejoice that you belong to Christ so truly that the world treats you as it treated him; that the Spirit rests on you (v. 14); that your faith is being refined; and that the glory coming is beyond all comparison (Romans 8:18). The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). You may weep and rejoice in the same hour. Joy here is not a feeling you produce, but a confidence God gives as you keep your eyes on Christ.

Should I expect persecution if I live faithfully? Yes, in some form, though its shape varies enormously. For some believers today it means prison, beatings, the loss of home or life; for others, mockery, exclusion, a career closed off, family rejection. Paul says all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). Do not seek it, and do not provoke it by foolishness (v. 15). But do not be surprised by it, and do not conclude that God has abandoned you when it comes. And pray for the persecuted church around the world, which is bearing the fiery trial in its full heat today.

In a sentence. Dear friends, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that has come on you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed when his glory is revealed.

On a Tuesday. If you are suffering for Christ, name it to God as fellowship with his Son, not as a sign of his absence. If you are not, find out about one country where Christians are being persecuted now, and pray for them by name this week. The body is one; when one part suffers, all suffer with it.

For worship. He walked into the fire first. The world’s hatred, the mockery, the scourging and the cross: he bore it all, and when his people suffer for him, he does not stand at a distance. He is in the furnace with them, as he was with the three young men in Babylon, and they share his sufferings so that they may share his glory. The fire cannot consume them; it can only refine them. And the day is coming when the one who suffered with them will be revealed in glory, and their joy will break out in a shout that fills the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.

If you are insulted for the name of Christ. Insulted, oneidizesthe, means reproached, reviled. For the name of Christ: because you bear his name and belong to him. Note the precision. Not for being difficult, or tactless, or socially awkward. Peter will make the distinction explicit in the very next verse, and he is careful never to let a Christian claim the blessing for trouble he brought on himself. And insult is the specific form named. Not imprisonment or death at this stage, but reviling, the ordinary daily contempt of neighbours. Which is what most Christians under pressure actually face, then and now: not a courtroom but a reputation quietly destroyed. Persecution was often verbal: mockery, slander, exclusion.

You are blessed. Blessed, makarioi: the Beatitude again, as in 3:14, echoing Jesus: blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account (Matthew 5:11–12). Peter keeps returning to a sermon he heard on a hillside.

Because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you. Then the reason, and it is one of the most remarkable statements in the letter. The Spirit of glory and of God is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s glory with him. The verb rests, anapauetai, rests, abides, settles, is the one used in Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the LORD rests on the shoot from the stump of Jesse: a messianic text. Peter says the same Spirit who rested on the Messiah settles on an insulted congregation in Bithynia. And there is very likely an echo of the glory cloud that rested on the tabernacle, when the glory of the LORD filled it and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35). The presence that filled the tent now rests on people being sworn at in the street. Like Stephen, whose face shone like the face of an angel as they gnashed their teeth at him, and who saw the glory of God (Acts 6:15; 7:55). Which inverts the whole appearance of things. The neighbours see a group whose reputation is in ruins. Peter says the visible shame is the outward face of an invisible glory, and that the Spirit is not merely with them despite the insults but is resting on them precisely there.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add: on their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified. The earliest manuscripts lack it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only persecuted believers have the Spirit. All believers have him (Romans 8:9). It means that in persecution the Spirit’s presence is specially manifest and real.

How can I know the Spirit is resting on me when I feel nothing but humiliation? Peter does not say you will feel it; he says it is so. The Spirit’s presence is a fact grounded in God’s promise, not a sensation you must manufacture. Often believers who have suffered for Christ look back and see it: a strength they did not have, a peace that made no sense, words that came when they needed them (Matthew 10:19–20), a love for their enemies they could not explain. In the moment, trust the promise. The insult is real, but so is the glory, and only one of them will last.

In a sentence. If you are insulted because of the name of Christ, you are blessed, for the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked for Christ this week, at work, online, at a family meal, take heart: God’s glory rests on you. Say so to yourself, quietly, while it happens: the Spirit of glory is here. Then answer with gentleness, or with silence, but not with shame.

For worship. The Spirit who hovered over the waters of creation, who filled the tabernacle with glory, who rested on Jesus at the Jordan like a dove, now rests on the mocked and the slandered people of Christ. The world sees only their disgrace; heaven sees the glory cloud settled over them. He does not abandon his people in their humiliation; he chooses that very place to dwell. Glory to the Father who sends him, glory to the Son who poured him out, and glory to the Spirit who rests on the weakest saint as on a temple.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.

But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer. Peter will not let the blessing of verse 14 be claimed by a Christian who has earned his trouble. Suffering is only blessed if it is undeserved. The distinction has run through the letter (2:20; 3:17) and he states it once more, bluntly. Evildoer, kakopoios, is criminal, wrongdoer, the very accusation pagans were making against Christians (2:12). Do not prove them right.

Or as a meddler. Then the fourth item, and it does not belong with the first three. Meddler, allotriepiskopos, is found nowhere earlier in Greek literature, and Peter may have coined it. It means something like an overseer of other people’s business: a busybody. Set beside murder and theft it is startling, and the placing is the point. Peter puts interfering in other people’s affairs in a list with felonies, because in a small suspected minority the busybody does real damage. It may describe Christians who stirred up trouble by interfering in their neighbours’ lives, tactlessly condemning pagan customs, or causing unnecessary offence. A Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours’ business will generate hostility and then mistake it for persecution. Christians can bring suffering on themselves by foolishness.

Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian. The word Christian appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; and here), and this is the only place where a believer takes it up as a name to be worn. It was coined at Antioch (Acts 11:26) and was almost certainly an outsiders’ nickname: Christ-people, Christ-ites, partisans of Christ, perhaps used mockingly. Here it appears to be becoming a legal charge. Half a century later the governor Pliny asked the emperor whether Christians in Bithynia were to be punished for the name itself, even without any crime, and executed those who would not deny it.

Let him not be ashamed. Ashamed, aischynesthō. There is no shame in suffering for Christ: I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation (Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8, 12). So Peter takes the label the neighbours were using as an insult and tells them to wear it. That is what he means by not being ashamed: the name is being thrown at them, and the instruction is to catch it. And no one knew better than Peter what it was to be ashamed of the name. In a courtyard by a fire he had said, I do not know the man (Matthew 26:72).

But let him glorify God in that name. In that name, en tō onomati toutō: because he bears the name Christian. The shame is not merely to be endured but converted. The mockers supplied the word; the Christian is to make it an occasion of praise, which takes the sting out of an insult more completely than any denial could. What was intended as an insult becomes a badge of honour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian who suffers is suffering for Christ. Sometimes we suffer for our own folly or sin. We must examine ourselves honestly.

How do I tell the difference between being persecuted and being a nuisance? Ask honestly what the people opposing you are objecting to. Is it your faith in Christ, your refusal to sin, your honest witness? Or is it your tone, your tactlessness, your habit of correcting everyone, your neglect of your work, your political rage dressed in Christian language? Ask a wise friend, because we are poor judges of ourselves. If you find you have brought the trouble on yourself, apologise and change; that is not compromise but humility. If after honest examination the offence is Christ himself, then stand firm and rejoice.

Does this mean I should keep my faith private to avoid trouble? No. Peter tells them not to be ashamed of the name, and to be ready to give an account of their hope (3:15). Keeping out of other people’s business is not the same as keeping quiet about Christ. You can speak of him openly, kindly and without apology, while refusing to be a busybody who polices your neighbours’ lives. The aim is that if you are opposed, it will be for the name, and for nothing else.

In a sentence. If you suffer, it should not be as a murderer or thief or any other kind of criminal, or even as a meddler. However, if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but praise God that you bear that name.

On a Tuesday. If you face criticism this week, ask honestly: is this for Christ, or for my own fault? If for Christ, wear the name with joy. And look for one place in your life where you have been a meddler, giving opinions where none were asked, or managing someone else’s life, and stop.

For worship. They meant it as a sneer: Christ-people. And it is the most glorious name a human being can bear. It ties us to the Anointed One, the King, the Priest, the Prophet; it tells the world whose we are. The one who gave us his name was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), though we had been ashamed of him. Peter, who once denied the name by a charcoal fire, wrote these words and then died for the name in Rome. And every believer who bears it gladly under scorn is a living doxology to the God who has written his Son’s name on us.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And “If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” Therefore let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God. A startling sentence, and it reframes everything the letter has described. Time, kairos, is the appointed season. Judgement, krima. Household of God, oikou tou theou, is the church, God’s temple and family (2:5; 1 Timothy 3:15). The idea is Ezekiel’s. When judgement fell on Jerusalem, the command to the executioners was: begin at my sanctuary (Ezekiel 9:6), God’s own house first. And Malachi foretold that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple and sit as a refiner, purifying the sons of Levi (Malachi 3:1–5). Peter is saying that the suffering these congregations are enduring is not merely persecution from outside; it is the first movement of God’s own sifting, and it begins with his people. For believers this judgement is the refining fire of suffering, purifying them (v. 12). That is not a comfortable thought and it is a clarifying one. Their trials are not outside God’s programme, and they are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

And if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? Outcome, telos, end. The argument runs from lesser to greater and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement. If God’s refining is this painful for his own children, how terrible will his final judgement be for those who reject the gospel? They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:8–9). The reader is left to do the arithmetic about his persecutors, which is a far more sobering thing than being told. And note the phrase: those who do not obey the gospel. The gospel is not only an offer but a summons, and to refuse it is disobedience.

And If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31 as it stands in the Greek Old Testament. Scarcely, molis, means with difficulty. Not that salvation is uncertain or only barely achieved, nor that the righteous are saved by a narrow margin or barely enough grace. It means saved with difficulty: through fire, through great trial and suffering, through the process this letter has been describing. Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Salvation is entirely secure, because God guards us (1:5), and the road to it is hard, and Peter has never pretended otherwise. If the righteous pass through such fire, what of the ungodly?

Therefore let those who suffer according to God’s will. Then the conclusion, and it is the finest sentence in the chapter. According to God’s will, kata to thelēma tou theou: suffering is not outside God’s control (3:17). Not one of these sufferings has slipped past him.

Entrust their souls to a faithful Creator. The verb entrust, paratithesthōsan, is the deposit word: commit, hand over for safekeeping, as one deposits valuables with a trusted friend before a journey. It is the word Jesus used on the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46), echoing Psalm 31:5, where David prays: into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God. Peter takes both halves of that psalm verse, the committing and the faithful God, and puts them together. And the thought is the one used of Christ in 2:23, handing his case to the just Judge. The title chosen for God is exact: Creator, ktistēs, used of him nowhere else in the New Testament. A man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it, and faithful, pistos, means the deposit will be there when he asks for it. The God who made you is faithful; he will care for what he made.

While doing good. Doing good, en agathopoiia. Note that the entrusting is done while doing good: not instead of acting, but in the middle of it. Trusting God does not mean passive resignation. Keep doing good, even while suffering. The hand that commits the soul to God goes on working for the neighbour.

What it does not mean. Scarcely saved does not mean believers may not make it. Peter has already said they are guarded by God’s power (1:5). It means salvation comes through great tribulation, not ease. And judgement beginning at the household of God is fatherly discipline, not condemnation (Hebrews 12:5–11; 1 Corinthians 11:32).

Is God punishing me through my suffering? Not in the sense of making you pay for your sins, which Christ has fully paid. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). But God does discipline his children, out of love, to make them holy (Hebrews 12:6, 10), and he uses suffering to refine and purify. So the question to ask is not, what is God making me pay for? but, what is my Father teaching me, and how can I grow? Sometimes suffering exposes a sin to turn from; often it is simply the road all his children walk. Either way, it comes from a Father’s hand, not a Judge’s sentence.

How do I actually entrust my soul to God? By handing over, in prayer, the things you cannot control: your life, your future, your reputation, the outcome of the trial, the people who are hurting you. Say it to him plainly, as Jesus did: into your hands. Remind yourself of who he is: your Creator, who made you and knows you, and faithful, who has never broken a promise. Then go on doing the good in front of you. When anxiety returns, entrust again. It is not a single act but a lifelong habit, and the dying Christ shows its last and greatest form.

Does this verse teach that hell is real and eternal? It points to it. If even the righteous pass through refining fire, the end of those who do not obey the gospel is far worse, and Scripture describes that end as conscious, eternal punishment, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46). Peter does not dwell on it, and nor should we with relish. But he does not soften it either, because only the truth about judgement makes sense of the urgency of the gospel and the wonder of grace. The fire that the ungodly will face is the fire Christ endured in the place of all who trust him.

In a sentence. For it is time for judgement to begin with God’s household; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And, “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should commit themselves to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.

On a Tuesday. Pray Jesus’ words today: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. Say them over the thing you are most anxious about. Then do one good thing for someone else, right away, while the trouble is still unresolved. And pray for someone you know who does not obey the gospel; the question of verse 17 is meant to move us to plead with God, and with them.

For worship. Into your hands. The Son spoke those words as he died, and the Father did not fail him; on the third day the deposit was returned, glorious and alive. Into the same hands we commit our souls: the hands that formed the stars, that shaped us in the womb, that have never let a single one of their own fall. He is our Creator, and he is faithful. The fire may be hot and the road may be hard, but we are saved, and we will be saved, and the faithful God who made us will keep what we have entrusted to him until that day.
