5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The last chapter has three movements: elders are to shepherd God’s flock (vv. 1–5); the whole church is to humble itself under God’s mighty hand, cast its anxieties on him and resist the devil (vv. 6–11); and closing greetings place the letter in “Babylon”, almost certainly Rome (vv. 12–14). Its climax is one of the finest benedictions in the New Testament: after a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder. Shepherd God’s flock willingly, not under compulsion; eagerly, not for money; by example, not by domineering. When the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive an unfading crown of glory. Younger people should submit to the elders, and everyone should put on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God's flock willingly, eagerly and by example — not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The chief Shepherd is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to elders as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to tie on the servant’s apron of humility.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:

Meaning first. 1 Peter 5 brings the letter to a close with instructions for a suffering church. Peter, writing as a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not for money or by domineering, knowing that the Chief Shepherd will give them an unfading crown of glory (vv. 1–4). Younger people should submit to the elders, and everyone should clothe themselves with humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (v. 5). So humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand, casting all your anxieties on him because he cares for you (vv. 6–7). Be alert, because the devil prowls like a roaring lion; resist him, firm in faith, knowing fellow believers worldwide suffer the same (vv. 8–9). After a little suffering, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (vv. 10–11). The letter ends with a summary (this is the true grace of God; stand firm in it), greetings from “Babylon” and Mark, and a final word of peace (vv. 12–14). It is the chapter of a man who has been a shepherd, a stray, a sleeper in Gethsemane and a broken net mended by Christ, and who passes on to frightened churches exactly what was given to him.

So I exhort the elders among you. So, oun, therefore: because judgement begins at God’s household (4:17), its leaders must be faithful. Exhort, parakalō, appeal, urge. Elders, presbyterous, plural: the leaders of each local church, also called overseers and shepherds (vv. 2–4; Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). Every congregation Peter writes to has more than one, and he speaks to them first, because a suffering flock needs faithful shepherds more than anything.

As a fellow elder. Consider what Peter does not say. He could have written as an apostle, and the letter opened that way (1:1). Addressing church leaders about how to lead, he sets the title down and takes the same chair they are sitting in. Fellow elder, sympresbyteros, co-elder, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He seems to have made it for this sentence, and it is the credential he wants in play: not authority over them but experience alongside them. Remarkable humility. Peter, the leading apostle, does not claim supremacy but stands alongside the elders as one of them.

And a witness of the sufferings of Christ. Witness, martys, eyewitness, one who testifies: the word that would come to mean martyr, because so many witnesses died for their testimony, Peter among them. That is a claim only a handful of men could make, and it carries more than the fact of having been present. Peter saw Jesus’ suffering firsthand: in Gethsemane, at the trial, and perhaps from a distance at the cross. He had watched from the courtyard, and had failed there. He also bore witness to it in preaching and by his own suffering. When he tells elders to shepherd the flock, the words come from the man who was told three times on a beach to feed the sheep, after denying he knew the Shepherd at all.

As well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed. Partaker, koinōnos, sharer. The tenses are worth noticing. He was a witness of the sufferings; he is a partaker of a glory not yet revealed. Peter puts himself and them in exactly the same position, between a suffering already seen and a glory still coming, which is where this whole letter has located its readers since the first chapter (4:13). And there may be a memory in that word. Peter had seen glory revealed once, on the mountain, when the Lord’s face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light (Matthew 17:1–8; 2 Peter 1:16–18), and Peter had wanted to build shelters and stay. He writes now as a man who knows the glory is real and that it is not yet time.

Where Christians differ: was Peter the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter head of the universal church, with authority passed to the bishops of Rome as his successors. Verdict: Peter calls himself a fellow elder, not a supreme pontiff. Christ is the Chief Shepherd (v. 4), the cornerstone (2:6), and the head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18). Peter was a leading apostle and the first to preach to Jews and Gentiles (Acts 2; 10), but the foundation of the church is the apostles and prophets together, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and Paul could rebuke Peter publicly (Galatians 2:11–14). The New Testament knows nothing of a papacy or of Peter’s authority being passed to Roman bishops. Local churches are led by a plurality of elders, under Christ.

Does Peter’s calling himself a fellow elder tell against the papacy? Roman Catholic teaching sees Peter as the first bishop of Rome with authority over the whole church (compare Matthew 16:18–19). Here Peter, writing probably from Rome (v. 13), places himself alongside the elders, not over them, and points them to Christ, the chief Shepherd. Nothing in his letters claims a supreme office or successors. Christians who order their churches differently, under bishops or under congregational rule, still agree that every church leader answers to the one Chief Shepherd.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Peter’s apostolic authority was the same as an ordinary elder’s. He was an apostle and eyewitness, writing Scripture. But he exercised his authority humbly, as a fellow servant.

In a sentence. To the elders among you, I appeal as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings who also will share in the glory to be revealed:

On a Tuesday. Pray today for the elders of your church by name, and ask God to keep them humble, faithful and unafraid. If you are an elder, sit for a moment where Peter sat: between the sufferings you have seen and the glory you have not, and ask whether your leadership this week looks like the one who was a witness of both.

For worship. Peter saw him suffer, and Peter saw him shine. The face that was spat on in the high priest’s courtyard was the face that blazed like the sun on the mountain, and both are the face of our Lord. He who was humbled to the uttermost is now exalted to the highest, and every under-shepherd of his flock, from Peter in Rome to the faithful elder in the smallest chapel, will one day stand in the glory that he has promised to share.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.

Shepherd the flock of God that is among you. Shepherd, poimanate: tend, feed, care for as a shepherd. It is the command Jesus gave Peter: tend my sheep (John 21:16), and now Peter passes it on. Shepherding includes feeding (teaching the word), leading, protecting from wolves, seeking the lost, binding up the injured and caring for the weak (Ezekiel 34:1–16; Acts 20:28). Peter has already given the titles of shepherd and overseer to Christ (2:25), which fixes the terms: these men are under-shepherds, and the flock is not theirs. The flock of God that is among you says it twice over. It belongs to God, and the elder is among it rather than above it. They are accountable to him.

Exercising oversight. Exercising oversight, episkopountes, means overseeing, watching over, and the word bishop comes from it. Two verbs, and they are the two words the New Testament uses for church leadership: shepherding and overseeing. Elders and overseers are the same office. Then three pairs follow, each a temptation and its remedy, and together they are the most searching description of pastoral motive in Scripture.

Not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you. Under compulsion, anankastōs, means by constraint, reluctantly, because they must. Willingly, hekousiōs, means voluntarily, gladly. The first danger is doing it because you have to: from duty, or because nobody else will, or because you cannot see how to stop. In a persecuted church, being an elder made you a target, and the temptation to serve reluctantly was real. Peter adds as God would have you, kata theon, according to God, which locates the willingness: not natural enthusiasm but a work taken up under God. Leadership should come from a willing heart that loves God and his people, not from pressure, guilt or duty alone.

Not for shameful gain, but eagerly. Shameful gain, aischrokerdōs, means greedy for dishonest money, as in 1 Timothy 3:3, 8 and Titus 1:7. Money, and Peter assumes elders were paid something or the warning would be pointless. Elders may be paid (1 Timothy 5:17–18), but money must not be the motive. The word for the alternative, prothymōs, means eagerly, wholeheartedly, with zeal: the opposite of a man calculating what the post returns.

Not domineering over those in your charge. The third is power, and it is the one that ruins most. Domineering, katakyrieuontes, means lording it over, ruling harshly: the very word the Lord used when he said the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you (Mark 10:42–43). Peter was in the room. He had been arguing about who was the greatest. Those in your charge, tōn klērōn, are the portions, the allotted ones: the people entrusted to each elder as a share is allotted, not owned. Leaders must not be bullies or tyrants, manipulating, controlling, or treating the flock as an audience for their own importance.

But being examples to the flock. Examples, typoi, are patterns, models, the mark left by a seal (1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:7). Lead by example, not by force. Shepherds in the ancient Near East did not drive their flocks from behind with dogs; they walked ahead, and the sheep followed the voice they knew (John 10:4). And the alternative is not weak leadership but a costlier kind. A man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying, and that is a far harder standard to meet on a Tuesday.

What it does not mean. Not domineering does not mean elders have no authority. They lead and must be obeyed (v. 5; Hebrews 13:17). It means their authority is exercised humbly, by example, for the flock’s good.

What should a church member do if an elder is domineering or abusive? Speak to him first if it is safe, honestly and respectfully, as you would any brother (Matthew 18:15). If that fails or the matter is serious, take it to the other elders, who share responsibility for oversight; this is one reason the New Testament gives churches a plurality of elders. Paul says a charge against an elder should be received on the evidence of two or three witnesses, and that those who persist in sin should be rebuked publicly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). If there is abuse or a crime, it must be reported to the authorities. Elders are under-shepherds, not owners, and they answer to Christ and to the church.

In a sentence. Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care, watching over them, not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but eager to serve; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.

On a Tuesday. Whatever leadership you have, in a home, a group or a workplace, lead by example and service this week, not by control. Ask which of Peter’s three temptations is closest to you: reluctance, money, or power. Then do the opposite once, deliberately. And if you are not a leader, make your elders’ work a joy (Hebrews 13:17): thank one of them this week.

For worship. He is the Good Shepherd who walks ahead of his sheep. He never served under compulsion; he came gladly, saying, I delight to do your will. He never served for gain; he made himself poor that we might be rich. He never lorded it over his flock; he knelt and washed their feet, and then laid down his life for them. And he still shepherds his church today, feeding it with his word, binding up its wounds, carrying its lambs, and raising up under-shepherds who, for all their weakness, show his flock what he is like.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.

And when the chief Shepherd appears. Chief Shepherd, archipoimēn, head shepherd: Jesus Christ (2:25; John 10:11; Hebrews 13:20). The word occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible, and it settles the whole passage. There is one Chief Shepherd, and every elder addressed here is under him. Appears, phanerōthentos, is revealed: at his return. It also answers the three temptations of the previous verse at their root. A man who genuinely believes the flock belongs to someone else, who is coming back, will not serve grudgingly, or for money, or by domineering, because none of those makes sense if you are minding somebody else’s sheep and he is due home.

You will receive the unfading crown of glory. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem: a circle of leaves, olive at Olympia, pine at the Isthmian games near Corinth, celery at Nemea, and everyone watching knew how quickly it browned. Victory wreaths withered within days. So Peter’s adjective is chosen with care. Unfading, amarantinos, is from the amaranth, the flower the ancients used as a symbol of what does not wither. He used the same root of the inheritance in 1:4. The wreath handed to an athlete was dead within the week; this one is made of something else (1 Corinthians 9:25; 2 Timothy 4:8). And note what the crown is made of: the crown of glory most likely means the crown that consists of glory, as the crown of life in James 1:12 means the crown which is life. The reward is not a decoration to wear but a share in the glory Peter has just said he is a partaker of.

A reward for the unseen. Which is a striking thing to promise elders in a persecuted network of house churches. Their work was unpaid or barely paid, unnoticed outside their own street, and dangerous. Faithful shepherds may receive little thanks on earth. Peter tells them the recognition is coming from the only person whose opinion is final.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only elders receive crowns. All believers share in glory. But Christ will specially honour faithful shepherds.

Is it right to serve God for a reward? Yes, if the reward is what God offers and the motive is love for him. Scripture repeatedly holds out reward as an encouragement (Matthew 6:4; Hebrews 11:6), and Jesus himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). What is wrong is serving for the wrong reward: money, praise, power, the admiration of the congregation. The crown of glory is not wages that put God in our debt; it is a gift of grace crowning the work grace produced. And the faithful will cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10), because the best part of the reward is the one who gives it.

In a sentence. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.

On a Tuesday. If you serve faithfully without recognition, in the crèche, at the door, in the hospital visit nobody hears about, look ahead: the Chief Shepherd sees, and he will reward. Do one piece of unseen service this week and tell no one. And when you are tempted to resent being overlooked, remember whose wreath you are working for.

For worship. The Chief Shepherd is coming home. He will gather his flock, count every sheep, and look for the under-shepherds who kept them. The world’s crowns wither on the winners’ heads; his do not. He wore a crown of thorns so that his servants could wear a crown of glory, and the glory is his own, shared with them. When he appears, every hidden labour of love will be seen, and the faithful will lay their unfading crowns at the feet of the one who made them faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Having addressed the leaders, Peter turns to those most likely to chafe under them. Younger, neōteroi: younger people in the church, who might be tempted to be impatient or rebellious, or perhaps a group of younger men who served the church practically, like the young men who carried out Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:6, 10). Elders here may mean the office or simply older people; probably the office, continuing from verses 1–4. Be subject, hypotagēte, is the same word as 2:13, 18; 3:1. Either way the instruction is the same posture the letter has asked of citizens, slaves and wives.

Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another. Then the scope widens and takes everyone in: all of you. Humility is for everyone, not just the young, and it is towards one another, elders to members as much as members to elders. The verb, enkombōsasthe, is unusual and vivid. It means to tie something on, and it was related to the apron a slave fastened over his clothes before serving. Peter is telling the whole congregation to put on the servant’s apron. And of all the men who could have chosen that image, Peter is the one who had watched it happen. In the upper room the Lord rose from supper, laid aside his outer garments, tied a towel round himself, and washed their feet, and Peter had objected, loudly, and been told: if I do not wash you, you have no share with me (John 13:4–17). The picture he reaches for here is one he originally refused.

For God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, and James uses it too (James 4:6): evidently a text the early church leaned on hard. The word for opposes, antitassetai, is military: to draw up in battle order against. God does not merely decline to help the proud; he takes the field opposite them. And grace, being a gift, can only be received by open hands, which is why humility is not one virtue among several here but the posture in which anything at all can be received. God pours grace on the humble as water runs to the lowest place.

What it does not mean. It does not mean young people have no voice or gifts. Timothy was young and a leader (1 Timothy 4:12). It means respect for godly leaders, and humility for everyone.

What does humility actually look like? It looks like being willing to do the lowly job without being asked or thanked; listening more than speaking; admitting when you are wrong, quickly and without excuses; rejoicing when others are praised; asking for help; receiving correction without sulking; and thinking of yourself less, rather than thinking less of yourself. It is not putting yourself down, refusing compliments, or pretending you have no gifts. C. S. Lewis observed that a truly humble man would not be thinking about humility, or about himself, at all. The root of it is seeing yourself rightly before God: a sinner saved by grace, with nothing you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7).

I am young and disagree with my church leaders. What should I do? Respect them, pray for them, and speak to them. Submission does not mean you must have no opinions, or that elders are never wrong. It means you approach them with humility rather than contempt, assume the best of their motives, ask questions before making accusations, and support their decisions where conscience allows, even when you would have done it differently. If a matter is serious, raise it privately and respectfully. Do not stir up a faction. And be willing to consider that age and experience may see what you do not yet see, just as you may see what they have missed.

In a sentence. In the same way, you who are younger, submit yourselves to your elders. All of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, “God opposes the proud but shows favour to the humble.”

On a Tuesday. Tie on the apron of humility this week. Find a way to serve someone, especially someone you might think beneath you, and do the job nobody wants: the washing-up, the stacking, the visit to the difficult person. And when you are corrected this week, by a spouse, a boss, an elder, a child, say thank you before you say but.

For worship. The Lord of glory tied on a servant’s towel. The hands that flung the stars into space poured water into a basin and washed the dust from fishermen’s feet, and then were nailed to a cross. He humbled himself, and God has highly exalted him. That is the God we worship: not one who sets himself against the lowly, but one who comes down to them, and who pours his grace into every heart low enough to receive it. He opposes the proud because they would rob him of glory; he gives grace to the humble because they have nothing but what he gives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter tells his readers to humble themselves under God’s strong hand, so that he will lift them up in due time, and to throw all their worries onto him because he cares for them. They must stay sober and alert, because their enemy the devil prowls like a hungry lion looking for someone to devour; they are to resist him, firm in faith, knowing that believers throughout the world are going through the same sufferings. After they have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, establish and strengthen them. To him belongs power for ever. Peter adds that he has written briefly through Silvanus to encourage them and testify that this is the true grace of God, and they must stand firm in it. He sends greetings from the church in “Babylon” and from Mark, asks them to greet one another with a kiss of love, and wishes peace to all who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.

Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God. The therefore follows the proverb: since that is how God deals with pride and humility, put yourself on the right side of it. Humble yourselves, tapeinōthēte, is passive in form: be humbled, accept the humbling. The mighty hand of God is an exodus phrase: it is how the Old Testament describes God bringing Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Exodus 3:19; 6:1; Deuteronomy 9:26). It is also his hand in disciplining them. And it cuts both ways, which is why it is the right image here. The hand is heavy; it is also the hand that delivers. Accept God’s dealings with you, including suffering, without resentment or resistance. The same hand that humbles also exalts.

So that at the proper time he may exalt you. Proper time, en kairō, in due season: God’s timing, not ours. Exalt, hypsōsē, lift up. The lifting is his work and his timing. As he exalted Christ after his humiliation (Philippians 2:8–9; James 4:10), so he will exalt his people. A man who insists on being raised now has taken the job out of the right hands.

Casting all your anxieties on him. Then verse 7, and the grammar matters more than most readers realise. Casting all your anxieties on him is not a separate command. It is a participle attached to humble yourselves: the casting is how the humbling is done. That connection is easily missed and it is the heart of the verse. We do not usually think of worry as pride. Peter does: holding on to your anxieties is a way of insisting that the situation is yours to manage, and handing them over is an act of self-lowering. Pride insists on carrying them alone; humility hands them over. Casting, epiripsantes, is a decisive verb: throw it, the word used of the disciples flinging their cloaks on the colt for Jesus to ride (Luke 19:35). Not setting down gently, and not sharing. It echoes Psalm 55:22: cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you. And all, pasan, leaves no category too small to bother him with. Anxieties, merimna, cares, worries, is the word Jesus used when he said do not be anxious about your life (Matthew 6:25–34).

Because he cares for you. The ground of the whole thing, and it is not that he is capable but that he is concerned. The word, melei, means it matters to him, he is concerned. There is a play of sound in Greek between our merimna and his melei: our care, his care. We are not burdening an indifferent God. Peter is writing to people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, and the last word of the sentence is that they are on somebody’s mind. The God who keeps the stars in their courses has you in his thoughts, by name.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should never plan or take responsibility. It means we should not be crushed by worry, but trust God with what we cannot control.

Is anxiety a sin? This verse is an invitation, not a rebuke: he cares for you. Some anxiety comes from pride and self-reliance, and needs to be cast on God in humility (v. 6). But some anxiety has bodily causes and is an illness, and seeking help from a doctor or counsellor, or taking medication, is no lack of faith. Bring the burden to God, again and again, and use every means he provides.

How do I actually cast my worries on God? Specifically and repeatedly. Name each worry to him in prayer, one by one, out loud or on paper: not a vague request for peace, but this diagnosis, this debt, this child, this meeting. Tell him what you fear will happen. Then deliberately hand it over: Father, this is yours; I cannot carry it. Do what is yours to do about it, and leave the rest. When the worry comes back, and it will, cast it again, without scolding yourself. Pair it with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6–7), which reminds the heart of how often he has carried you before.

In a sentence. Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that he may lift you up in due time. Throw all your worries onto him, because he cares for you.

On a Tuesday. Write down every worry you are carrying, large and small. Then pray through the list, casting each one on God, and at the end write across the top: he cares for me. Keep the list. In a month, look at it again and see what he did with them. And notice where pride is making you hold on: the worry you refuse to give up because you think you must fix it yourself.

For worship. The hand that is mighty enough to part the sea is gentle enough to take our smallest care. He does not sigh when we come with the same worry for the hundredth time; he cares for us. He carried the whole weight of our sin on the cross, and he is not going to drop the lesser burdens now. He humbles us to lift us; he takes our anxieties to give us his peace; and at the proper time, on the day of his appearing, he will raise his humbled people to share his throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.

Be sober-minded; be watchful. Two sharp imperatives, and the first has appeared before (1:13; 4:7). Sober-minded, nēpsate, clear-headed. Peter’s repeated counsel to a frightened church is a clear head and open eyes. The second word, grēgorēsate, stay awake, keep alert, is the one from Gethsemane: watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:37–38). Peter did neither, and slept, and within hours had denied his Lord three times (Mark 14:66–72). He is not issuing a command he has never failed. He knows the cost of not being watchful.

Your adversary the devil. Adversary, antidikos, is a courtroom word: the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor. Devil, diabolos, means slanderer. And that is a precise description of what these readers were experiencing: they were being accused, publicly and continuously. Satan accuses believers before God (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10), the accuser of our brothers, and slanders them through human persecutors. He is real, personal and hostile.

Prowls around like a roaring lion. Prowls, peripatei, walks about. The picture is hunting, and notice what a roaring lion is doing. A lion stalking prey is silent; the roar comes to panic the herd and drive something out of it (Psalm 22:13; Ezekiel 22:25). The noise is a weapon, and it works on the nerves rather than the body. The devil uses fear, persecution and intimidation to make believers flee from faith. Under Nero, within a few years, Christians in Rome were sewn into the skins of wild beasts and torn by dogs, and in later persecutions they were literally thrown to lions.

Seeking someone to devour. Devour, katapiein, swallow up, gulp down. Seeking someone: the hunt is selective. He is looking for the one that has drifted from the group, the isolated, the weak, the careless, which is exactly what persecution does to a congregation.

Resist him, firm in your faith. Resist, antistēte, stand against, as in James 4:7: resist the devil, and he will flee from you. The command is to stand, not to attack. And firm, stereoi, is a solid word: settled, steadfast, not moving, like a rock, which is the opposite of the scattering the roar is designed to produce. Peter, the rock, urges firmness. Resistance comes through faith: trusting God and his word, taking up the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:16). Not by our own strength, and not by fleeing from faith.

Knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world. Then the encouragement, and it is unexpectedly practical. Brotherhood, adelphotēs, as in 2:17. Throughout the world, en tō kosmō. Not a promise of relief but of company. You are not alone. Believers everywhere face the same trials. Isolation is the lion’s method, and the answer is the knowledge that you are one of many, which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to five provinces rather than a private note.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every difficulty is a direct satanic attack, or that we should be obsessed with the devil. It means we should be alert, recognise his tactics, and resist by faith. He is a defeated enemy (3:22; Colossians 2:15).

How does the devil actually attack Christians today? Mostly not with dramatic manifestations, but with the same tactics Peter names: accusation, fear and isolation. He accuses, telling you that you are too sinful for God to forgive, or that your faith is fake. He frightens, making obedience look too costly. He isolates, drawing you away from church and Christian friends until you are alone. He also deceives, with false teaching and with temptations dressed as freedom. The answer is the same as Peter’s: stay awake, stay in the word, stay with the flock, and when he accuses, answer with the blood of Christ. He is a lion, but he is a lion on a chain.

In a sentence. Be alert and of sober mind. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in the faith, because you know that the family of believers throughout the world is undergoing the same kind of sufferings.

On a Tuesday. Where might the devil be trying to isolate or frighten you? Stand firm in faith, and connect with fellow believers this week: go to the meeting you were going to skip, phone the friend, join the prayer group. And if an accusing voice is telling you that you are beyond forgiveness, answer it out loud with Scripture: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

For worship. The lion roars, but the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. Our adversary accuses, but our Advocate speaks for us before the Father, and his blood answers every charge. The devil prowls, seeking the lone sheep, but the Shepherd has never lost one that the Father gave him. And around the world tonight, in prisons and villages and great cities, the brotherhood stands firm in the same faith, held by the same hand. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under our feet.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

And after you have suffered a little while. Peter does not remove the suffering from the sentence. It stands, and it is bounded. A little while, oligon, is the same phrase as 1:6, measured against the eternal glory in the next clause (2 Corinthians 4:17). Suffering is real but temporary.

The God of all grace. The title is chosen for the moment. Not the God of all power, though he is; the God of all grace, pasēs charitos: every kind of it, sufficient for every situation these scattered congregations were in. Saving grace, sustaining grace, strengthening grace, the many-coloured grace of 4:10. My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ. Called, kalesas: God’s effectual call (1:15; 2:9, 21; 3:9). The calling looks past the suffering to the destination, and the destination is his own glory (Romans 8:30). Peter said in verse 1 that he is a partaker of it; here he says they are called to it. God has not called us to suffering as the end, but through suffering to glory. In Christ: in union with him, which is the only place the glory is found.

Will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. Then four verbs, piled up for assurance, and they build. And the emphatic word is himself, autos: God personally. Not through an agency or a process. Restore, katartisei, is the mending word: used of setting a broken bone and of repairing nets, which Peter had done for a living. When Jesus first called James and John they were in their boat mending their nets (Mark 1:19), the same verb. It assumes damage: the suffering will break something, and God will set it. Confirm, stērixei, means to make firm, steady, set fast. It is the word the Lord used when he told Peter: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32), and here Peter does just that. Strengthen, sthenōsei, is to fill with strength. And establish, themeliōsei, is to lay on a foundation, to ground something so it cannot be shifted. God will repair what suffering breaks, and make his people firm, strong and settled. This is the perseverance of the saints: God will finish what he started (Philippians 1:6). And it comes from a man who had been broken and repaired by name.

To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen. Dominion, kratos, power, might. Peter has just named the prowling lion; he ends by saying whose the dominion actually is. The devil roars, but God rules.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that suffering will end in this life. Restoration may be partial now and complete in glory. But it is certain.

What if I feel broken beyond repair? Then this verse was written for you. Peter promises that God will restore, and the word assumes real damage: a broken bone, a torn net. He does not say the breaking did not happen or did not matter. He says God himself will mend it. That mending may begin now, slowly, through his word, his people, prayer and time, and sometimes through doctors and counsellors he provides; and it will be complete when Christ appears. Peter had been broken by his own denial, and Christ restored him on a beach. The God of all grace has never yet met a soul too broken for him.

In a sentence. And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast. To him be the power for ever and ever. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Pray this promise back to God today, in the first person: you yourself will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish me. Name the broken thing you want restored. Then trust him to do it in his time. And look for one person in your church who is broken by suffering, and be one of the hands God uses to strengthen them, as Peter was told to strengthen his brothers.

For worship. He is the God of all grace. Not of some grace, rationed out to the deserving, but of all grace, for every need, without end. He called us to his own eternal glory, and he will not leave us halfway. He mends what is broken, steadies what is shaking, strengthens what is weak, and sets on rock what was sinking in sand, and he does it himself. The suffering is for a little while; the glory is for ever. To him be the dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.

By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion on the second missionary journey, who sang hymns with him at midnight in the jail at Philippi (Acts 15:40; 16:19–25; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1), a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37), and now carrying Peter’s letter. By, dia, through: he may have been Peter’s secretary, helping with the polished Greek of a Galilean fisherman, or the bearer of the letter, or both. It is a lovely detail that Paul’s companion helps Peter: the apostles were not rival parties.

I have written briefly to you. Briefly, di’ oligōn, in few words, as in Hebrews 13:22. Five chapters, and a lifetime of experience compressed into them.

Exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Exhorting, parakalōn, and declaring, epimartyrōn, testifying. That is Peter’s own summary of what he has written, and it repays notice. This is everything in the letter: the gospel of grace, including suffering for Christ. After five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, he calls the whole thing grace. Not advice, not endurance training. True grace, alēthē charin, genuine grace. Suffering does not mean grace has failed; it is part of God’s true grace.

Stand firm in it. Stand firm, stēte, stand. The summary of the letter: hold your ground in God’s grace. Their part is simply to stand in it. Peter does not say produce it, or earn it, or even fully understand it. Stand in it, as a man stands on solid ground in an earthquake.

She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings. She is almost certainly the church there, God’s chosen lady (2 John 1), and Babylon is very probably a code name for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8; 17:5; 18:2. Jewish writers of the period used the name for the great pagan power that had destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, as Babylon had in 586 BC. Like Babylon of old, Rome was the great world empire, the capital of idolatry and the place of exile for God’s people. Early tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life, where he was martyred under Nero. It is a fitting last image for this letter. Peter writes to exiles from the empire’s capital and calls it Babylon, the place of exile, reminding them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in a foreign country as the church in Bithynia. And likewise chosen, syneklektē, chosen together with you, hands them back the word he opened with (1:1).

And so does Mark, my son. John Mark, the young man who abandoned Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13), was the cause of their sharp disagreement, and was later restored, so that Paul could call him very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). My son is affection, not paternity: Peter’s spiritual son. Peter had gone to Mark’s mother’s house in Jerusalem when the angel freed him from prison, and found the church praying there (Acts 12:12). Early tradition, from Papias, says that Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down in his Gospel what Peter preached. Two men who had both failed, both been restored, standing together at the end.

Greet one another with the kiss of love. Kiss of love, philēmati agapēs: the customary greeting among family members, used in the early church as a sign of family affection (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20). Slave and master, Jew and Gentile, greeting each other as brother and sister. The letter that has spoken so much of hostility ends with an instruction to touch each other.

Peace to all of you who are in Christ. Peace, eirēnē, the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything as it should be. For suffering exiles, the last word is peace, found in Christ. Offered to people who had very little of it, from a man who would shortly die in the city he calls Babylon. It was the first word the risen Lord had spoken to Peter and the others in the locked room: peace be with you (John 20:19). Peter ends where his Lord began.

What it does not mean. Babylon does not refer to the literal city in Mesopotamia, which was largely deserted by then. Nor does Peter’s presence in Rome establish a papacy; it shows he served there and died there as a faithful witness.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The point is warm, holy affection between brothers and sisters, expressed in the form one’s culture uses. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may be used; elsewhere a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. The form may vary by culture; the warmth should not.

What does it mean to stand firm in grace? It means refusing to move off the ground God has put you on. Do not slide into earning your standing by performance, as though suffering meant you had not done enough. Do not slide into despair, as though suffering meant grace had failed. Do not slide into compromise, as though grace could be kept while denying Christ. Stand on what this letter has told you: you are chosen, born again, ransomed, guarded, loved, called to glory. Keep coming back to it in the word, at the Lord’s Table, among his people. Grace is not only how you began; it is where you stand every day until he comes.

In a sentence. With the help of Silas, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you her greetings, and so does my son Mark. Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Read 1 Peter through in one sitting this week; it takes about twenty minutes. Then write one sentence summarising what the true grace of God means for your life right now. And greet someone at church next Sunday warmly, especially someone on the edge, as family.

For worship. This is the true grace of God: that the Father chose exiles, the Spirit set them apart, the Son ransomed them with his blood; that he caused them to be born again to a living hope, guarded them by his power, refined them in the fire, and called them to his eternal glory. It is grace from the first verse to the last, grace that holds in Babylon and Bithynia, grace that turned a denier into an apostle and a deserter into an evangelist. We stand in it, and it holds us. And over every scattered, slandered, suffering child of God, the last word is his: peace, in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.
